#8938. The 6 Best Walking Pads for Staying Active During the Workday

Improve your focus and get your steps in seamlessly with one of these walking pads.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Stuck at your desk all day? Us, too—and we work for a running publication. (Oh, the irony!) Well, fret not, fellow office warriors: Walking pads and under-desk treadmills are here to save the day—and boost your step count. These low-profile treadmills slide right under your standing desk, making it easy to walk and work at the same time. Thanks to a renewed focus on health, whether you’re working from home or heading into the office, walking pads have quickly become a staple in home offices and shared workspaces alike. So, whether you’re aiming to close those rings or boost your daily steps, a walking pad can help you stay active throughout the workday without missing that 3 p.m. meeting.

🏃🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Walking for Weight Loss Guide can make it happen!

Recent studies support the benefits of movement while working: office employees using treadmill desks have reported improved energy, greater focus, and a boosted mood over just a few months of consistent use. Plus, the convenience of walking pads means you can exercise regardless of the weather or your schedule—no gym membership required. With so many walking pads on the market, each offering a unique blend of features and portability, at a range of prices, finding the right model can be overwhelming. Not to worry, though. We put tens of thousands of steps on these machines to find the best ones for you.

If you’re looking for portability, a cushioned deck, affordability, and a walking pad you can use while you’re in the office without people on your meeting hearing your treadmill? This is the one for you. We’ve had it at HQ for years, and it’s consistently in use by our team. It has seen thousands of miles, and it’s still going.

It’s got a well-cushioned deck that absorbs impact, a motor built for heavier walkers, and it’s relatively wide for a walking pad. It is, however, a bit short front-to-back, but it’s fine for most people. If you’re a giant like my brother? You might want a different model, otherwise, this is just about perfect.

If your social feeds are overflowing with DeerRun under-desk walking pads, you’re not alone. This TikTok-famous gadget is everywhere, and for good reason: It’s a simple, space-saving treadmill that you can control with a remote or an app.

The app’s got your back, letting you dial up the speed without breaking a sweat (or your focus). And topping out at just over 3 mph, it’s more of a gentle stroll than a full-on sprint.

The deck’s a cozy—if kinda tight—35 by 16 inches, which means it’ll tuck neatly under your desk. It’s easy to use and that glorious cushioned feel is pure bliss for your feet while you’re getting those steps in.

This is our office’s new BFF. The most frequent user, Hype Director Aly Ellis, said that her favorite feature is the convenience, noting “I prefer this one to one with arms because it allows me to adjust the desk height when I need to for comfort purposes.” She’s also a big fan of the fact that it lights up, but mostly because it’s cool. I agree. She does worry about losing the remote, as we all do, but fun fact! You can operate it via the app, so there’s no real worry there.

It’s quiet and sturdy, has a 12 percent incline, and has a high weight limit, so larger-bodied walkers should feel comfortable on this walking pad.

This is easily the most compact on this list. It folds up to about the size of a queen blanket, but it doesn’t feel flimsy or cheap. WalkingPad has made it its business to build high-quality walking pads that are made for your home or office.

I like this one because it’s no fuss, no muss, has a large 48-inch by 16-inch walking surface, weighs only 50 pounds, and it’s whisper quiet.

The Urevo Strol 2.0 walking pad is the under-desk treadmill you want if you tend toward boredom. It has a ton of built-in programming, and the ability to connect to a ton more like Zwift.

Once you link the app to your phone, you can control everything right there. But, if that’s not your style, traditional controls are easy to access and use. It’s a smooth walk, quieter than previous models, and you can move it around easily.

The combination of the sturdy tablet holder and smart app integration creates a user-friendly experience that blends exercise with productivity or entertainment effortlessly in any space.

If you’ve ever wondered how hard you can push yourself while you work, do I have the walking pad for you. This puppy inclines all the way to 14 percent, which—whoa—and it does it with the power of a brushless motor, which makes it quieter (though it can’t quiet your huffing and puffing), and that same motor will last a lot longer than others thanks to its construction.

The whole thing is remote controlled, so when you’re fighting for your life and you don’t want your Teams meeting to see it, you can quickly adjust on the fly.

When shopping for the best under-desk walking pad, keep these factors in mind:

Size and Portability: Ensure the walking pad’s dimensions fit under your desk and in your workspace. Consider weight and whether the machine has wheels for easy storage or movement.

Belt Size: Wider belts provide more stability and comfort, while narrower pads are better for tight spaces. Longer deck lengths work best for those with a longer stride.

Speed Range: Most walking pads offer speeds from 0.5 to 4 mph—enough for gentle walking to brisk paces. Some 2-in-1 pads allow faster speeds when used away from a desk.

Incline Options: A few models feature adjustable inclines for varied intensity, though many are flat for multitasking. If you want more of a workout, look for pads with at least a minor incline capability.

Weight Capacity: Check each machine’s weight limit, especially if you need extra support or want a more robust frame.

Noise Level: Choose a quiet pad for minimal distraction, particularly if you share your space with others or take calls frequently.

Ease of Use: Look for simple controls (often via remote) and clear displays. Consider features like app compatibility, folding capabilities, and maintenance requirements.

Price: Budget models are available for under $200, while high-end or commercial-grade options cost significantly more. Decide which features are worth extra investment for your specific needs.

So, what’s the difference between a treadmill and a walking pad? There are a lot of parallels for sure, and functionally they’re very similar. However, the real difference between a treadmill and a walking pad happens under the hood. Walking pads have smaller, quieter motors that don’t allow you to pick up the pace dramatically, but they keep them quiet enough to use while you work or read. They’re also a lot lower to the ground, and that low step height makes them a great choice for folks who have joint and mobility issues. They’re shorter and narrower than traditional treadmills so that they fit easily under desks. Luckily, they’re also easier to store, and many of them fold into little packages or can be stored on their side. And the point many people love the most? They’re usually a lot cheaper.

Our team performed all walking pad testing either in our offices for hundreds of hours or in our own homes, reflecting the real-world environments where these products are most used. Each unit was assessed with a focus on:

Speed and Incline: We measured each pad’s speed range and, where available, incline adjustments, making sure transitions were smooth and controls responsive.

Noise: We operated pads during conference calls and regular work to evaluate how quietly each model ran.

Design and Portability: We checked for ease of setup, the ability to move and store the pad, and whether the design fit under multiple desk types.

User Experience: Testers of varying heights and stride lengths used each pad for sessions extending beyond an hour, noting comfort, usability, and any unique features or challenges.

Every product featured here was rigorously tested for durability, performance, and portability in the Runner’s World offices and in the homes of our editors, ensuring our recommendations are both practical and trustworthy. #8937. 10-Minute Full-Body Stretch for Dog Owners

Longtime yoga teacher Amber Burke, graduate of two YogaWorks teacher trainings and former leader of a teacher training program at the University of New Mexico-Taos, shares her favorite stretches to do before walking her dogs. You can also explore other ways to stretch your entire body.

Confession time. I love my dogs, but I don’t always love walking them. Dog walking, I have found, bears little resemblance to normal walking. It is far more physically demanding than I ever imagined in my pre-dog-owning years, and sometimes it’s even a little scary. I have wrenched my back when my two big rescue mutts decided to dart in front of me while playing tug-of-war. I have been pulled after squirrels and tugged straight into lampposts. I have fallen into bushes. I have faceplanted. It is a small miracle that my shoulders are still attached to my body and I have (almost) all of my teeth.

Even when a dog walk goes smoothly, I usually end up feeling a bit crooked, hunched over, and frazzled by the end. If, like me, you walk big dogs, two or more dogs, high-strung or strong-willed dogs, and live anywhere with squirrels, you might value some yoga poses and movements that strengthen and stretch your shoulders, improve your balance, and stabilize your back, hips, and legs to help you survive the demands of your next dog walk.

This standing practice can be done in just a few minutes before your next dog walk, or simply do one or a few of these exercises while your dogs are busy running in the dog park. No mat or lowering yourself to the ground required. You will need a strap—or dog leash, after you’ve untangled yourself from it.

The top priority for dog walkers is shoulder stability. Dogs yank, and when your dogs go after a squirrel, you don’t want your shoulders to go with them. Train your shoulders to resist every yank with this variation of Mountain Pose (Tadasana).

How to: Stand tall with your feet hip-distance apart in Mountain Pose and your arms alongside your body, squeezing inward in at your sides. Bend your elbows. Roll your shoulders up and back, and then down your back. Draw your shoulder blades toward each other, imagining that you’re creating a crease between them. Pause here for several breaths, then release.

This exercise helps strengthen the muscles that keep your shoulder blades in place and reverses that forward-rounding back hunch that might result from holding a leash in front of you.

How to: Take a hold of a leash (or strap) behind your back with your palms facing forward, about shoulder-distance apart, or if your hands meet behind you, interlace your fingers behind you. Keeping your shoulders back and your arms straight, pulse your arms up and down several times, lifting them as high as is comfortable. Repeat for several rounds, then release.

Dog walking takes your arms—and your attention—forward and down as you keep an eye on your dog, any potential obstacles, and tempting trash items. This exercise moves your body in the opposite direction, broadening across your chest and stretching the fronts of your shoulders.

How to: Reach your arms straight in front of your chest. Hold a leash between your hands, taking them slightly wider apart than shoulder-width. As you inhale, lift the leash overhead and lower it slightly behind your shoulders; as you exhale, bring it back in front of you, keeping your arms relatively straight the entire time. (If your arms bend a lot, move your hands wider on the leash.) Do this for several rounds.

You can also pause with the leash behind you, if that gives you a good stretch, for a few breaths. Then lower your arms and release the leash.

If you have more than one dog, it’s a good idea to be ready for that cumbersome moment when they criss-cross their leashes, going in opposite directions. This stretch allows you to practice that arm position by stretching the muscles along the backs of your shoulders and in between your shoulder blades.

How to: Cross your arms at the elbows in front of your chest. Your arms will be slightly bent. Make soft fists, then reach your hands away from each other as if you are trying to straighten your arms in opposite directions. Pause here for a few breaths, then release your arms and switch sides so the opposite arm is on top.

It‘s all too easy to twist an ankle if your dog pulls you sideways while you’re stepping off a curb or if you’re simply paying more attention to your furry friend than your own footing. Heel lifts help to strengthen your ankles and your balance.

How to: Stand with your feet together or hip-distance apart and your arms by your sides. Gaze at a steady point on the ground or, for more of a balance challenge, at a fixed point on the horizon. Press down with the balls of your feet. As you inhale, lift your heels; as you exhale, slowly lower your heels, without letting the ankles splay to the sides. Do this several times.

When your dog jumps on you unexpectedly, the last thing you want to do is take a tumble. This dynamic pose variation helps you cultivate leg strength and balance to prepare you to stand strong.

How to: With your feet together or hip-distance apart, gaze at an unmoving point in front of you. Press down into the balls of your feet, then lift your heels. Bend your knees, lean your chest slightly forward, sink your hips toward the ground, and reach your arms straight out in front of your chest in a Chair Pose variation. For more of a challenge, bend your knees more deeply to bring your hips closer to the ground, and try to keep your posture more upright instead of leaning forward, drawing your belly toward your spine. Pause for several breaths, then lower your heels and arms as you return to standing.

If your dogs have ever tried to take off, you know how important it is to be able lower your center of gravity fast so you can resist their pull. Get ready to drop down into a sturdy position by practicing Squat (Malasana).

How to: Stand with your feet a little wider than hip-width and turn your toes out slightly. Bend your knees and lower your hips as far as you like, tracking your knees over your toes. Bring your elbows inside your knees and your hands together in prayer position in Squat. Broaden across your chest and lift your heart space. Stay here for a few breaths, then press your feet into the ground to rise back to standing.

Dog walkers do a lot of forward folding—we bend down to pet our dogs, to pick up after them, to take their harnesses on and off, and to pry things that they really shouldn’t be eating out of their mouths. Pyramid Pose (Parsvottanasana) warms up your hamstrings and mobilizes your lower back to help you do all that with greater ease.

How to: Press down through your left foot and step your right foot around 12 inches behind you. Place your hands on your hips. Hinge from your hips and fold your chest forward as much as is comfortable, or about parallel to the ground. Bend your front knee if you like. Stay in Pyramid Pose, petting a dog if you like, or drape your upper body over your front leg and let your head relax for more of a more intense stretch. To come out of the pose, walk your hands up your front leg. Then change sides.

Dog walkers need to be able to preserve their stability, and also change speeds and directions on the fly. You might need to dart sideways out of the way of another walker who isn’t paying attention, or quickly escape an approaching off-leash dog. Use this move to practice fast footwork and energize your legs.

How to: Standing with your feet together, hinge from your hips and reach your chest forward. Cross your right foot behind your left, planting the ball of your right foot as far outside your left foot as feels comfortable. Bend your left leg slightly. Reach your arms toward the left, then step your right foot back to the starting position. Then cross your left foot behind and outside your right foot and reach your arms toward the right. Move from side to side several times, building momentum and going as slowly or quickly as you want. Then return to standing.

The front of your thighs might be feeling the work of the previous poses—and months or years of dog walking. Dancer’s Pose (Natarajasana) provides a stretch for the quadriceps, as well as a backbend that gently counterstretches all the forward reaching and bending of dog walking. It also gives you another chance to strengthen your balance.

How to: Shift your weight into your left foot. Bend your right knee and draw your right heel toward your buttock. Loop your leash or strap around your right foot or ankle, draw the strap over your right shoulder, and hold it with one or both hands in Dancer Pose variation. Stay here for a few breaths, or use both hands to lift the strap overhead and press your right shin behind you, arching into a backbend. Draw your elbows toward each other and lift your chest. Lower down and change sides.

Do you find yourself holding onto the leash for dear life? All that gripping can create tightness in the hands and wrists. Here’s a way to relieve that tension.

How to: Reach your arms in front of your chest and interlace your fingers with your palms facing forward. Straighten your arms as you press your palms away from you. Stay here for several breaths, or lift your arms overhead to add a full-body stretch. Then release your hands and lower your arms by your sides.

In addition to stretching your back and hamstrings, Standing Forward Bend (Uttanasana) can also be mentally relaxing, allowing you to breathe out the stresses that come with daily life…and dog walking.

How to: Plant your feet hip-distance apart. Fold forward, walking your hands down your legs and bending your knees as much as you need. Place your hands on the ground or your shins in Standing Forward Bend, grasp opposite elbows, or let your arms hang toward the ground in Rag Doll. Relax your neck. Pause here for several breaths, then walk your hands up your legs to return to standing.

After you’ve returned home from your dog walk, give yourself several minutes of well-deserved rest. You made it!

How to: Recline on your yoga mat, with or without dogs. (Only you know if they will enhance your relaxation or distract you from it!) Sigh out any remaining tension. Allow your shoulders to soften toward the floor with your  hands out to the sides or resting on your body in  Savasana. You don’t need to be on guard anymore. Give yourself over to relaxation, the way dogs know how to do when the fun is over. For a few minutes, surrender your weight to the earth, and let yourself be a big warm animal, gently breathing.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

This redemption is accessible because Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from the two most popular transferable points currencies in the ChooseFI ecosystem:

All transfers are instant. This matters because ANA business class availability on partner programs is scarce, and when you find a seat, you need to move fast. You cannot afford to wait 3–5 days for points to post.

Here's a non-obvious but critical piece of tradecraft: you do not search for ANA award availability on Virgin Atlantic's website. Virgin Atlantic's search engine is limited for partner award space. Instead, you search on United.com, because United and ANA are both Star Alliance members and United shows ANA partner award availability accurately in its search results.

Find the space on United.com, confirm the flight numbers and dates, then call or use the online booking tool at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com to complete the booking.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This means as long as you earn or redeem even one mile every three years, your balance stays alive. Keep that in mind as you accumulate — a small card transaction through the program every couple of years is all it takes to protect a hard-earned balance.

You need 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles for a one-way business class ticket. Before anything else, confirm you have this balance — or the equivalent — in Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou Points, or Bilt Rewards. All four major transfer partners post instantly, which is a genuine advantage here given how quickly availability disappears.

With miles now in your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account, complete the booking at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com. Use the flight numbers you identified in Step 2. You should see $0 in fuel surcharges — only government taxes (typically $50–$100 for trans-Pacific routing).

Airlines partner with each other through alliances and bilateral agreements, allowing their frequent flyer programs to book seats on each other's flights. The pricing inefficiency occurs when Partner A prices Partner B's premium cabin at a different rate than Partner B charges through its own program. Virgin Atlantic maintains a fixed partner award chart that prices ANA business class at 90,000 miles regardless of demand or seasonality. ANA's own dynamic pricing can push award costs significantly higher during peak periods. This arbitrage between partner pricing and the operating airline's own program is the foundation of most airline travel rewards sweet spots.

If you've been diligently earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards and you want to experience what a truly premium long-haul flight feels like — without paying $8,000–$12,000 out of pocket — this is your redemption.

It's particularly well-suited to the FI-minded traveler who values experience over stuff. You're not flying business class because you can't manage without it. You're flying it because 90,000 points delivering $8,000–$12,000 in value is one of the most efficient uses of a points balance available anywhere in loyalty programs today.

For the ChooseFI traveler who has optimized their earning strategy and is ready to deploy a meaningful points balance on a once-in-a-decade trip, this is one of the most compelling redemptions on the board.

## Why This Redemption Is Rated Moderate This isn't a beginner redemption, but it's absolutely within reach for someone who understands the basics of transferable points programs. Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. The learning curve is real but short. The reward — flying ANA "The Room" over the Pacific for $60 in fees — makes every minute of research worthwhile.

#8934. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”

#8933. The Best Cargo E-Bikes of 2026, Tested by Editors Who Used Them for Groceries, Kid Hauling, and Daily Commutes

From budget longtails to family-ready front-loaders, these picks can help replace car trips.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Each year, I ride many different bicycles. From high-performance road bikes to full suspension mountain bikes to basic hybrids, I’ve swung a leg over eight or ten styles of bicycles in the past six months. But switching to an electric cargo bike has made the biggest positive impact on my overall quality of life. Thanks to a cargo bike, I’ve been mostly car-free for the last several months.

Traditional bicycles are great for your daily commute, running errands, and cruising around. However, if you need to carry more than you can squeeze into a backpack or maybe some panniers, most commuter bikes or e-bikes aren’t up for the job. Common tasks like grocery shopping, carrying large items, or transporting children can be tough on even the best of them. That’s what makes cargo bikes great—they can carry everything (and more!) that you can imagine.

As their name suggests, cargo bikes are designed to carry heavy, large, or awkward loads. Their extra hauling capacity makes cargo bikes incredibly useful for families, commuters, and riders in cities, suburbs, and small towns across the country. Bicycle brands produce cargo bikes in several distinct layouts to meet the needs of riders seeking to carry or move more stuff by pedal power.

Almost any bicycle purpose-built to carry passengers or extra gear—such as packages, bags, or boxes—can be called a “cargo bike.” Cargo bikes typically feature reinforced frames, racks or mounting points, and come with higher payload capacities than traditional commuter, city, or townie bikes. Bike brands and third-party manufacturers also offer a wide array of accessories to outfit a cargo bike for your specific needs and use cases.

Bicycling’s editors are huge fans of cargo bikes, and we use them regularly for our daily commutes, running errands, dropping kids at school, and family rides. Like other bicycle types, cargo bikes come in all shapes and sizes—and there’s almost certainly one that’s perfect for you. Finally, while non-assisted cargo bikes are available, electric-assist cargo bikes are now far more common. So all of the models we test use electric motors.

Buying Tip: Consider where you will store your cargo bike. Their large size and extra weight can make cargo bikes difficult to store if you don’t have a garage or dedicated bike storage. If you need to park your cargo bike outside, get a heavy-duty bike lock and a bicycle cover to keep it safe.

Some cargo bikes are loaded with features but cost too much, while others are low-priced but don’t ride well. However, the Aventon Abound LR is the rare $2,000 electric cargo bike that doesn’t feel like a compromise—And that’s why it’s our Best Overall pick.

The Abound LR is built to handle daily life—daycare drop-offs and pickups, grocery runs, and commuting—without the premium price tag of its competitors. Plus, it rides with more polish than some bikes costing twice as much. This makes it a great option for families and utility‑minded riders. The LR can handle kids, panniers, and weekly shopping trips without stretching the budget. It’s ideal for those who value comfort and stability over top‑end speed.

If you’re comparing this Aventon to other electric cargo bikes, it feels more polished than budget longtails like the Lectric Xpedition 2.0 and Rad Power’s Rad Wagon 5. Yet, the Abound LR costs far less than premium mid‑drive cargo rigs from Tern, Cannondale, and Trek.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it’s one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around. The dual-battery model ($1,799) boasts an incredible 120-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. This makes the XPedition an option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

“The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

However, concessions had to be made somewhere to reach this low price, and the result is a somewhat cheap feel. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but it is erratic at times. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend.

Tern’s Quick Haul Long is enticing because it delivers the core functionality of the pricier GSD series at a lower price. While the Quick Haul Long’s frame isn’t as sleek as the GSD and lacks a suspension fork, the bike still has everything needed to be a true car replacement.

The Quick Haul features include hydraulic disc brakes, a robust double kickstand, a built-in frame lock, trailer attachment points, and an impressive maximum weight limit of 419 pounds. Tern also offers a wide range of accessories to customize the bike to your individual needs. Even when loaded with two kids and a trailer full of groceries, the Bosch Cargo Line motor handles the load with ease. However, don’t expect a speedy ride when fully laden. The bike can handle the load (and you’ll get where you want to go), but it won’t zip to its maximum pedal-assist speed of 20 mph when weighed down.

If you like the look, features, and price of Aventon’s Abound LR but want a smaller package, the SR is the bike for you. The SR has the same 440-pound carrying capacity and 60-mile range as its longtail sibling, but on a shorter wheelbase chassis. This makes it ideal for riders with space constraints (such as apartments and RVs) or anyone seeking a quick ride around town.

The Specialized Globe Haul ST packs 419 pounds of cargo capacity into a surprisingly compact frame. With powerful brakes, dialed geometry, and well-thought-out features, it’s ready for commuting, grocery getting, neighborhood errands, or getting a child to daycare. Without active suspension, the Haul relies on massive 3.5-inch tires for its ride comfort, which work well on all but the roughest roads.

My partner, Julia, purchased a Haul ST after reading the Bike of the Year review. She uses it for commuting in Boston and describes the Haul as zippy. She said, “The power levels are flexible, and I can easily adjust them to how I want to ride or tackle hills.” She also likes the cargo configurations for carrying groceries and running errands. Julia also likes the Haul’s geometry; “It’s nice to ride upright, and it gives me more visibility.”

The new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

While it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

The Fetch+ 4 is Trek’s take on the classic Dutch bakfiets. This bike is essentially the minivan of bikes—it carries up to four kids. It includes two child seats, but you can add accessories to improve your passengers’ comfort. These include a full cover for the basket to keep everyone out of the wind and rain. To power the Fetch, Trek uses Bosch’s BES3 system with a Bosch Cargo Drive motor. It delivers power via a Gates Carbon belt drive for virtually maintenance-free operation.

Most families know Radio Flyer for its iconic red wagons, tricycles, and ride-on toys, but did you know the company also made a range of electric bikes? I use “made” here because, unfortunately, Flyer is backing away from e-bikes to concentrate on its core business. However, if you buy this bike, you’ll still have after-purchase support and the brand will have spare parts available.

The Loop is a 20-inch-wheel mid-tail model equipped with a 750W hub motor (87Nm torque) and can carry up to two children as passengers. Like a good family bike, Flyer loads the Loop with safety features, including a fully enclosed rear wheel, long front fender, turn signals, and four-piston Magura hydraulic disc brakes. Flyer offers the Loop in one universal frame size (fitting riders 4’11” to 6’3”) and four color choices.

Health & Fitness Editor Monique LeBrun tested the Loop with her six-year-old daughter for several months. “I’ve never ridden an e-bike before, so I was a little skeptical about it, but I really enjoy riding the Radio Flyer,” she said. Lebrun notes that “the seat is very comfortable, and I love that it has a low frame so I can easily step on and off the bike.”

The Tern GSD redefines what a car-replacement bike can be. It’s easy to picture running errands on a cargo bike if you live in a city or a town with great cycling infrastructure. However, many people live in suburbs or other areas not exactly designed for bike commuting. The GSD’s Class 3 Bosch pedal-assist motor, massive cargo capacity, and solid battery range make long hauls realistic, even for riders who live miles from town.

Riders from 5 feet to 6’6” can share the same bike, thanks to quick-release adjustments on the seatpost and handlebar. The bar can even rotate forward for tall riders who want extra reach. The bike also features premium touches you won’t find on low-cost cargo bikes—like a suspension fork, Magura 4-piston hydraulic brakes, an integrated lock, and a suspension seatpost. Practical design details make storage and transport surprisingly manageable: the handlebar folds at the headset, the seat drops quickly, and the whole bike can be tipped upright to rest on its rear rack—perfect for tight garage corners. However, be aware that the GSD’s extra weight can make loading it into a vehicle a two-person task.

Do you need to carry absolutely everything and want to do it in style? If so, an Urban Arrow might be right for you.

This front-loader, basket-style cargo bike is designed for families and people carrying large items like multiple kids, large dogs (plural), a Costco run, or a couch—All things people can carry with an Urban Arrow. Thanks to its 75 Nm Bosch Cargo Line motor and 545Wh battery, it has the torque and range to carry you and your stuff up hills and to your destination without breaking a sweat.

Domestic and international cargo bike popularity has exploded in the past decade, says Xtracycles founder and longtail cargo bike pioneer Ross Evans. There are generally four main styles of cargo bikes: longtail, short-tail, front loader, and the bakfiet (a Dutch term that translates to ‘box bike’). You can also find trike varieties for riders needing to transport heavy loads or more than two children.

➡️ Longtail cargo bikes are the most agile and lightweight design. They transport cargo or passengers on an extended tail section behind the rider.

➡️ Short-tail cargo bikes are a variant of longtail bikes, but with a shorter rear extension that makes them more compact and better suited for those tight on space.

➡️ Front loader bikes place the payload in front of the rider, generally on a low-slung platform adaptable to suit many needs.

➡️ Bakfiet-style bikes feature a large basket (typically in front of the rider) for carrying cargo or transporting multiple passengers.

Moving hundreds of pounds on a bike without a motor is great...if you want to get a workout. But most riders and families don’t want that stress or extra work. That’s why we recommend electric motor-equipped cargo bikes. “Electricity and cargo bikes go together like PB&J,” Evans says. E-cargo bikes feature pedal-assist electric motors that can deliver more than 50 miles of range. This makes cargo bikes more accessible to riders who want car-like convenience in a bike-sized package.

However, the tech comes at a price: Electric cargo bikes are pricier than their non-electric counterparts. Unless you live somewhere completely flat, we think an e-cargo bike is the best choice. Electric motors vastly improve a cargo bike’s usability and can save you money in the long run by making it a more effective car substitute.

Once you’ve purchased a cargo bike, you’ll want the right accessories to maximize its utility. Start on the manufacturer’s website: Many brands sell panniers, racks, and child seats to match their cargo bikes. Alternatively, if your style is more “dump it and go,” bakfiets use a single spacious box—typically upfront—that’ll fit all your stuff (there are still seat belts for your kids). The best way to determine which style or bike you prefer is to take bikes for test rides.

Approach an e-cargo bike and accessory purchase the same way you would if buying a car. Try and test as many options as possible. Prioritize your most common cargo needs. While it can be fun to think in aspirational terms, a bike suited to your daily needs means you use it more often.

These bikes are thoroughly put through their paces by the Bicycling test team. We don’t only test them—we live with them. We haul groceries, drop kids off at school, and squeeze in as many rides as possible to see if these e-cargo bikes can truly replace our cars for daily life. Test Editor Dan Chabanov puts them through the ultimate car-replacement experiment on the streets of his hometown of Philadelphia, and Deputy Editor Tara Seplavy tests them on her daily commute to the office. A

t our Easton, Pennsylvania headquarters, the rest of the team gives these bikes a daily beating, using them to run errands around town (because let’s be honest—e-cargo bikes are just plain fun to ride). We also speak with the product managers behind the designs to understand their choices, and compare each model to its closest competitors to see how they stack up. Bottom line: we test these bikes like we’d use them in real life—because we actually did.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8931. 11-Minute Stretch and Breathwork Routine to Soothe Your System

Radiance Basden is a certified yoga teacher and passionate advocate for stress reduction, mental resilience, and restorative wellness. Here, she guides readers through a gentle movement and breathwork practice that’s even better when done outside.

It’s a beautiful day to breathe on purpose.

Incorporating grounding practices—including breathing exercises, yoga, and mindful stretching—into your daily routine is one of the the simplest ways to teach your body that it’s okay to relax.

If you have the opportunity to do this sort of breathwork outdoors, the experience can be even more beneficial. When I need to regain my equilibrium, I spend time in nature. After all, outdoor spaces are scientifically proven to soothe your system. Listen to the sounds, notice the world around you, breathe in the fresh air, and embrace the power of simple movements done with intention. You’ll be surprised by how quickly you can come back to yourself.

Begin in a comfortable seat, preferably on the edge of something supportive, whether a chair, couch, bench, even a rock. Place your feet flat on the ground. Both before you start and throughout your practice, check in with yourself and make sure that your shoulders, face, and hands are relaxed.

Rest your hands on your knees—palms facing up to receive energy, facing down for extra grounding. If you feel called to do so, gently close your eyes. Start with 3 deep breaths, slowly inhaling through your nose, slowly exhaling through your mouth.

Now, it’s time to bring in humming breath. Inhale through your nose, and as you exhale, make a humming sound. Continue to hum for the entire length of your exhalation, however long that might be.

Repeat this 5 times or however many you’d like.

Take 3 deep breaths, allowing yourself to sit in stillness while mentally checking in with your body.

Can you still feel the vibrations of your humming?

Make sure your feet are planted about shoulder’s-width distance apart. When you’re ready, begin to move through some hip circles. Circle toward the right, leading with your shoulders and guiding your torso forward, around, and back.

When you’re ready, switch directions and enjoy 8 more circles.

As you move through your hip circles, pay attention to any parts of your body that feel particularly tense or tight and spend some time there. Pause to rock, deepen your stretch, or bring in whatever movement or breath you might need to relax the area.

Next, embody your breath with a seated flow through Cat-Cow. With your inhalation, arch your back and lift your chin toward the sky, bringing your hands to rest on the sides of your hips in a seated variation of Cow Pose.

With your exhalation, round your spine and tuck your chin and bring your hands to rest on the front of your knees in a seated variation of Cat Pose.

Repeat this pattern of movement 10 times, moving with the pace of your own breath.

With your next exhalation, clasp your hands and extend your arms forward in a variation of Seated Forward Bend.

Take 1 full breath here before inhaling your arms up to the sky and exhaling them down at your sides.

Stand up and prepare for a variation of Breath of Joy. Inhale through your nose to throw your arms up overhead, taking a slight backbend in the process.

Exhale through your mouth, making a whooshing sound. Bend forward, bend your knees, and throw your arms back behind you.

Repeat this pattern of movement for 1 full minute.

With you next exhalation, come into Mountain Pose. Stand tall here for 5 cycles of breath through your nose.

Now, for your last bit of breathwork, take 3 more slow breaths, inhaling through your nose and exhaling through your mouth.

#8930. How Runner’s World Training Plans Helped Four Runners Crush the New York City Marathon

Their stories will inspire you to train for your best marathon.

Among the more than 61,000 runners who crossed the finish line of the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon were 18 Runner’s World+ members who were part of the Race With Runner’s World+ team. Two were first-time marathoners while 16 others set big goals, such as adding to their World Marathon Major collection and hitting new PRs. No matter their specific ambition, some team members used these Runner’s World+ training plans to power themselves to the Central Park finish line.

Whatever your goal distance and time, you can find a plan by exploring our full training plan collection, including the ones our members used to return to the marathon, earn a sixth star, and run a PR.

🏃‍♀️ Want to run some of the best races in the country with us? Bookmark our Race With Runner’s World+ program page, which gives Runner’s World+ members of all backgrounds and levels a chance at free entry into select races.

Prior to New York, 46-year-old Erin Dewalt ran her last marathon in 2022, a race that she described as a “disaster.” Then, she finished in more than four hours and had an overall rough race day experience.

After a four-year marathon hiatus, Dewalt knew she needed a smart training plan to ensure she would arrive prepared for the NYC Marathon start line. The RW Break 3:45 plan aligned well with her weekly training volume of around four runs per week. For inspiration, she printed the calendar and stuck it to her fridge, checking off completed runs and moving workouts as needed.

The result for Dewalt in the Big Apple? A 3:26:18 marathon performance—breaking the 3:45 barrier by nearly 20 minutes. “I was spot on [with hitting my goal],” Dewalt said after crossing the finish line. “I wanted to enjoy it and have fun but also run around three and a half hours.”

Like Dewalt, Scott Shellabarger printed a Runner’s World training plan, but he used the Break 3:15 plan. In fact, he used it for two races: the NYC Marathon in November and the Flying Pig Marathon in his hometown of Cincinnati, Ohio, in May. “I actually used it for the last marathon I ran, for the Flying Pig, and that’s where I got my PR at,” Shellabarger said. “The training plans are fantastic.”

Not only did the plan help him set a personal best of 3:18:33 at Flying Pig, but it also helped him earn his Six Star Medal in New York and score a 2028 Boston Marathon qualifying time for his age group. Though he didn’t quite break 3:15 with his 3:21:27 performance, it marked his second-fastest marathon to date.

With a hectic schedule as a coach, Courtney Sobanski knew she needed a training plan that could fit into her everyday life. With our 3-Day training plan, Sobanski managed workouts successfully around other responsibilities—and remained injury-free. Our 3-Day plan features three key workouts a week—and any other days of easy running or cross-training you complete count as extra credit.

At the New York City Marathon, Sobanski crossed the finish line in 4:19:09 and told Runner’s World that she showed herself she could still run strong following foot surgery two years ago. “I’m just overcome with emotion that I actually did it and I can [run marathons] again,” Sobanski said following her race.

Ashley Osburn, 41, used the Break 4:30 plan to have every part of her training block mapped out in front of her—intervals, hills, tempo runs, long runs. Osburn said the plan made workouts approachable, and she appreciated the two weekly rest days built into the schedule for better recovery.

Though she didn’t quite reach her sub-4:30 goal in New York due to fueling missteps, Osburn intends to take another shot at the time barrier again in the future. “I will absolutely use [the training plan] again for my next marathon,” she said.

All of our Race With Runner’s World+ members had different goals and training plans pushing them toward the NYC finish line. But they all had a common shared experience of relishing the ecstatic crowds and infectious energy along the course through the five boroughs. “The crowd support all the way through was just amazing,” Dewalt said.

Ashley is Editor of Content Hype at Hearst’s Enthusiast & Wellness Group. She is a former collegiate runner at UNC Asheville where she studied mass communication. Ashley loves all things running; she has raced two marathons, plus has covered some of the sport’s top events in her career, including the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials and multiple World Marathon Majors.

#8928. A 28-Year-Old Brooklyn Runner Died After Being Stabbed During an Evening Run. Police Are Still Searching for Her Attacker.

Katie Suarez’s death has left runners grieving and residents demanding better safety measures.

(Editor’s note: A 27-year-old man who worked for the city’s public school system was arrested and charged with the murder of Katie Suarez on Saturday, November 7, the New York Times reported.)

On Friday, October 30, Katie Suarez headed out at night along Brooklyn's Shore Parkway Greenway, a waterfront route she'd become quite familiar with from her regular runs around the neighborhood. The 28-year-old was stabbed in the neck that evening and died Monday, November 2, at NYU Langone Hospital-Brooklyn, her family confirmed.

The attack came just two days before the New York City Marathon, when the city was already buzzing with runners gearing up for Sunday's race. (Suarez was not registered for the event.) More than 60,000 people would be making their way through the five boroughs that weekend, but Suarez never got to finish her own run. Her death has since shaken the running community, particularly women who know all too well the safety concerns that can come with heading out alone.

Suarez usually met her parents after finishing up at the TD Bank near Caesar's Bay Shopping Center in Bath Beach where she worked, and joined them for the commute home. On the day of the attack, she switched into her running clothes and took off along the waterfront while her parents waited for her to return.

According to The New York Times, her father, Nery Suarez, called just before 8 p.m. to check on where she was. Katie told him she was only about half a mile away and would be back soon, but when more time passed without any sign of her, Nery and his wife, Yasira, became worried and went out looking for her.

Nery eventually found his daughter unconscious just off the running path near Bay 17th Street. She had suffered severe injuries to her neck and was rushed to the hospital, where she remained on life support until her death.

"I'm just left with this pain, and, oh my God, remembering my daughter as she was," Yasira told the New York Daily News on Tuesday. "She just wanted to run.”

As of November 6, police had not identified or arrested a suspect. NYPD Chief of Detectives Joseph Kenny said Monday that investigators were still trying to determine what led to the attack, though they had no reason to believe Suarez was specifically targeted and "right now, it seems that it's random.”

Finding evidence has been especially difficult along the section of the greenway where Suarez was attacked, which is dark and has no reported surveillance cameras. Investigators have searched the surrounding area using everything possible, from drones to police dogs and scuba divers, while also hoping passing motorists might have recorded something useful.

"We are looking for Teslas, we're looking for Uber drivers," Kenny said, explaining that dashcam footage could help police determine whether the attacker crossed the Belt Parkway while escaping.

The lack of lighting has also brought up plenty of concerns from people in the neighborhood who regularly use the path. At a vigil held Wednesday night, neighbors gathered near the waterfront to remember Suarez and discuss what needs to change to make the area safer after dark.

"There's no lights anywhere. It's very dark. A lot of trees, can't see anything," resident Ann Florio-Lopez told ABC7 New York.

Another woman at the vigil said she'd already changed her routine because of the attack, telling the station she “stopped walking at night.”

Runners outside Brooklyn have been speaking up as well, especially with the attack happening so close to marathon weekend. Fast Women shared Suarez's story on Instagram, expressing disappointment that her death hadn't received more attention within the running community. The account also pointed to complaints from locals who had reportedly been asking for better lighting and security along the greenway for years.

For Suarez's younger brother, Christopher, running has taken on a new meaning. He told 1010 WINS that Katie was always looking out for him, often calling to check in whenever he wasn't home at his usual time.

Now Christopher wants to honor her by running “all the miles she wanted to run” and the races she’ll never get the chance to do.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#8927. I Used to Buy Cycling Kit for How It Looked. Now I Buy It for How It Gets Me Through the Ride—My Three Rules for Cycling Kit

Versatility, comfort, and durability matter most when choosing kit that improves your ride.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

After spending almost two decades riding and years running bike shops, I have narrowed down my priorities for key criteria when buying cycling apparel. I’m looking for a product that is durable, performs well in varying conditions, and is comfortable over miles on the bike.

Apparel falls into different categories depending on the rider. For some, it falls into a category of fashion. Those riders want their choice of apparel to tell a story about who they are on the bike.

For other riders, safety is the biggest driving factor. This group is intentionally easy to see by their bright colors riding by. While other riders solely look for a great deal, digging through clearance racks at bike shops as the seasons change.

Finding kit that performs the way we want our bike to perform can give us a better experience on our ride compared to getting whatever the cool kids are wearing—just for fashion’s sake. Here I’m going to dive deeper into each of the priorities I have for my jerseys and bibs to shed some light on why there’s value in this shift—especially this time of year.

What I look for in a jersey, especially for fall, is one that will vent well on the way up, but keep me comfortable on the way back down. I love a good gilet, especially leaving it open on the way down a road. If my jersey can do what the gilet does then that’s one less piece of kit I have to buy and bring. Lately I’ve been using the Dottore Hybrid Long Sleeve jersey from Q36.5 and it checks off all those boxes.

I tried this jersey out on a recent trip to Italy where we had a roughly 2,500-foot climb followed immediately by an equal descent. The temperature was hovering around the mid-fifties and usually, I would bring a vest for a ride like this. However, I was told this jersey should be perfect for these conditions, so I wanted to give it a proper test. On the way up I didn’t feel a need to unzip the jersey at all and on the screaming descent I never felt cold. Somehow Q36.5 figured out how to give the best of both worlds in one jersey.

Many of us think of a good pair of bibs being the key component to comfort on the bike—and in some ways that’s not wrong. Comfort on your sit bones can be greatly improved by getting the right saddle and sometimes a bike fit to determine what that saddle is and how the saddle should be positioned. But a good pair of bibs can still greatly improve comfort on the bike even after you get a fit and get the right saddle.

Not all chamois pads are created equal, and not all bibs hold the chamois in the place you need after miles of pedaling. Part of the challenge with bibs is you don’t really know until you get on the bike to ride—and good bibs aren’t exactly an inexpensive purchase.

“An unlined full length bib like the Velocio Luxe Tights offers a more comfortable go to bib for when you need to cover you legs but don't need to have fleece warmth,” says Trevor Raab, our resident bike racer and photographer at Bicycling. What I typically look for in bibs is a pair with minimal seams, has a chamois pad that offers both padding and ventilation, and good support and structure from the overalls to help hold the bib in place.

The final piece of my puzzle for gear and apparel is durability. Part of the reality is that just like bikes, apparel has pieces that are more consumable than others and will need to be replaced over time.

I’m someone who tends to stress test both bikes and apparel from hitting the ground. I haven’t found any apparel that holds up to a good impact to the pavement or gravel— as can be seen by many of my bibs having a tear on one of the hips. However, not all material holds up the same over time.

From the bibs that I have tried I either haven’t put enough miles in them or I have put over a year of miles on them and there is a noticeable impact to the comfort of the chamois. But something to note: more padding isn’t inherently better in a chamois. From a durability perspective and my experience, the thicker pads compress over time and aren’t necessarily more comfortable on the bike. The pair I’ve gotten the most miles on this year are the Q36.5 Dottore Bib Shorts. I’ve put a few hundred miles in them and they are still as comfortable as the first ride. Every rider I talk to that has tried this pair of bibs has experienced the same thing.

It’s important to acknowledge the pricing of some of this high-end kit is not a small investment. Shifting your perspective of apparel as just clothes to looking at apparel as gear can make it easier to understand. Too many times when I worked in a shop someone would spend thousands of dollars on a bike only to buy low-priced apparel. There’s nothing wrong with buying entry-level kit to get started. But if you are someone who spends thousands on your bike, then it’s likely ride quality matters to you regardless of the price. If you start to think about your apparel as gear, it’s easier to see that great apparel can impact your ride just like riding on a great bike.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. #8926. Are High-Intensity Workouts Messing With Your Cortisol?

If you’ve scrolled through social media lately, you’ve probably seen wellness influencers claim high-intensity exercise increases cortisol, the infamous “stress hormone” that, in excess amounts, can lead to fatigue, weight gain, trouble sleeping, high blood pressure, and elevated blood sugar.

Many influencers say to switch to a no-stress, low-sweat regimen. And while low-intensity exercises such as Pilates, treadmill walking, or yoga are valid ways to work out—and serve as excellent cross-training activities for runners—HIIT workouts (like hill repeats, sprint intervals, and tempo runs) are key if you’re training for a race or looking to build speed and power.

But are high-intensity runs actually messing with your hormones, or is the wellness side of the internet spreading misinformation? We’re here to separate fact from fiction.

Cortisol is a hormone made by your adrenal glands, which are located on top of your kidneys and are part of your body’s endocrine system.

“Cortisol helps regulate metabolism, blood pressure, and the immune response, and it makes energy available when the body is under stress—including during exercise,” says Dr. Aysegul Eren, M.D., endocrinologist and medical director of the Adrenal Program at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center.

This hormone rises when your body faces increased physical or metabolic demand, such as exercise, illness, fasting, low blood sugar, or psychological stress, Eren explains. During exercise, cortisol naturally spikes as a way to provide energy to your body so it can perform. Viewed through that lens, cortisol is an important part of your body’s response to exercise and your ability to complete workouts.

“Higher-intensity exercise reliably causes a temporary cortisol rise, generally related to exercise intensity,” Eren says. “This is normal physiology, not something harmful to prevent.”

How long cortisol remains elevated depends on the stressor, according to Dr. Feyza Erenler, M.D., an endocrinologist at Tufts Medical Center. It may be minutes to hours for a brief stimulus like exercise, she explains.

A 2021 meta-analysis of 10 studies on HIIT, published in the Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, found that cortisol increased immediately after exercise, often fell below baseline about two hours later, and returned to baseline within 24 hours.

“There’s no evidence that a specific number of HIIT sessions causes chronically high cortisol,” Eren says. “The more relevant concern is overtraining—chronic training without adequate recovery—which can lead to persistent underperformance. ‘Too much’ is individual, depending on training load, sleep, nutrition, recovery, and other stressors.”

In fact, research shows physical activity can actually lead to lower cortisol levels. A 2026 study in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that those who did 150 minutes of moderate- to vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise (50 to 85% of their max heart rate) every week for a year saw a reduction in long-term cortisol levels.

Symptoms frequently attributed to “high cortisol,” such as fatigue, poor sleep, anxiety, or difficulty losing weight, don’t indicate that a person has high cortisol, according to Erenler. “These symptoms are extremely common and nonspecific and can occur for many different reasons,” she says.

Signs of true high cortisol—not the brief, self-resolving spike during exercise—include bruising, muscle weakness (particularly in the upper legs), wide purple stretch marks, worsening high blood pressure or diabetes, and sometimes changes in fat distribution, according to Eren.

If you’re experiencing any of the above symptoms, Eren recommends discussing them with your healthcare provider rather than trying to diagnose yourself with high cortisol all on your own (or with the help of a chatbot). Chronic high cortisol levels that are undiagnosed can cause high blood pressure, diabetes, muscle and bone loss, higher infection risk, and cardiovascular complications.

But rest assured, cortisol disorders are rare. For instance, Cushing syndrome, a condition where you have too much cortisol in your blood for a long period of time, only affects 10 to 15 people per million each year, according to the Endocrine Society. Cushing syndrome is caused by a tumor on the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, not too much high-intensity exercise.

“During exercise, cortisol temporarily rises in response to the physiological stress and then decreases as the body recovers and the stressor resolves,” Erenler says. “In Cushing syndrome, cortisol exposure remains inappropriately elevated over time, and the normal regulatory mechanisms—including the normal circadian pattern and suppression of cortisol production—are disrupted.”

For most healthy people, there’s no need to try to suppress the normal cortisol response to exercise. Instead, the goal should be a sustainable training program that includes adequate recovery, sufficient sleep and nutrition, and variation in workout intensity.

“Don’t worry about the temporary rise in cortisol that occurs with exercise,” Eren says. “It’s a normal part of the body’s response to physical activity, not a sign that exercise is harming you.”

Erenler agrees and says the goal isn’t to eliminate cortisol—it’s to challenge your body appropriately and give it enough recovery to adapt to the stress you’re placing on it.
