Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

This story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

For three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

My mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

This was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the plans I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

They gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

My younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

The day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

On June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

The race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

By the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

My training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making plans; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

The trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

#8912. What Runners Need to Know About Rhabdo

After a tragic death in the running community, doctors want runners to know the risk factors for the condition.

Shortly after the New York City Marathon, tragic news broke: A 24-year-old runner, Rachel Apa, collapsed on the course and died in the hospital after doctors worked for six hours to save her life, according to the New York Times. Apa’s father told NYT the cause of death was rhabdomyolysis (a.k.a. rhabdo).

The news is shocking and saddening—as well as unsettling. Questions are popping up from runners on social media as to how something like this could happen to a young woman who was reportedly a former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University and had spent months training for the marathon.

To help answer some of those questions, we talked to doctors to explain what runners need to know about rhabdo, and how to stay safe.

First, know that rhabdo is relatively rare and dying from it is even rarer. Approximately 26,000 cases of rhabdomyolysis are reported annually in the United States, and the mortality rate starts at 10 percent but may go up to 50 percent in severe cases.

In short, rhabdo is a breakdown of muscle that in and of itself is not life-threatening. In fact, Derek M. Fine, MD, a nephrologist at Johns Hopkins Medicine, says that if you were to test creatine kinase (a.k.a. CK, a blood marker of muscle breakdown) in marathon runners after the race, “most” of them would show elevated levels of the enzyme.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that multiple CK tests are the only way to accurately identify rhabdo, though. Normal CK is between 20 and 200 U/L, but rhabdo is diagnosed when it reaches five times the upper limit.

“There’s always a little bit of muscle breakdown and the reason is because, at least in [a] marathon, you’re using the muscles so much that at some point they can run out of an energy supply,” Fine says, adding that the mitochondria can't keep up and make enough of what’s called ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which is your primary source of energy.

Rhabdo becomes dangerous when it becomes more severe. As muscle tissue breaks down, the body can release harmful substances into the bloodstream, including myoglobin, a protein that can damage the kidneys, and excessive amounts of potassium.

As for myoglobin, the protein can get “stuck” in the kidney and cause kidney failure or injury at various levels, Fine says. “It can be quite severe, but that usually takes a little bit of time to manifest,” he explains.

Fine says that high levels of potassium are probably a bigger risk than myoglobin. “When the muscle cells break up, you get a very large release of potassium into the bloodstream and that potassium then can cause cardiac arrhythmias,” he says. This can cause kidney failure (your kidneys are the organ tasked with getting rid of extra potassium) or potentially sudden cardiac arrest.

“Under normal circumstances, if it’s happening slowly and you’ve got decent kidneys, you pee the potassium out and it never gets that high in the blood,” he says. “If there's severe rhabdo and you have a huge amount of muscles breaking down, you can release a ton of potassium and your body can't get rid of it fast enough.”

In addition to the rapid release of these substances, rhabdo can sometimes lead to other issues that resemble sepsis or even multisystem organ failure, Fine says.

Still, rhabdo is not a common underlying cause of cardiac arrest, says Lili Barouch, MD, director of sports cardiology at Johns Hopkins Medicine and an endurance athlete herself. However, it can lead to abnormal heart rhythms due to severe electrolyte problems, primarily high potassium. And as Fine also explains, kidney failure (as well as other organ failure) can result in cardiac problems, she says.

It’s not just running that can increase risk of rhabdo—any heavy exercise can do damage to muscles, Barouch says, particularly exertional rhabdomyolysis. In fact, Fine says that there have been incidents of rhabdo reported in CrossFit athletes for this reason. Whether it’s a marathon or weight lifting, it’s in high-effort situations that the muscle breakdown can accelerate rapidly and lead to problems.

As for running, while training does induce microscopic damage to muscles that later repairs in a stronger way—a positive outcome—many people push harder in a marathon. “For a race, you’re usually going at a much higher level of effort and you’re really pushing yourself to your limit,” Barouch says.

This can be true for athletes of any level, but people who aren’t as highly trained who push really hard on race day may be at higher risk, Fine says. “The most common reason [for getting rhabdo] is you’ve got someone who overdoes it and who wasn’t trained enough,” he says. (This was not necessarily the case with Apa, just a potential risk factor for runners in general.)

Another risk factor is dehydration, Barouch says. “If someone’s dehydrated, the amount of those muscle breakdown products [your body produces] that can become toxic to the kidneys starts to really go up. You're unable to clear the toxins out of your body fast enough and that can cause more damage,” she says.

On the flip side, good hydration can help flush the myoglobin from the kidneys, per Fine. But, he points out that there’s a delicate balance between being over- and underhydrated: “While you’re running a marathon, your kidneys are getting messages from your brain to hold on to water, so if you keep putting water in there, the water dilutes out the sodium in the blood and you can get hyponatremia,” he says. The key: Drink to thirst and take electrolytes during a long or hot race, Fine says.

Carbohydrates could help as well. “Part of rhabdo could be if you’re not giving enough carbohydrates and energy [to your body], you can't make ATP [the energy currency you need to perform] and that’s where the muscle could break down,” Fine says.

Another factor for marathon runners is environmental conditions. “If it’s a particularly hot day, for example, that seems to be a big risk factor,” Fine says. In fact, there was an unusually large incidence (24 cases) of exertional rhabdomyolysis at the 2022 NYC Marathon, per a study in Nephron Clinical Practice, likely associated with the “unseasonably high heat and humidity” on race day, per the authors.

Younger runners may actually be at higher risk of rhabdo, likely because they’re more inclined to take risks and push harder than the older population, Fine says, potentially ignoring signs of rhabdo.

There’s also a genetic component to rhabdo, Fine says. So, if you have had rhabdo before, or have a family member who has had rhabdo, it could be worth looking into your own risk more closely.

It’s not super common, but genetic tests look at certain markers that might suggest someone is more susceptible to rhabdo. “It’s not like you're going to say, ‘Okay, I’m going to run a marathon, I’m going to go do prescreening genetic testing,’” Fine says. “But in someone who may have had this before, even if they said, ‘Well, I did CrossFit and I got rhabdo and I'm now going to try to run a marathon,’ that sort of person may be worth checking.”

Finally, certain medications (including statins and certain antidepressants) and underlying conditions (like McArdle disease and Duchenne muscular dystrophy) might predispose someone to rhabdo, Barouch says.

The experts agree that signs of rhabdo can be hard to identify because aches are pretty much unavoidable when running a marathon. Still, severe pain in the working muscles (e.g., the legs) is a red flag, Fine says, as are muscle weakness and swelling.

“Of course during a marathon, people tend to have muscle pain, but if it’s much more severe than usual or much more severe than expected,” that’s what to watch for, per Barouch. Severe muscle soreness after the race is also something to keep an eye on, she adds.

Another thing to look out for is urine color. “What one might see early on is very sort of dark orange, rust-colored urine, and that’s the myoglobin coming out,” Fine says. “If someone’s got muscle pain and their urine’s orange, they probably want to go and get checked out and maybe get hydrated and get a CK level checked in an emergency room.”

Per the CDC, the earlier you get treated, the more likely you’ll recover without long-lasting or permanent health effects, so don’t wait if you suspect you have rhabdo.

At the end of the day, it comes down to listening to your body. “As endurance athletes especially, we tend to push ourselves really hard for a race because we have personal goals, time goals, things like that, but you still have to listen to your body,” Barouch says.

If something feels off, don’t ignore it. “Marathons are not comfortable to run for anybody, but if your muscles seem extremely painful or if you start to have other symptoms, if you’re having breathing problems, chest problems, things like that, that seem out of the ordinary, [do] not ignore those warning signs either for rhabdo or another medical condition that might be building up,” Barouch says.

#8910. I Added 10 More Miles a Week to Marathon Training—and Seriously Felt the Difference at Mile 20. Here’s How to Do It Effectively.

How a modest mileage bump helped one marathoner finish stronger, feel better, and build confidence.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

4:09:48. That was my finish time at this year’s New York City Marathon. It was also—to the second—my finish time in the same race last year.

Putting aside the wildness of that (but what does it mean?) I learned a few lessons as I cruised through the five boroughs for the seventh time.

Specifically, although I ran the exact same time, my splits looked quite different. I ran the latter miles faster and they felt easier this year. And that comes down to one key training adjustment I made: adding more overall mileage to my week.

Here’s how and why I maximized my volume during this training cycle, and how it paid off in my strongest finish yet (even if not a PR).

I ran the London Marathon in April, and both New York and Sydney last year, using an artificial intelligence training app. I programmed in that I wanted to run three days a week so I could continue to strength train two to three days a week as well. Plus, I walk quite a bit as someone who lives in New York City (around four to five miles a day on top of any running).

But then I reported on a series of articles about durability for Runner’s World and I started thinking more about total weekly mileage and how much I had (or had not) been doing. Turns out, I peaked around 30 to 35 miles for all three of those marathons. It made me realize there was room for growth.

When I got the opportunity to run New York again this year, I figured out how high I could go mileage-wise without upping my risk for injury.

I started by talking to Andrew Kastor, head coach of the Asics Mammoth Track Club. Before our call, I sent him the training plan I planned to follow for this upcoming training cycle: the Runner’s World Break Four Hours plan. (I also intended to continue strength training twice a week.)

The peak week mileage for that plan: 48 miles, with at least four days a week of running. This may not seem like a ton to people who swear by super high mileage, but it is a steep increase relative to my previous builds. “Between 32 and 50 is night and day,” Kastor says. “You’re going to notice a big difference in your staying power after mile 20.”

Importantly, I built a pretty solid base before starting the training plan 16 weeks out from race day and felt ready to jump into week one when the time came. This plan also leverages mileage ranges, rather than firm numbers, allowing me to further customize it.

Kastor likes the approach of mileage ranges and uses it with many of his athletes. “It kind of takes a little bit of the edge off or the pressure off,” he says, because you can choose the lower end of the range if you’re feeling fatigued.

He also advised me to add in the optional up-to-three-mile run in my plan every other week (where you see 0 to 3 miles). “It’ll be worth it the last mile of the race or the last two miles of the race [when] you’re able to hold that 9:07 pace or that nine flat pace,” he says.

Kastor encouraged me to pay attention to how I was feeling as the training stacked up, and to pull back if I noticed symptoms of overtraining, like an elevated resting heart rate, reduced heart rate variability, or subjective measures like excessive fatigue or feeling flat in workouts. “If [the] legs are not bouncing back week after week, then that’s a sign of overtraining and that you need to pull back and not just pull back with mileage, but take two days off to let your legs recover and heal up,” he says.

I actually felt great throughout my training, which I also attribute to switching up my strength training a bit under the guidance of my physical therapist (I focused more on heavier weight and much less volume, while adding isometrics for tendon health.) Mentally, I also started looking more forward to my running days versus my off days, which is likely due to the fact that I was running more regularly.

In addition to watching for signs of overtraining, Kastor also emphasized the importance of recovery and nutrition when increasing mileage. “In order to do more mileage, you have to sleep well and eat well,” he says.

I focused specifically on eating more carbs than I ever have in training before. (I recently realized I was so focused on protein that I was coming up short on carbs.) As for sleep, I’m always pretty protective of that. So I just kept doing what I was doing: aiming for eight to nine hours a night.

Per Kastor’s suggestion, I also committed to a sports massage every other week during my training, and used the Therabody JetBoots PRO Plus immediately after long runs and occasionally in the evenings on other days. (I feel like they relax my whole nervous system before bed.)

Modern running shoes can also help you handle more time on your feet, Kastor explains. “Generally, because people can handle a little bit more volume with the cushion of the shoes, they’re not breaking down as much,” he says.

I trained in a higher cushioned shoe—the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28—which is known for its premium cushioned, long-lasting ride, according to Runner’s World reviewers. It provided me with a high-energy return and support for the extra miles.

When I spoke to experts in durability about how to increase it for late-race performance, they told me that weekly mileage plays a major role. Research, too, backs up the importance of volume, stating long runs of at least 90 minutes and higher training volumes overall improve durability. And other research suggests more volume (especially easy miles) can lead to faster marathon finish times.

“We start where the athlete is with their fitness and then we progress upward because volume is king,” Kastor says. “More is better as long as you stay healthy.”

He adds that there’s something about the repetition of running frequently that seems to help, citing his wife, marathon Olympic bronze medalist Deena Kastor, as an example. At one point, she was running upward of 140 miles, hitting 13 runs a week, he says. “She would wake up from a nap and be really sleepy, rubbing her eyes, lace up her shoes, and go for a run,” he says. “I think what’s overlooked generally is the role of the nervous system and [how it] plays into the efficiency of running mechanics. If you [run] over and over and over and over again, then you get really, really good at it.”

So, you know I did not PR after adding more mileage to my training plan. But! Take a look at the times for the final four miles in 2025 versus 2026:

I was clearly significantly stronger during the latter miles this year than I was last year, and it was amazing to see and feel that difference. In 2025, I’m honestly surprised I was able to hold the paces I did—I remember feeling pretty wiped, which is why I held back some this time. This year, I felt like I was cruising down 59th Street on the way to mile 25, and even later in the day, I felt good enough to walk almost a mile to dinner and back home.

I felt so strong at the end of this year’s marathon that I know the “mistake” I made was to not trust my training earlier in the race. I was so afraid that I would run out of steam if I held the 8:47 pace I hit at miles 4 and 5 that I pulled back.

So for me, the race was much more of a mental one than a physical one. Now I just have to trust that next time, I can hold faster paces earlier on and still finish strong.

At the end of the day, I realize that I was so focused on my physical training plan and even nutrition that I didn’t think about the psychology of it all. Because I’d run all my long runs at a much easier pace (with the exception of a handful that called for some tempo miles in the middle), I kind of freaked out at the idea of running 26 miles at a 9:00 pace. Now, I truly believe I can. And more mileage is definitely a big part of why.

#8909. Herniated Discs Are a Common Cycling Injury—Here’s Everything You Need to Know

Keep your back health on track with these tips from top docs and bike-fit experts.

Sometimes it happens with a bang, like when former Tour de France pro Marty Jemison was racing Tour of Flanders in the late 1990s. His saddle slipped to be nose up. He thought “no big deal” until one of the steep cobbled climbs, where he was in the saddle cranking out maximum wattage.“And my back just popped,” he says.

Jemison finished the race and the others that followed until he retired about 18 months later, though he had pain off the bike and for the first 30 or 60 minutes of riding, and knew something was wrong. That something was a herniated disc that became nearly debilitating after retirement, eventually required two procedures, and still flares up to this day if he’s not meticulous about his bike position and on top of his core work.

Other times, it’s the proverbial straw that breaks the camel’s (or the cyclist’s) back, as was the case with avid long-distance cyclist Mark Elsasser of Philadelphia who developed some sciatica in 2018. He was able to ride through it just fine, but couldn’t sit for any length of time before the pain was unbearable. The diagnosis: a herniated disc in his low back, which he resolved with physical therapy and has kept at bay by changing his position on the bike, going from a 0-rise to 5-degree stem. “My spine is less compromised being a bit more upright rather than nose down on top of the stem,” he says.

Herniated discs are fairly common in the general population, occurring most frequently among 30- to 50-year-old adults, and men more often than women. Interestingly, you may have one right now and not even know it. “We know from radiographical studies that 50 percent of those aged 40 may have some form of disc herniation. We might consider it normal, age-related changes, and many of those won’t be symptomatic,” says bike fitter and sports physiotherapist Bianca Broadbent, co-owner of The Cycling Physios based in the United Kingdom.

In fact, one research review published in the American Journal of Neuroradiology found that degenerative changes in the discs, which include herniated discs, are present in nearly 90 percent of adults 60 and older and often require no intervention. A herniated disc only causes pain if it’s pressing or otherwise irritating a nerve root in the spine

Join Bicycling All Access for more injury-prevention tips and training advice!

Your spine is comprised of 24 vertebrae. Between those vertebrae are fluid-filled cushions known as discs, which act as shock absorbers for your spinal bones.

“Imagine your spinal discs as jelly-filled doughnuts,” says Andrew Pruitt, Ed.D., the founder of the Boulder Center for Sports Medicine and CU Sports Medicine and Performance Center. “A herniation happens when the jelly inside pops out.”

You may hear people using other terms like “bulging disc,” “ruptured disc,” or “slipped disc.” Technically, a bulging disc is just that: It’s when the jelly inside the donut is pushing against the side enough to bulge out from the vertebrae but isn’t leaking out. A ruptured or slipped disc refers to an actual herniation, where the doughnut cracks, allowing the gel-filled center to squeeze out.

A bulging and/or herniated disc can cause pain by creating pressure on the nearby nerves. There’s some evidence that the leaked fluid from herniated discs also can cause chemical irritation and inflammation of the spinal nerve roots.

Again, it’s possible to have an asymptomatic herniated disc where you feel no pain. When you do have pain from a herniated disc, however, you’ll know it.

Pain from the herniated discs is sharp and radiating. Most cyclists experience herniated discs in the lower, lumbar back (we’ll get to why in a bit). So you may feel burning pain often known as sciatica that radiates from your lower back into your glutes and down one or both legs, sometimes even into your feet. You may feel pain similar to an electric shock when you stand or sit or walk. You may also feel radiating numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in your lower extremities.

So how does the jelly get out of the doughnut and start wreaking havoc on your spinal nerves? In a word: pressure. It can be extreme and sudden, like Jemison cranking on the cobbles. Or, in many instances, it can happen gradually over time, as was the case with Elsasser.

When your spine is in its generally straight, neutral position, the pressure from the top down is uniform on your discs, so the jelly inside those cushions is evenly distributed, Pruitt explains.

“When you bend forward, the jelly is pushed back, stressing the skin of that doughnut,” he says. “If you’re sitting all day, that jelly is pressing back there for eight hours. Now jump on a bike, and you add another two hours in an even more extreme position, pressing that jelly further and further, until—pop—it comes out.”

Though herniation can happen anywhere in the spine, in cyclists it happens most frequently in the lumbar (low back) region close to the base of the spine, or the L5-S1, the bottom-most disc that sits right on top of your tailbone, because that’s where we bend the most, says Menachem Brodie, C.S.C.S., head coach at Human Vortex Training and USA Cycling expert coach.

“For many cyclists, the L5-S1 is where they’re getting their flexion, and the lumbar spine has about six degrees of movement,” Brodie says. So if you’re not hinging from the hips and keeping your spine within its safe, natural range, you’re pushing those limits. Keeping your spine under that kind of stress for prolonged periods of time pushes you closer to the failure point.

Along those lines, research shows that riders with a lower handlebar position and greater flexion in that key lower back region were more likely to have low back pain. Though, importantly, the research also suggests that poor core strength and endurance could contribute to the spinal stress and low back pain in cyclists.

Of course, the bike isn’t the only place you can stress your spine. The gym can be another place riders put their spine under unhealthy stress, says Dane DeLozier, D.P.T., the biomechanics lab director at and co-founder of Revo Physiotherapy and Sports Performance. Maintaining a stable, neutral spine is very important when resistance training, especially when doing big lifts like deadlifts and squats as well as under velocity like with kettlebell swings, DeLozier says.

“When you have your spine under load, you want it to be neutral and very stabilized. You want to be hinging through your hips, not bending and extending your spine under load,” he says.

If you’re unsure of if you’re maintaining a neutral spine, DeLozier recommends setting up your phone and recording yourself (or having a friend video record you) so you can see if you are breaking or flexing under load.

The good news is a 2020 scientific paper, “Slipped disc: Overview,” reports that about 90 percent of people will get relief from their pain and restricted movement within six weeks even if they receive no medical treatment. That’s because the body gets rid of part of the prolapsed tissue or it shifts position so that the nerves aren’t irritated anymore, according to the overview.

You can help that process along with physical therapy, DeLozier says. “The vast majority of folks feel better and have a great outcome by doing mobility exercises for the hip and low back and decompression exercises for the spine.”

The exercises you do depends on your individual situation, but your physical therapist may recommend mobility, stability, and core strengthening exercises such as:

Press Up: Lie facedown with your feet together, toes pointed, and your forearms on the floor palms. Pull your shoulder blades down and in towards your spine and press into forearms to lift your chest off of the floor, keeping your neck long and hips on the floor. If mobility allows, you can press up further by placing hands below your shoulders to come into an up-dog position. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Repeat about 15 times.

Hip Flexor Stretch: Kneel with the affected knee on the floor, tighten your glutes, and brace your abdominal muscles while keeping your back straight. Pressing hips forward. Hold this stretch for 30 seconds. Do 3 times.

Bird Dog: Get on your hands and knees with your palms flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart. Slowly raise and straighten your right leg and left arm at the same time. Keep your hips aligned with the torso and not tilted to one side. Hold for 10 seconds. Return to start. Repeat on the other side.

Cycling itself, when done with a healthy riding posture, can also be a great rehab tool to strengthen the discs and surrounding structures, Broadbent says. In fact, a study done on high-volume road cyclists who rode nearly 100 miles a week for five or more years had beneficial adaptations to their discs and psoas (the biggest hip flexor muscle), which were beneficial for spinal health.

If you’re riding through your rehab, Brodie recommends “crocodile breathing” when you get off the bike. To do it, lie facedown with your forehead resting on the back of your hands and let your chest and hips sink into the floor. Inhale deeply into your belly, expanding your diaphragm for four slow counts. Pause for two seconds, then exhale for six slow counts.

Finally, while many herniated discs can be treated conservatively with physical therapy, some require injection therapy like nerve blocks, if the symptoms are severe, Broadbent says. In rare cases, spinal disc herniation can cause extreme pressure and swelling of the nerves at the end of the spinal cord causing a medical emergency known as cauda equina syndrome.

“If your bladder and bowels aren’t working properly, you have saddle numbness (off the bike as well), or you have sexual dysfunction such as unable to get an erection then you should seek urgent medical investigation,” Broadbent says.

Again, cycling can actually improve spinal strength and the health and hydration of your discs, says Broadbent.

Having a good bike position and the right saddle is key. “You want your spine in a healthy position that doesn’t strain those discs in your lower back,” Pruitt says. If you ride a gravel or a mountain bike, you’re likely already in a slightly more upright, more neutral spine position, he says.

An anatomical saddle will also allow you to put your weight on your perineum without putting harmful pressure on those sensitive tissues, so you’re able to reach the bars without bending too far and putting your spine in an unhealthy position. “Saddle technology improvements have really helped reduce degenerative disc disease,” he says.

Specialized Women’s Power Comp With Mimic

A super popular pick because of the neutral color and three width options.

The raised back cradles you to reduce pressure.

Perfect for racing and comes in two width options.

You also can protect your spine by doing core-strengthening exercises several times a week. Brodie recommends what are known as the “big three” exercises for spinal stability, developed by renowned back pain expert, Stuart McGill, Ph.D., Professor Emeritus of Spine Biomechanics at the University of Waterloo. These exercises stiffen the musculature throughout the core in a way that enhances stability in the spine.

How to do these exercises: The American Council of Exercise recommends performing three sets for each using a reverse pyramid rep/set scheme. Start with a higher number of repetitions for the first set, then decrease by 2 to 6 reps, then decrease by another 2 to 4 reps on the last set. So you might start with 8-6-4 reps and work your way up to 12-10-8 reps as you get stronger and build endurance. Hold each exercise for no more than 8 to 10 seconds.

McGill Curl-up: Lie on your back with one leg extended and the other leg bent, foot flat on the floor. Put your hands under your low back to maintain your natural arch. In one move, lift your head, shoulders, and chest off the floor, keeping your neck and back in the neutral position. Hold. Then slowly return to start. Do half a set. Then switch legs and complete the set.

Side Bridge: Lie on your right side, with your forearm on the floor and elbow underneath your shoulder. Bend your knees at a 90-degree angle. Place your left hand on the opposite shoulder for stability. Lift your hips off the floor so your body forms a straight line from your head to your knees. Hold. Then lower to the starting position and repeat to the other side. Work up to doing the move with your legs straight.

The Bird Dog: (As explained in the previous section)

You can make these exercises part of your warm-up, along with dynamic mobility moves before you get into your bigger lifts.

Off the bike, Brodie recommends practicing good spine hygiene by avoiding hunching forward when you sit and not sitting in a static position for prolonged periods of time, but rather shifting positions in your chair every 15 minutes and getting up, moving around, and doing a little standing stretch, extending your arms, reaching overhead and taking a deep breath every 60 to 90 minutes.

Finally, don’t overlook your mattress. A firm mattress with a pillow top will help support your spine while you sleep, Brodie says. “A lot of people overlook this and it can make a big difference in your back health.”

#8908. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Marathon

Use walk breaks to finish your first marathon—or even score a BQ.

Completing a marathon sits at the top of many runners’ bucket lists, whether it’s a World Marathon Major with thousands of fellow competitors or a small hometown race. It’s a goal that requires plenty of dedication and consistency—along with hundreds of training miles and regular strength workouts—no matter where you are in your running journey.

But you can make the 26.2-mile distance more manageable with a smarter training and racing strategy: adding short walk breaks into your runs.

Runner’s World’s guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, shows you how to successfully navigate marathon training and race day with intentional walk intervals. With the run/walk strategy, you can build your endurance for the marathon distance—while still prioritizing recovery and smarter training.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Marathon, we’ll teach you:

Training Principles for Consistent Success

Adding walk breaks into your training isn’t reserved for marathon newcomers, nor does it mean you’ll perform slower on race day. It’s a smart strategy runners of all levels can use—and it might even help you go faster than when you’ve previously run a full marathon without stopping.

Using walk intervals as a marathoner could help you:

Boston Marathon on your bucket list? Many run/walkers have earned a coveted Boston qualifying time using strategic walk breaks. “We’ve also talked to plenty of runners who have struggled with breaking a time barrier in the marathon,” says Chris Twiggs, chief training officer at Galloway Training. “But once they tried the run/walk method, they finally hit their goal. And in some cases, that meant earning a BQ.”

The faster you aim to go in your marathon, the shorter your walk breaks and the quicker your run pace. You’ll set your training and race paces using your Magic Mile, multiplying your timed mile by 1.3.

Use one of Runner’s World’s three run/walk plans—beginner, intermediate, and advanced—to tackle the 26.2-mile distance. Across either 20 or 26 weeks, you’ll incorporate run/walk workouts, easy walks, long runs, speed sessions, race pace work, and optional cross-training into your build to prepare your body for the demands of the marathon.

Ideal for: Runners who already do walks or short run/walk workouts and want time to build up their time on feet and endurance for 26.2 miles.

With the beginner plan, you’ll complete two 30-to-45-minute run/walk workouts, an easy walk of 20 to 45 minutes, two optional cross-training days, and a rest day each week. Long runs start at two miles and work up to 26 miles in week 23. Running close to the 26.2-mile distance in training will help your body build endurance and prepare for the demands of the distance ahead of race day.

For your long runs, keep your pace 90 seconds to two minutes slower than your predicted marathon pace. On your cross-training days, you can do strength workouts to build resiliency, or also complete other complementary exercises like cycling or swimming.

Ideal for: Runners who have some racing experience and consistently run/walk three times a week.

This plan follows some of the same training principles as the beginner plan, including two 30-to-45-minute run/walk workouts, two optional cross-training days, an easy walk day, and a rest day. Your long runs begin with five to nine miles and work up to 26 miles by week 17.

Ideal for: Runners who have already completed a marathon and want to finally break through a time barrier or run a new PR. You’ll also want a strong base before hopping into the plan.

Each week of the advanced plan includes two optional cross-training days, a 30-to-45-minute easy run/walk workout, and a rest day. You’ll start with higher mileage for long runs compared to the beginner and intermediate plans, beginning with 12 to 14 miles. You’ll also complete consistent speedwork and race pace miles throughout your marathon build.

One crucial speed workout you’ll grow accustomed to during your training: mile repeats. To complete the workout, you’ll warm up for one mile, then run a mile at a pace 30 seconds per mile faster than your race pace. Afterward, you’ll walk for five minutes and repeat both the quicker mile and the five-minute recovery interval. The number of reps will progress from four to 14 miles. For example, if your marathon race pace is 10 minutes, you’ll run a mile at 9:30 pace, followed by five minutes of walking recovery.

Race pace miles equal running faster than your easy run/walks and long runs. Run at the pace you plan to run on race day and use your goal run/walk ratio.

During your build, you’ll dial in your pacing plan, fueling strategy, and run/walk ratio. You’ll also train yourself to push back against the late-race “wall” of fatigue marathoners often face by completing slow long runs working up to 26 miles. It’s all part of a strong race plan rehearsal meant to help you feel strong come race day. Once you cross that start line, trust all of that training and weeks of practice to propel you to the finish.

One of the most important rules of thumb: Nothing new on race day. Stick with your routine that you built during your training block, and refrain from adding new fuel sources, gear, and pacing strategies to your marathon.

In the first third of the marathon, you should feel relaxed—not huffing and puffing. If you feel like you’re pushing yourself too hard during the first miles, slow down and take more frequent walk breaks. You should save pushing the pace for the very end of your race, and if you conserve your energy early on, you’ll have enough left in the tank to close hard toward the finish.

While time banking for a faster marathon is a myth, energy banking does exist. If you save your energy early on, you’ll likely find that toward the end of your race, you can tap into that energy and finish strong.

Ashley is Editor of Content Hype at Hearst’s Enthusiast & Wellness Group. She is a former collegiate runner at UNC Asheville where she studied mass communication. Ashley loves all things running; she has raced two marathons, plus has covered some of the sport’s top events in her career, including the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials and multiple World Marathon Majors.

#8907. This Seated Twist Stretches Your Spine, Engages Your Core, and Enhances Your Awareness

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about a seated twist first appeared in the March-April 1994 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

To encourage new perceptual skills in my students, I like to ask them from time to time to practice in a new spot in the yoga studio. If you’re like most people, after a few classes you find yourself regularly gravitating to the same location, often within a few inches of accuracy.

The mere suggestion to place your mat in the front of the room instead of the cozy corner may make you decidedly un-comfortable. Changing positions enables you to see yourself and the world from a different vantage point, much as a photographer might circle a subject to get pictures from different angles.

It’s not surprising, considering the propensity of our species to form habits, that we tend to perceive our bodies from one perspective, including some aspects of ourselves while leaving others out.

Thus our perception of our body may become like a two-dimensional sketch, deprived of the volume, form, and texture that would extend our awareness into the three-dimensional realm. While Eastern cultures have investigated and honored the inner layers of the body as the key to our physical, mental, and spiritual health, most Western cultures have concerned themselves primarily with the body’s superficial layers. Because of this bias, most of us have come to view our movements as entirely dictated by the muscles and bones, unconsciously deleting other systems from our awareness. Keeping the mind on the outer layers, we become unable to feel or act from our deeper selves.

One of the body systems that brings us most succinctly into a deeper sense of self are the organs, the contents of the musculoskeletal container. Awareness of the organs gives our movements volume, form, and a sense of ripe fullness. Through the health and vitality of the organs, the outer layers gain their strength and form.

Just as we might bring our attention to the sensation of a muscle stretching, we can bring our attention to the sensation of an internal organ. When we change the vantage point of our awareness to bring the inner body into the foreground (an inner adjustment analogous to moving to a different place in the yoga studio), the way we experience ourselves and the quality of our movement will be quite different.

For most of recorded history, yogis have been engaged in just this kind of research, exploring the effects that the asanas (as well as pranayama and meditation) have on the deeper, subtler bodily systems. The ancient practitioners noted which movements and practices stimulated, purified, sedated, or neutralized the energy currents moving deep within the body, correlating these phenomena to health, longevity, and the elevation of consciousness. By contrast, they were not terribly interested in the state of their hamstring muscles, and traditional texts make few references to such structures.

Movements that twist the body compress, elongate, and massage the inner organs. Unfortunately, twists are often practiced exclusively from the perspective of the musculoskeletal system; we use the strength of the muscles and the leverage of the bones to force the body into rotation without ever inviting the soft inner contents along for the ride. Focusing on the internal organs not only reduces the possibility of injury, but stimulates and tones these deep structures by bringing our attention to them, just as electrical activity is created in our muscles simply by visualizing them flexing.

In this article, we’re going to look at how changing the vantage point of our awareness affects the practice of Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi (Marichyasana III), a seated twist.

Bringing attention to the inner body is a way to physically organize our presence on this center. Knowing that there is nowhere to “get to,” we can proceed with the full knowledge that we are on our way.

The following exercise was adapted from Sensing, Feeling, and Action by Bonnie Bainbridge Cohen. Sit on a cushion or blanket with your legs crossed. Close your eyes and let yourself settle. Bring your awareness to the soft inner contents of the torso surrounded by the musculoskeletal container. Imagine your body as two concentric cylinders with the soft internal organs on the inside and the harder musculoskeletal system surrounding them. Feel how the rise and fall of the breath swells from the core and communicates itself to the outer layer.

Now gently bring your awareness to each of your major organs. In the chest is the heart, slightly to the left of center, with the lungs on either side. In the upper left quadrant of the abdomen is the stomach; in the upper right quadrant of the belly is the liver, which extends up underneath the rib cage. The small intestines occupy most of the central and lower belly. In the lower right quadrant of the belly, the small intestine becomes the large intestine, which makes a hairpin turn to run up the right side of the belly (the ascending colon), across the top (the transverse colon), and down the left side (the descending colon), finishing as the sigmoid colon and rectum.

You may want to refer to an anatomy text for a more in-depth discussion of the internal organs. For now, sense their general position and volume, using your breath to palpate them. The kidneys lie on either side of the spine above the waist. The uterus is deep in the abdomen above the pubic bone.

Now bring your attention to your skeletal structure, as if you were seeing the body with X-ray vision. Extend your right arm over your head and bend to the left, focusing your attention on the bones moving. Repeat this to the other side.

Returning to the first side, initiate the side bend from the skeleton and then Shift your attention to the underlying organs, focusing on elongating the organs on the right side of the body and compressing the organs on the left. Did you go further? How did the quality of the movement change as your focus shifted?

Now initiate the side bend as a movement that arises from the organs. Breathe into and elongate the organs on the right side of the body, letting the skeleton follow. How did this experience differ from the one in which you had your mind on the skeletal system alone?

The organs are the seat of our deepest emotions; we physically experience strong feelings as sensations in the viscera (for example, the butterflies of fear or the tight knot of anger). Therefore, many people find that when they initiate movement from the organ system, the movement seems to arise out of their deepest self—that is, there is not a dualistic sense that the mind is “doing something” to the body. By contrast, when you perceive the body as nothing but a skeleton, it may feel as though your mind is manipulating your body like a puppet on a string.

Now integrate this new awareness of your organs into a simple twisting posture.

Some preliminary suggestions may make your task easier. One of the obstacles to twisting freely is the inability to sit upright with the normal curves of the spinal column intact. When the legs are extended, this problem may be further exaggerated because the hamstrings may pull on the base of the pelvis, causing the back to round (Figure 1: Incorrect). In this position, you are actually sitting on the base of the spine rather than on the sitting bones, and the collapse of the outer body makes it difficult to breathe freely.

To make sitting—and therefore twisting—a little easier, this first variation calls for both legs to be folded. By deactivating the hamstrings, we allow the pelvis to move more freely into an upright position.

Sit cross-legged with the buttocks elevated on a blanket or cushion. Place the right leg so the shin is upright, with the sole of the right foot directly in front of the left ankle. Inhaling fully, allow the abdomen to expand freely. On your exhalation roll the abdomen to the right, guiding the abdomen back against the spine to encourage the twist. Bring your left elbow onto the outside of the right knee (Figure 2).

With each breath, allow the soft inner body to move circularly in the direction of the twist, very much as if you were doing a belly dance. Once the lower torso is turning freely to the right, direct the breath more fully into the right side of the chest. Expanding the right lung with the inhalation, encourage the thoracic spine to move in and up. As you exhale, release the left lung from the center of the chest out into the shoulder, allowing the muscles along the back of the body to follow the changing shape of the lung.

As this occurs, the shoulder blade and then the arm will move further around.

Replace the elbow against the knee as necessary. When you feel you have reached your limit, stay for a few more breaths, simply letting the inhalation and exhalation oscillate the body slightly to and fro. Release on an exhalation and then repeat on the other side.

Now extend both legs in front of you, placing a blanket underneath your buttocks if necessary to create an erect sitting position. Sit with your back one arm’s length from a wall. Bend your right knee, placing the heel of the right foot in line with the sitting bone of the right side of the pelvis. Extend downward through the length of the left leg, simultaneously pressing the right foot down into the floor. Feel how this groundedness through the bones rebounds up through the body as the energy flows through the soft organs and the bones to support the erect carriage of the torso. When you release the downward movement of the legs, notice how the spine sags and the whole torso wilts.

Sense how the movements of the muscles and bones affect the shape of the internal organs, and vice versa.

As you inhale, direct the breath into the mid and upper chest. With each exhalation, successively turn from the lowest part of the belly to the head. Bring your elbow onto the outside of the right knee and place your hand against the wall, making sure that you are far enough from the wall that the shoulder is not elevated toward the ears (Figure 3). Use your arm to lift and support the torso, but do not overpower the soft movements of the inner body by using the arm to forcefully turn the outer muscles. Instead of using the arm as a “dictator,” let your arm become a “guide.” In the same way, wait for the inner body to yield to the movement, then encourage it with the guiding arm.

Take a few more full breaths before releasing and repeating the movement on the second side.

In this exercise you will focus on the contents of the spine—the spinal cord—to bring deeper awareness to your movement. Begin by sitting in Staff Pose (Dandasana) with both legs extended. Bend the left knee and place the heel of the left foot in line with the sitting bone. Now place the left hand immediately behind the left buttock and use it to support the trunk.

Before beginning the twist, take a moment to bring a few central images to mind. Start by bringing your awareness to the contents of the skull. Sense whether the brain is balanced equally between the front and back of the skull. Exiting the brain is the brain stem; then the spinal cord runs through each vertebrae like thread running through a string of beads.

Think of your spinal cord as the tail of your brain and the vertebrae as individual beads, each with its own size and shape.

As you bring your awareness to the brain stem, notice how the spinal cord curves inward so that the cervical vertebrae stack up underneath the head. As you continue your mental journey down the back, the soft spinal cord curves outward, following the convex curve of the thoracic spine. As you move your attention down toward the base of the rib cage, the spinal cord loops back in and the five lumbar vertebrae stack directly under the center of the chest. Continue on down to the massive sacral bone which curves outward and articulates with the two wings of the pelvis.

Having established this anatomical map, begin to sense how the bones of the spine are positioned in relationship to the soft spinal cord. Are there any areas of the spinal cord that feel compressed, perhaps even red and sore from being pressed and rubbed by the bodies of the vertebrae? Are there vertebrae that feel as if they were glued together, or areas where the bones feel rotated or collapsed on one side? Use your breath to gently move your vertebrae as if you were rearranging very precious antique furniture in a room. Adjust the vertebrae so they glide over the spinal cord easily.

As you enter the twist, continue to gauge your movement to avoid any irritation to the spinal cord. (While the brain is insensitive to pain, the outer sheath of the spinal cord is richly supplied with sensory nerve fibers.) Imagine that you are initiating the movement from the level of the spinal cord. If you overpower the spine with the strength of the arm, the result will often be irritation in the spine during the twist and an ache in the back long after your practice is finished.

Once the torso has rotated so the chest is facing the left knee, you can take the “hand lock” by bringing the right arm around the outside of the left shin. Link the fingers or, if possible, hold the left wrist with the right hand. Exhale and draw the hands away from the shoulders, allowing the spine to lengthen strongly upward.

If taking the hand lock compresses the front of the abdomen and collapses the spine, you are moving your skeleton further than the organs can support. Be conscious of using your breath to shape the internal organs. Keep the front of the abdomen open and draw the base of the left rib cage in toward the waist to encourage full spinal extension. Turn the head to look back at the foot of the extended leg (Figure 4). Take a few more breaths and then release. Repeat on the other side.

To clarify the distinction between initiating movement from the inner body and dominating with the outer muscles, you might try the previous exercises again, this time exerting force with the outer body by using the arm as a strong lever. Notice the tone in the muscle tissue when you exert force from the outside, as opposed to the quality when you allow the inner body to give to the movement in its own time. Also notice how the two different ways of initiating movement create different psychological states.

Within each of us is a longing for wholeness. Like the spiraling shape of the twist, our spiritual path must constantly turn back toward the still center within us. The longing to “get somewhere” through yoga is a distortion of our true urge to return back to the undifferentiated, unchanging core from which all life expands.

#8906. Can the Tour Be Pogačar-Proofed? The 2027 Tour de France Route Is Designed to Keep the Racing Close.

More time trialing and fewer summit finishes could give Remco Evenepoel, Jonas Vingegaard, and the rest of the peloton a chance to take the fight to the five-time champion.

It’s early November, which means the Halloween candy is on sale, the piles of leaves in my yard are getting harder to ignore, and the routes for the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France have finally been unveiled. After weeks of refreshing Tour rumor sites, here’s what stood out to me about the men’s route.

First, let’s address the Slovenian elephant in the room: There’s little anyone can do to defeat a healthy, in-form Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates XRG), who will head into the 2027 Tour as the overwhelming favorite to take a record-breaking sixth overall victory. Certainly, the organizers seem to feel the same way.

Rather than create a race designed to defeat him, which currently doesn’t seem possible, they’ve laid out a course that could at least prevent the five-time champion from running away with it in the first week. The 2027 Tour packs more than 53,000 meters of elevation gain and 28 second-, first-, or hors catégorie climbs into its 21 stages. But there are only three summit finishes, and the first doesn’t arrive until the end of Stage 9, atop the Grand Colombier.

That means fewer chances for Pogačar and his team to jump out to a huge early lead on the Tour’s general classification and then ride defensively, slowly wearing down the opposition until the final week. That’s when the Slovenian usually delivers the coup de grâce, adding a few more stage wins to his ever-growing tally.

Yes, there are a couple of punchy uphill finishes in the opening week, at the end of Stages 4 and 5, and Pogačar will do well on them. But the time gaps shouldn’t be huge, so I expect a tighter bunch of riders at the top of the GC heading into the first individual time trial on Stage 7.

Speaking of time trials, the 2027 Tour features 71 kilometers of them across Stages 7 and 16, the most we’ve seen since 2012. It’s hard not to see that as a nod to Belgium’s Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull–Bora–Hansgrohe), the four-time world time trial champion who finished second in the Tour this past July.

If he can improve his preparation for this year’s Tour, and he’s only 26, Evenepoel could use those time trials to his advantage. The first might even give him a chance to give Pogačar a scare before the mountains arrive at the end of the opening week.

But waiting until Stage 9 for the first mountain stage doesn’t mean the opening week will be easy. A slew of long, tricky stages will be tough for one or two teams to control. And at least until the Stage 7 time trial, plenty of riders should be in contention to spend a day or two in yellow and willing to take a few risks and big swings to make it happen. That’s the downside of designing a route that attempts to delay the GC fireworks until the second week. More riders feel they have a chance to wear yellow, which can lead to more risk-taking and, unfortunately, the possibility of more crashes.

Throw in tight roads, punchy climbs and descents, some rain during the three opening stages in the United Kingdom, and perhaps a few days of crosswinds, and you’ve got the exact right mix to create unpredictable and downright chaotic racing.

If Pogačar is going to run away with another Tour, I expect we’ll know by the end of Stage 11, the final day in the Alps and the second of the race’s three summit finishes. If his rivals, including Evenepoel, Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard (Visma–Lease a Bike), and France’s Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM Team), can somehow limit the damage on Stages 9, 10, and 11, we could have a much more compelling Tour than what we’re used to.

A run of sprint and transitional stages follows before the final week, when the second time trial and two days in the Pyrenees await. With any luck, we’ll still have a GC battle worth watching by then.

That’s what the organizers appear to be hoping for with this route. But given what we’ve seen from Pogačar and his UAE squad in recent Tours, I’m not sure it will happen. While the time trial kilometers seem to acknowledge Evenepoel as one of Pogačar’s greatest threats, I also see the route as a not-so-subtle gesture to Seixas, the young Frenchman many consider the rider most likely to be Pogačar's successor.

Seixas, now 20, raced his first Tour this past summer and finished fourth overall. The 2027 course should give him a chance to continue growing as a Tour contender without throwing him in at the deep end the way this year’s route did. The French would be thrilled to see him finish on the final podium, and with the Tour’s most intense stages broken into two- or three-day chunks, with time to recover and regroup in between, that kind of result looks well within his reach.

I’m also eager to see how two-time Tour champion Vingegaard tackles the race. Recent routes have forced Vingegaard and his Visma–Lease a Bike team to burn a lot of matches early, leaving them powerless when Pogačar and his UAE teammates throw down in the second and third weeks. The 2027 course should allow Vingegaard to ride a bit more under the radar, hopefully keeping him fresh for the Stage 7 time trial and the first summit finish on Stage 9. If all goes to plan, the Dane could enter the third week ready to challenge Pogačar in a way we haven’t seen since Vingegaard won his second Tour in 2023.

As for specific stages, I’ve already marked a few as days I won’t want to miss.

The Tour begins in the United Kingdom with three stages that should generate some intense battles among sprinters and Classics riders. Of the three, Stage 3 looks like the hardest. Its 223 km route includes a slew of punchy climbs, making it a perfect day for riders like Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin–Premier Tech), Wout van Aert (Visma–Lease a Bike), and Tom Pidcock (Pinarello–Q36.5 Pro Cycling Team).

Then there’s Stage 10, a 171 km ride from Annecy to Sallanches that features six categorized climbs and previews the course used in August’s world championship road race. Coming right after the Tour’s second rest day and sandwiched between summit finishes on Stages 9 and 11, this should be an exciting and hard-to-predict day for the GC contenders.

Stage 14 takes the riders 199 km from Montpellier into the Cévennes, covering many of the roads immortalized in Tim Krabbé’s The Rider, one of the best cycling novels ever written. Seriously, if you’ve never read it, find a copy and enjoy! The stage ends on an airstrip just past the summit of the Côte de la Croix Neuve, a famous climb that always generates an exciting finish.

After taking a back seat in recent Tours, the Pyrenees close out the mountain racing in 2027, highlighted by Stage 18. The Tour’s “queen stage” runs 174 km from Pau to Saint-Lary-Soulan, with 5,400 meters of elevation gain and perhaps the two toughest climbs in the entire race: the Col du Tourmalet and a summit finish on the Col du Portet. If the race hasn’t been decided heading into Stage 18, it should be by the end, even with one relatively milder day in the Pyrenees still to come.

And what about Stage 21? Maybe you heard the pre-announcement rumors that the organizers would skip the cobbled Côte de la Butte Montmartre. Thank goodness they proved false. Adding a few trips over the climb to the final stage in 2025 has proven to be one of the greatest innovations in Tour history, and I’m thrilled they kept it in for another year.

Overall, the 2027 men’s Tour stacks up like this: 3,479 kilometers (2,162 miles) spread over 21 stages, with seven flat stages, six hilly stages, six mountain stages, two individual time trials, and three rest days.

With about eight months to go before the riders hit the road in Edinburgh, a lot can still happen. Most of the top contenders haven’t even confirmed their 2027 programs, which means there’s a chance, however unlikely, that at least one of them might not participate.

But as long as Pogačar is racing, the result, for better or worse, might be a foregone conclusion. And that’s not necessarily a bad thing. He is a once-in-a-lifetime talent, resetting the record books of the sport the way Eddy Merckx once did.

But as the saying goes: it’s the journey—not the destination—that matters here. Yes, we should enjoy speculating about who will and who won’t win the Tour de France—and how and when they manage to do it. But we can’t forget that the Tour de France offers at least 21 chances for something exciting and unexpected to unfold. Next year’s route might not prevent the inevitable, but it will certainly produce lots of great racing along the way. And I can’t wait.

#8905. Don’t Get Locked Into a Spring or Fall Marathon Cycle. A Run Coach Explains Why You Should Race in Other Seasons.

Here’s how to adjust your training timeline for better weather, faster performances, and more motivation.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When choosing a marathon, most runners focus on the details of the race itself: size, location, weather, elevation, and crowd support. Those are crucial considerations, of course, but they only account for one day, compared with the months you spend training for 26.2 miles. So, you also need to factor in what those months of training could look like depending on the race you choose.

Once you do that, you may realize that racing your marathon in the winter or summer actually benefits you more than racing in the spring or fall. In fact, some runners find that the PRs just out of their reach during those more popular racing windows were simply waiting for them in a different season. The missing piece? Moving the timeline of their marathon cycle to maximize factors like consistency.

A run coach who’s competed in every season explains how to pick a race that sets you up to perform at the right time each year and how flipping your training and racing seasons just might lead to more fun, less stress, and even faster times.

Some of the biggest, most exciting 26.2s occur in the fall and spring—take six of the World Majors, for example. But these marathons can also come with less-than-ideal training timelines, Elizabeth Corkum, a.k.a. Coach Corky, an RRCA-, UESCA-, and USATF-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World.

When race day falls in September, October, or April, you’ll likely have your most important workouts and long runs on tap for the least ideal weather of the summer and winter months: brutal heat and humidity or short days with ice and cold temperatures, Corkum explains. Many runners, though, deem these tougher training conditions a fair trade for a shot at a cool, dry day in the low 50s when they toe the starting line.

Some runners would rather flip the script: Do the bulk of their training and peak mileage weeks in nicer weather, instead of hoping for ideal conditions on race day.

If you don’t enjoy running as much when you’re waking up at 4 a.m. in the summer to beat the heat or waiting until the sun goes down to squeeze in miles just before bed, you may benefit from switching your main training season. Some options to consider might be the California International Marathon (CIM) in December or the Houston Marathon in January, Corkum suggests.

Or, maybe you find yourself worn down from trudging through sleet and slush, bundling up for runs in below-freezing temps, logging miles in the dark when the days shorten, or simply confining yourself to the treadmill because it’s the only place that isn’t slick with ice. In that case, you might want to complete your heaviest training in the spring for a summer race. Some great options to consider are Grandma’s Marathon in June, the San Francisco Marathon in July, and the Gold Coast Marathon in July.

For many runners, the greatest benefit of doing the bulk of their training during the fall and spring is that they enjoy the process more. They’re excited to get out the door each day to put in the miles when the weather is cool and crisp from September through November, or they’re finally catching glimpses of green and spring blooms from March through May.

“The mental impact of just grinding day after day in the bitter cold or brutal heat can sometimes make running feel less fun, and I think there is some mental exhaustion that can come from doing that in summer and winter,” Corkum says. “Some people love it and they thrive on it—but many don’t.”

When runners can train in the conditions they feel their best in, they’re usually able to get their miles in more consistently and the entire marathon cycle becomes more enjoyable, she adds.

Once you make the switch, you may not only find that it’s less challenging for you to adhere to your training schedule but that you also have more mental energy and motivation. While these benefits are psychological, they can lead to real physiological training improvements, too.

Besides the mental boost that comes from logging miles in the spring and fall, you might find that your body responds better to training in milder conditions, as well. This may allow you to train harder and recover more quickly.

“October and November are months during which I sweat less and running is not as taxing,” Corkum says. “My heart rate is 5, 10, even 15 beats lower at the same effort because of the weather. And because of that, all my easy runs are even easier on my body.”

Corkum has found that she can usually handle about 10 to 15 more miles each week, and this higher training load, for her, doesn’t require as much recovery as it would during the hotter months of the year. “There’s a huge benefit if we can add more mileage with less stress on the body. If we’re able to run more, that can make us much better runners,” she explains.

A study of more than 119,000 runners published in Sports Medicine in 2024 backs up Corkum’s recommendation: Higher averages of easy-running mileage were associated with faster race performances. So consider which season allows you to safely and comfortably log more miles each week.

Regardless of the season you choose for your marathon, good weather isn’t guaranteed. Corkum says runners should prepare for the possibility that even races like CIM, which has a strong track record for being cool and overcast, could experience an unexpected pop of heat. So, she encourages runners to incorporate some type of heat training—especially if you’re not getting much exposure to hot and humid temps during runs.

“We don’t need to be running in uncomfortably hot and humid conditions every single day to be ready for a warmer race day. Passive heat training—sitting in a hot tub, bathtub, steam room, or sauna—can help us heat adapt, too,” Corkum says.

Another tip Corkum gives her athletes? Do your research. “Go online to check the average temperatures and dew points of a race for the last 10 years or so. Look at the outliers, too,” she says. This information helps you determine if race day and the training season will offer the conditions you want.

And finally, learn to adapt when—despite your best preparations—race day doesn’t go your way. Ask yourself how you’ll adjust your expectations, fueling, and pacing instead of forcing the effort, because that can change your experience of the day and even your finish time, Corkum says.

The season for your best marathon performance will largely depend on your ability to prioritize the aspects of training and racing that feel most important to you, Corkum explains. So when choosing your marathon, consider how much emphasis you’re putting on both race day and the months of the journey.

“Of course, we all want the perfect day for our marathon. But it’s the months of training beforehand that get us there feeling fit and confident,” she says. Keeping both pieces in mind can help ease race-day pressure and elevate your entire marathon cycle regardless of the time of year—or time on the finish clock.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.
