#8885. No Alps, No Pyrenees, and No Paris. The 2027 Tour de France Femmes Will Still Deliver Exciting Racing, but the Women Deserve More of Cycling’s Iconic Backdrops.

A three-day start in England and a finish atop the Puy de Dôme give us plenty to look forward to. But some of the organizers’ choices leave me wondering what this Tour could have been.

The route of the 2027 Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift was revealed in late October, featuring a Grand Départ in the UK, a jaunt through central France, and a summit finish atop the Puy de Dôme. The sixth edition of the revived women’s Tour will kick off on Friday, July 30, and conclude on Saturday, August 7, after nine days of racing.

In just five editions, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift has become the pinnacle of the women’s WorldTour calendar. And looking at the 2027 route, we’re in for another nine days of aggressive racing, a hard-fought GC battle, and opportunities for a wide range of stage winners. Yet some route choices leave me lukewarm, and a few things are missing altogether. There’s no trek into the Alps or Pyrenees, no individual time trial, and still no Paris finale.

Now, I don’t doubt that the women’s peloton will make the most of the route it’s given, but whether it’ll match the spectacle of previous editions is another question.

First, the highlights, starting with the three-day Grand Départ in England.

The 2027 route puts a lot of the fireworks up front, so there’s no easing into this Tour. It opens with a short, punchy 86km stage from Leeds to Manchester. Officially classified as flat, it still packs in three categorized climbs. So while the sprinters may get their chance at the first yellow jersey, it’s not guaranteed. Then comes a bumpy stage two that, a local tells me, is much harder on the legs than it looks on paper. And then we’ll get the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift’s first team time trial in London.

Leeds, Manchester, London. The 2027 edition will put women’s racing in front of millions. That’s a huge opportunity to draw roadside crowds and reach new audiences. Those opening stages could also give the GC an intriguing shape. An early winner backed by a strong team performance in London might carry a rider in yellow deep into the race.

Then there’s the Puy de Dôme. The volcano occupies a special place in cycling history, having hosted 14 men’s Tour de France stage finishes, including the famous 1964 head-to-head between Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor.

A more recent memory of the Puy de Dôme is that of Matteo Jorgenson’s heartbreak on stage nine of the 2023 Tour. The American attacked alone with almost 50km remaining, only for Canadian Michael Woods to catch and pass him some 450 meters from victory. Jorgenson ultimately finished fourth.

It’s easy to imagine the volcano hosting another exciting chapter in the Kasia Niewiadoma (Canyon//SRAM) and Demi Vollering (FDJ United–Suez) rivalry.

In 2025, the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift delivered six different stage winners and three riders in yellow. This year, it was six and five respectively. The 2027 route should again give a broad cast of riders their chance, with plenty of terrain for versatile stage hunters alongside opportunities for the sprinters and climbers.

That’s something I like about the Tour. A Tour stage can define a rider’s season; just look at the breakthrough victories of Maëva Squiban (UAE Team L'Imad), Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education–Oatly), and Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance–Soudal) in years past.

The route opens the door to well-rounded riders, but the overall will still likely be decided on the final two mountainous days. But if climbing decides the Tour, I’d like to see some high-mountain racing in the Alps or Pyrenees. If the intention is to give more riders a shot at the GC, then I want to believe that they can actually take the yellow home, rather than just borrow it for a few days.

Of course, Vollering and Niewiadoma excel on punchy terrain too. And that’s part of my concern: different profiles don’t guarantee different outcomes. Perhaps the shorter climbs will keep more riders in contention, but I’m not convinced this route broadens the fight for yellow as much as it prolongs it.

Then there’s London. I’m excited about the setting, but the racing format leaves me underwhelmed. I prefer an individual time trial where every rider controls her own performance. No matter the timing rules, a team time trial tends to favor stronger, bigger teams, with more money to spend on a deeper roster, equipment, testing, and optimizing. A rider from a team with fewer resources could leave London with a time loss that reflects her team's budget more than her own performance.

Eighteen kilometers may limit the damage, but as 2024 showed, when Niewiadoma-Phinney won the overall by just four seconds, every single second counts.

While Britain gets the big-city showcases, I feel roadside fans in France get a bad deal. The route bypasses the country’s largest cities on its way to a finale where spectator access remains uncertain.

Strict environmental protections are in place on Puy de Dôme, and organizers are still exploring if they can admit a limited crowd at the summit. I understand the need for protection, but a repeat of 2023’s empty upper slopes would be a lonely way to welcome in the Tour winner. If fans aren’t welcome, surely it’s worth asking whether this is the right place to finish.

And while a summit finish can deliver exciting racing, I’m still waiting to see the women’s peloton finish on the cobblestones of Paris, same as the men. Wout van Aert’s victory in 2025 and Mathieu van der Poel’s all-out effort in 2026 were absolute highlights of those Tours for me. The Montmartre circuit has shown how much racing in Paris can offer, beyond a ceremonial procession. After watching Vollering and Niewiadoma duel in France and again in Montréal, with Marlen Reusser never far behind, I want to see what these women could do on those streets.

#8883. Inspired by Fall Marathon Season? Here’s What You Need to Do to Prepare for 26.2

Follow these nine coach-approved training tips now for a strong finish later.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The spirit of the fall marathon is undeniably contagious: the roaring crowds, the crisp autumn air, and massive community energy. If you spectated this year, watching the hundreds (if not thousands) of runners race toward the finish line might have you yearning to lace up your shoes and hit the starting line next season. But before you jump into training, hit pause and make sure you’re prepared for success.

“Training to run a marathon will revolutionize your life, but it will also test you in brand-new ways,” says Susie Crossland-Dwyer, an avid marathoner and ultramarathoner, coach, and founder of studio s in Cincinnati. “A lot goes into a healthy, successful training season and what you do leading up to it.”

Here are nine tips that coaches want every marathoner to know to get to race day healthy, strong, and fast!

You’re about to set out on four-plus months of intense weekly mileage. That’s really tough on your body. To sidestep an overuse injury, having a steady foundation is crucial. A review of research on runners’ injuries published in the Journal of Sport and Health Science found that the injury incidence rate among runners is 40.2 percent, and overuse from ramping up mileage or intensity too quickly causes more than 70 percent of the injuries.

“As you begin your marathon season, start with base building and don’t just jump right into doing all the miles and all the speed workouts,” advises Crossland-Dwyer, who recommends spending at least three months gradually working up to 20 to 25 miles per week before starting an official marathon training program.

“Strength training, specifically your core and hips, is the most effective way to prevent injuries,” says Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect. “As you ramp up your mileage for the marathon, this will be essential to you staying healthy through the training segment.”

Studies have found that strength training can also boost your performance by improving your running economy. You don’t need a certain base of strength before starting your training plan, he says, but you should include two to three weight workouts each week.

Along with weight training, “try plyometrics to get your body used to absorbing impact, single-leg exercises to prevent muscle imbalances, and mobility drills to keep your range of motion and joints healthy,” advises Meg Takacs, NASM-CPT, a run coach and founder of the Movement & Miles app.

Carb-loading before race day is what most novice runners are familiar with when starting on their marathon-training journey, but it’s only one aspect of your diet that’s important.

“Nutrition is key for successful training and a successful race—from carbs to water, electrolytes, and salt capsules,” says Takacs. “The goal is to stay ahead of any deficits before they happen because once you’re in a hydration or nutritional deficit, it’s almost impossible to come back.”

Buy water bottles to carry with you on long runs (sip water or a sports drink every 10 to 15 minutes), plus gels or gummies to nibble on every 30 minutes to stay fueled and strong through your long runs ahead.

We’re not talking about the race itself—though, yes, you’re going to be on your feet for a long time for that, too. But it’s important to know the kind of time commitment you’re going to be looking at for the next 16 or so weeks leading up to race day.

You’ll be devoting a couple hours, at least, likely every Saturday or Sunday morning to a long run, plus your other weekly runs. But also, says Crossland-Dwyer, “Training for a marathon isn’t all about running. In fact, a big portion of your weekly training hours should be spent preparing, with prehab exercises and prerun activations, doing strength-training, and recovering with mobility work, adequate rest and refueling, and extras like compression and cold therapy.”

Yes, destination races are popular, and if you’re pretty sure this whole marathon thing is going to be a one-and-done experience for you, you might as well pick an epic course. But don’t ignore races in your backyard.

“It’s so fun to see your city streets opened up for you,” says Erin Beck, vice president of innovation, product, and experience at Xponential Fitness, who’s run 21 marathons. “Seeing your city from a different vantage point than usual can keep your mind off of the treachery of 26.2 miles.”

Yes, you have several months until race day. But don’t wait to find your favorite clothing and shoes. “Purchase the gear you’ll need now, including shoes for training, the shoes you’ll race in, your potential race kit, and options for different weather conditions,” Gaudette says. “That way, you can test everything out during a few training runs to ensure it’s comfortable.”

Don’t forget about accessories: Having the right details for you, from the fuel belt that bounces the least on your hips to the socks that help you sidestep blisters, will make training all the more comfortable.

If you’re not sure where to start, check out a local running store or online forums for recs from knowledgeable contributors.

Runners joke about bloody nipples for a reason. Rubbed-raw skin there—or your inner thighs or armpit or your upper arm where it shifts against your shirt or sports bra—is inevitable at some point (or several) during marathon training.

Blisters from ill-fitting shoes or the wrong socks could be in your near future too. “Unfortunately, the only way to really know what clothing will contribute to this to test it out, which is why it’s good to have everything you might wear early,” says Gaudette.

In the meantime, buy an anti-chafing stick or cream now and lube up before every long run ahead to protect your skin and slash the chances that you’ll be in a lot of pain later.

All the anticipation of gearing up for your race will likely be mixed with nervousness, too. Remind yourself that you can do this because so many people like you have done the same.

“You don’t have to be Eliud Kipchoge to run a race—and you don’t have to know who that is to run a race, either!” says Beck. “The only thing you have to be in order to be a marathoner is bold enough to try one.”

Every successful marathoner has a training plan to follow. So before you dive into marathon training, you’ll want to find a plan that spans at least 16 weeks and fits your fitness level and your goals.

Do you just want to finish? Are you looking to break three, four, or five hours? Can you meet the weekly mileage in week one of the plan? Think about these questions and find the plan that works to guide you to the starting line and finish line feeling strong.

#8882. ⁠Before You Spend on Gravel Suspension, Try Wider Tubeless Tires for a Simpler, Smoother Ride

Wider tires can add comfort and traction on chunky gravel without the weight of suspension parts.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Just the other day a friend getting into gravel was asking me about suspension parts for his relatively new gravel bike. He was considering different suspension components as a means to gain comfort while he rides—especially on chunkier gravel. He mentioned his frame isn’t compatible with a suspension fork, but was looking at parts like a suspension stem and suspension seatpost. If this sounds like you read this before hitting add to cart on those parts.

When I ran a shop I installed plenty of suspension parts on bikes for people who felt it was the only way they could be more comfortable on the bike. Certain riders fit the bill for a suspension seat post or suspension stem. A few customers had prostate issues and a suspension seat post helped them stay on the bike longer. Others had wrist or hand issues and they benefited from a suspension stem. But even those riders could get additional comfort from a simple change.

After trying all the suspension components I could add to my own bike (as well as trying a full-suspension gravel bike), I have realized that throwing suspension at a gravel bike doesn’t necessarily fix the issue of being more comfortable on the ride. In the shop, customers would ask about installing a suspension fork on a hybrid or gravel bike, but not all frames are even compatible with a suspension fork.

Adding suspension parts to the bike can change the overall feel of the bike, not to mention the weight those parts typically add. When riders are looking for more comfort on their gravel bike the component swap I pick first is simple—wider tires. Here we’ll talk about the benefits of wider tires and why going tubeless gives your ride that extra bit of cush.

Step one of getting more comfortable on your gravel bike is setting up your tires as tubeless if they aren’t already set up that way. Tubeless systems allow you to run your pressure lower compared to running tubes, which in combination with a wider tire offers more comfort. Running tubes with a lower tire pressure leaves you susceptible to pinch flats, but tubeless systems remove the tubes from the equation.

One easy way to check if your tires are set up as tubeless is to loosen the nut at the bottom of your valve and gently press it into the rim. If you press it in and air starts to come out, then tighten the nut back up—congratulations, your tires are set up as tubeless!

If they aren’t tubeless, then it’s time to check compatibility. Check the specs of your bike to see if your rim and tire are tubeless-compatible. If they aren’t you’ll have to explore new wheel and tire options, but if they’re compatible you can convert them to tubeless. Some bikes come stock with tubeless-compatible rims and tires, but don’t come set up tubeless out of the box. Tubeless systems require specific rim tape or rim strips to properly set them up. I’ve seen plenty of bikes come with tubes installed, but with rims taped with tubeless tape. Again, check your individual bike’s specs to see if this includes your bike.

If you need to pull the tubes out of your tubeless-compatible wheels and tires, then you’ll need a few things. First is a good set of tubeless valves. My favorite are Muc-Off Tubeless Valves. They come with a valve core remover tool on the valve cap, come in different lengths depending on your rim depth, and there are a myriad of colors to add a little pop to your bike. You’ll also need tubeless sealant. I’ve tested more sealants than I can remember, but the tried-and-true sealant I go back to is Stan’s Sealant. Tara Seplavy, Bicycling’s Deputy Editor, walks through setting up your tubeless tires here.

A bike rarely comes stock with the widest tire that fits in the bike. For example, the Trek Checkpoint SL5 is equipped with 700x42mm, but can fit up to 700x50mm tires when there are no fenders on the bike. Always check the technical specifications for your specific make and model to see how wide you can go. Over the last few years, bike manufacturers have been pushing the envelope to allow for wider and wider tires on bikes. If you have a previous model-year bike that doesn’t mean you can bank on the current model’s tire clearance fitting your bike. Be sure to check the correct generation for your specific make and model. If you go with a tire wider than the maximum width for your bike, you risk damaging the fork and frame.

On my own gravel rig, I recently bumped from 700x40mm tires to 700x45mm tires and noticed the difference immediately. I stuck with the same tire make and model—the Pirelli Cinturato H. The extra five millimeters of width immediately gave more comfort and traction on chunkier gravel and some local singletrack; even with the same tire tread. Five millimeters might not sound like a lot, but it added significant comfort while putting out rides longer than one hundred miles.

Wider tires are the right choice for many—even if you aren’t pushing your mileage into the triple digits. Recently I bumped up the tire width on my dad’s gravel bike. Adding wider tires to his bike (as well as a slightly thicker handlebar tape) leveled up his comfort level while riding. Whether you are taking your gravel bike on singletrack, chunky gravel, hundred-mile rides, or just want a little more comfort on your local lunch loop, go tubeless and bump up your tire width.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8880. What the Mythology Behind Tree Pose Reveals About Unlocking Your Inner Strength

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

Yoga Journal’s archives series is a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Tree Pose mythology first appeared in the January-February 1989 issue of Yoga Journal.

According to Joseph Campbell, the symbol of the tree in Indian mythology is deeply rooted in the pre-Aryan civilization of the Indus Valley, which flourished around 2000 B.C. In particular, one of the iconographic seals excavated earlier this century from the ruined city of Harappa shows a nude goddess standing in the branches of a sacred pipal tree, surrounded by female attendants and other supplicants engaged in a fertility ritual or sacrifice.

The motif of a tree-goddess sheltered in the boughs of a tree reappears in all subsequent periods of Indian art, whether Buddhist, Hindu, or Jain. Buddha himself attained enlightenment under a pipal tree, also known as the bodhi tree, or Tree of Wisdom, and early Buddhists shared with the more primitive fertility cult the popular belief that trees are divine beings with magical properties. Hence, at the early Buddhist stupas at Sanchi, figures of female tree guardians (yakshas) are given special prominence on the ornamental gateways leading to the egg-shaped monument.

The belief in the magical powers of trees and tree-spirits lingers on even today in rural India, as shown by the following anecdote from the early life of the Indian saint Nityananda. “He sometimes wore a loincloth, sometimes was nude, and lived a life of great simplicity;” writes biographer M. U. Hatengdi. “His home was in the rocks, caves, and forests. It was a familiar sight to see him perched on some tree top, standing stiff…”

“Crowds often gathered below the tree on which he stood, crowds that were mixed without regard for caste or creed. After a time, the Master would shower them with leaves: these leaves were greatly prized as medicine. One day a man who had lost his sight stood among the crowd beneath the tree…He continued pleading with the Master to restore his sight, explaining that as it was, he was not able to earn a living and so was a burden to his family. After a considerable time, Nityananda came to him and rubbed the man’s eves with leaves from the tree…On arising the next morning, the man was able to see and his sight remained restored.”

Nityananda was a saint who practiced the most severe of yogic austerities. During his early years, he ate food only when it was offered to him by others. He wore a loincloth not from modesty but at the insistence of his disciples. “He had a total disregard for the elements or for his nightly resting place…and would sit or lie down any place, from the doormat and dunghill to the cattleshed and even the dry lavatories, just to avoid crowds.” He believed that vairagya (total renunciation or absence of desire) was essential for his spiritual progress.

Vrksasana (Tree Pose) itself derives from a traditional act of austerity. According to scholar Georg Feuerstein, the practice of standing on one leg (known as Eka Pada Sthana) has been followed in India for at least two thousand years, and is referred to in the Mahabharata. In that great Indian epic, Pandu stands on one leg all day long in order to propitiate the god Indra (1.123), and Manu (the father of the human race) stands on one leg for a thousand years (III.187).

The most beautiful and dramatic representation of the practice of Eka Pada Sthana is found in the huge relief-sculpture at Mamallapuram, near Madras, dating from the seventh century A.D. Here, as Heinrich Zimmer writes, “A huge wall of rock, rising vertically in the fierce sunshine of southern India, has been converted into a prodigious masterpiece, teeming with hosts of gods, titans, genii, serpent princes, human beings, and animals, all converging towards a great cleft in the middle of the composition,” which represents the descent of the Ganges from heaven to earth.

This ancient Shaivite myth relates how the holy sage Bhagiratha performed great acts of austerity for a thousand years to compel the gods to let the heavenly river Ganges flow down to Earth, and how he then persuaded Lord Shiva to receive the full weight of the cataract on his head, lest the Earth be destroyed by the impact of the falling water. At Mamallapuram, we see the stoic figure of Bhagiratha standing on one leg, with his arms raised overhead in supplication, at the very moment when Shiva gives his consent and all the orders of creation burst into celebration at the flow of the sacred river.

The Descent of the Ganges as depicted at Mamallapuram can be interpreted as an allegory of our spiritual journey. Through clarity of purpose and unwavering dedication, the solitary yogi reaches a place of inner stillness—as quiet as the rock, as empty as the void.

But in that emptiness, like the emptiness that existed before creation, there is potential for a tremendous surge of psychic energy (the Ganges). This energy can overwhelm or corrupt the individual, as all power tends to corrupt, unless it is offered back to its divine source (Lord Shiva) and received as a sign of grace, not as confirmation of an inflated ego. When we surrender in this way, we begin to experience the vibratory movement of the world, and we know at last the joy of creation.

#8879. Clipless Pedals Can Feel Intimidating—Here Are Some Tips to Make Those First Clipless Rides Feel Smoother

Expert tips for cleat setup, pedal tension, and safe unclipping before your first ride.

When a rider switches from flat pedals to clipless pedals, they typically aren’t thinking about the differences of pedals like Shimano SPD or SPD-SL, Wahoo Speedplays, or egg-beater pedals. Many times, they haven’t heard of Time pedals or the different Assioma or Garmin models. The first thought many have is, “How do I get out of the pedal once I’m clipped in?”

Not all people considering the switch realize this—as contradictory as it sounds, clipless pedals refer to a pedal system where you are clipped into the pedal. If you aren’t familiar with the system, think about being clipped into a ski binding. Some pedal options offer different release settings—similar to how a DIN setting on a ski binding can be adjusted to offer different levels of force needed to release the ski boot from the binding.

Here we’ll dig into what clipless pedals are, how they can benefit you on your ride, tips for setting up your pedals and cleats, and tips for those daunting first few rides with your new pedals.

I have plenty of friends who swear by the saying, “flat pedals win medals.” However, there is a reason you’ll only see clipless pedals at world tour road races or on the majority of gravel bikes at your local gravel grinder. When you ride clipped in you end up using more of your leg musculature during each revolution of your pedal stroke.

In short, this means you’re typically more efficient when using clipless pedals compared to flat pedals. For clarity, you don’t need to ride clipless pedals to be a cyclist. But for those riders looking to take their riding to the next level, it’s worth giving them a try.

Because you’re literally attached to the pedal, you use not only your quads in the downstroke part of the revolution, but you also work your hamstrings, hip flexors, and glutes as you pull up. All of those muscles at work translate to more power while you’re riding, especially as you refine your pedaling technique. To get started, here’s your expert-backed guide to pedaling with clipless pedals—without falling over.

“Cleat placement is paramount,” says Issac Denham, owner of bike fitting studio Befitting Bicycles in Wayne, Pennsylvania. “Since incorrect cleat placement can lead to injuries, we suggest booking time with a bike fitter to place your cleats. Having a professional install your cleats also ensures that they won’t be installed improperly or even upside down.”

For those riders that want to try clipless pedals, but don’t want to jump into a precision fit, start with cleats in a neutral position. This means setting the cleats up in the middle of the slots in the shoe with the cleats relatively straight. Just make sure the left and right cleats are in roughly the same position—this will give you a good baseline moving forward.

It will take time doing the guess and check method for cleat placement, but this method gives you the chance to play around going clipless before you invest hundreds into a bike fit. If you start to develop pain after using clipless pedals, stop pedaling. This is likely due to cleat position and that is when it is time to see a local trusted shop for direction.

“Many clipless pedals have adjustable pedal tension. This is basically how hard the built-in spring holds the cleat in the pedal,” says Dan Chabonov, Bicycling test editor. “Setting this tension as low as possible means you need less force to clip in and out of the pedals and can make the learning process a little easier.”

While most clipless pedals already come set at the lowest tension setting from the manufacturer, you can also easily make the adjustment.

“Typically out of the box, pedals are set up with the least amount of release tension,” says Becky Quinn, former pro and bike fitter. “The pedal tensioner is on the rear of the pedal. There is a small 3mm bolt that requires a 3mm Allen wrench to adjust the tension. It can be turned counterclockwise to loosen the tension or clockwise to tighten it. There is a small window on the back of the pedal that has a small horizontal pin that moves up or down depending on which way you turn the tensioner.”

If you adjust the tension on your pedals, make sure you confirm that the pins are in the same place on both the left and right pedal, so the release tension is the same on both sides.

Practice does indeed make perfect when it comes to learning how to pedal with clipless pedals. The goal is to become so comfortable with the movements that they become part of your muscle memory, so you don’t have to look down at your foot or pedal for longer than a quick glance.

When you’re just starting out pedaling with clipless pedals, do it inside first. “Practicing indoors either on a trainer, or even leaned up against a wall, can be a great place to start where you don’t have to worry about falling down or looking silly,” says Denham.

When I ran a shop and was getting people set up on clipless pedals, I would suggest they get on the bike inside, ideally on a trainer or next to a wall to stabilize themselves, then put on a show or a movie. It sounds monotonous (and the people you live with might give you an odd look or two), but simply clip in, clip out, clip in, clip out, over and over. Do it looking down at your shoe, then when that’s comfortable practice doing it without looking down. Feel it out inside and you’ll be much better off when you head out the door.

To clip into your pedal, start with the pedal positioned at the bottom of the pedal stroke.

“Softly lift the front of the pedal with your toe to flip it over so that you can engage. Your toe will be slightly pointed downward. Slide your foot forward until the tongue of the cleat stops on the lip of the pedal,” Quinn explains. “Once you can’t slide your foot any further forward, continue to pedal forward and add pressure to the pedal. It will click in. Sometimes you will need to rotate your heel inward or outward at the 6 o’clock position to engage securely.”

Then it’s time to clip out: “In order to practice clipping out of your pedals, place one leg all the way down to the bottom of the pedal stroke (6 o’clock). Then, firmly rotate your heel outward. Be sure to not roll your ankle,” Quinn advises. “The motion should be similar to that of smashing a bug under the ball of your foot.”

If there is a single gem of advice we would love to pass on to every cyclist who has ever learned how to ride with clipless pedals, this would be it: Unclip the foot you intend to put down when you come to a stop before you come to a stop. “This is the most important piece of the puzzle,” says Quinn.

Once you unclip, “here is the most critical piece: Keep the unclipped foot on the pedal but continue to pedal a half stroke,” Quinn adds. “Once the foot that is still clipped in gets to the 6 o’clock position, coast and stand up. Your butt needs to get off the saddle. Continue to apply your rear brakes until you are almost at a stop. When you are about to come to a complete stop, apply your front brake and step down with the unclipped foot.”

Many cleat and pedal systems will follow a similar process with the general idea being: line up the cleat on the pedal and add downward force to clip in once the cleat is aligned.

Remember how we said switching to clipless pedals is a cycling rite of passage of sorts? Well, so is falling over as you’re learning. Practicing while riding on grass can make the falls a little easier, and falling with the proper technique (yes, there’s a technique for falling, too!) will lower your chances of serious injury.

“You will fall. We all have done it and it’s okay,” says Quinn. “Just remember that if you start to fall over, turn your buttocks so you land on it. It is the most padding we have on our bodies. Putting out an arm can break a wrist. You most likely will only get a bruise on your butt.”

The most important thing is not to get in your head, beat yourself up, or give up. Falling over at least a few times has happened to every single cyclist who rides with clipless pedals.

I’ll never forget one of my first rides with clipless pedals. I rolled over to the group in the parking lot overly confident, forgot I had to unclip my foot from the pedal, and slowly tipped over—still attached to the bike. It happens to everyone when you’re first making the switch, but some practice at home can make the transition a little less painful.

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

Determine which transferable currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, those are your fastest options — transfers to Flying Blue are instant. Log into your credit card portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards or americanexpress.com/rewards) and confirm you have at least 53,000 points available per person traveling in business class.

Initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

Return to FlyingBlue.com, log in with your miles now posted, and complete the award booking. Select the Promo Reward fare, confirm the passenger details, and review the fee breakdown carefully — verify that surcharges are eliminated or minimal. Pay the government taxes (typically $50–$150 transatlantic) with a credit card.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

By monitoring monthly promotions, maintaining transfer-ready points across multiple programs, and booking when your route appears at a discount, you can consistently fly lie-flat to European destinations for 50,000-62,000 miles. The fuel surcharges are a real cost to factor in, but even with that overhead, promo business class awards deliver 5-12 cents per mile in value. Set the monthly reminder and let the system work.

#8877. I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body. (Photo: Getty Images)

I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace. I nailed it, but couldn’t help thinking it felt harder than it should have.

“It’s just nerves,” I told myself. “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”

The next day, I felt exhausted, and my ribs were sore and tender to the touch. I started to wonder if I’d pulled a muscle in my rib cage while breathing heavily during my training run. I, of course, turned to Google. “Ribs sore from running.” “Ribs hurt after running.” Most of the posts advised that I’d feel better in a day.

But I didn’t feel better the next day. Instead, I noticed a small pink mark on my stomach, and now my ribs felt both sore and tingly. My Google searches grew more alarming: I could have shingles.

I scheduled an appointment for that same day, and my doctor confirmed it. She took one look at me and said, “I’m so sorry, you have shingles.”

Shingles is a painful viral infection that looks like a terrible rash and usually involves nerve pain that can last for months. The virus comes from dormant chickenpox in your body that can reappear when you’re stressed.

My doctor asked about stressors in my life. “I haven’t really been that stressed,” I promised, saying my family life and my career were extremely smooth. “But I have been training for a marathon,” I said.

“That could do it,” she told me. “Your body is clearly telling you that you were pushing too hard.”

I’m 43, younger than the typical shingles patient, but I’m part of an unfortunate trend. Shingles cases are on the rise and the biggest increase is among people in their 30s and 40s. One study found overall shingles cases nearly doubled between 2005 and 2021. Another found cases in Americans under 50 quadrupled from the late 1940s to 2000, and are still going up, according to data from the CDC.

A big reason for the increase among millennials is that we fall into a gap: 50 and up, and you can get the shingles vaccine; 30 and under, and you’ve had the chickenpox vaccine, which will make getting shingles way less likely.

That age range is also most common among marathoners, so my big question was whether running, especially hard training, can give you shingles. Unfortunately, that specific question hasn’t been extensively studied, so there’s no clear-cut answer. But doctors are drawing correlations between heavy training and whether it decreases the body’s immunity overall.

There’s research that shows immunity dips after heavy training, says David Nieman, DrPH, FACSM, director of the Human Performance Laboratory at Appalachian State University. He pointed to a study involving mice and the herpes virus.

“When you infected the mice and then forced them to run to exhaustion, there was a higher mortality rate in those mice than mice that just did moderate activity and rested,” he says. “Moderate activity actually helped a little bit, but by far the really bad response was in the mice that ran to exhaustion.”

In another study, researchers gave horses the flu and then ran them really hard. Those horses developed a longer-lasting, more intense bout of the flu compared to the horses who were infected but didn’t run hard, he said.

But Nieman and other researchers agree that moderate exercise can actually boost your immunity. James Turner, a professor at the Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation Sciences school at the University of Birmingham, says it’s far more common that inadequate sleep, diet and psychological stress suppress immunity than exercise, even really hard training.

“Research on both prolonged exercise and marathon running shows that antibody responses are not suppressed and might actually be higher,” he says.

Meanwhile, Dr. William Schaffner, MD, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health who’s an expert in shingles, says it’s too soon to say definitely that lots of stress leads to the virus. He points out there’s no evidence that soldiers in combat or police and firefighters have an increased risk of shingles.

“When people get a shingles episode, there is a tendency to look back in their lives to see if there might be some sort of inciting event or stressful event and there’s a tendency to link the two,” he says. “But the question is, is that just coincidence because there’s a lot of stress in life, or was it a causal relationship? I think we’ll still have to say that hasn’t been definitively settled.”

Instead, for Schaffner, the likeliest explanation for the increase in shingles is because the chickenpox vaccine is decreasing our exposure to chickenpox. We used to all get chickenpox as children, and so the virus was more common in the wild. That gave our immune systems a boost. Now that there’s a vaccine, that isn’t happening, which means we may be more likely to get shingles, he said.

Whether my running caused my shingles or not, as soon as I had my diagnosis, my next questions were about my marathon. My doctor said my symptoms would likely peak in four days to a week, and so it still seemed possible I would be ready for race day. I rushed out to get a seven-day course of Valtrex—if you start an antiviral treatment quickly enough, it can stop the spread of the shingles rash.

But as the week passed and the rash grew along my rib cage to my back, it only continued to feel worse. I was achy everywhere, and my ribs felt like they were constantly being stabbed with tiny needles. A week later, I called it and canceled my marathon plans, harboring a hope that within a few weeks I would be better and could rebound to run my BQ.

What I did next probably hurt my cause rather than helped it. As soon as I felt a bit better, I would go out and do a race-pace run, which would give me a painful setback that lasted for several days. This likely was making my bout with the virus longer, Nieman says.

He reminded me of the mice who were running to exhaustion and not getting well. The mice really needed to keep it low-key to get an immune boost, not drain.

“If they did 30 minutes of something like a brisk walk equivalent, that would help a little bit,” he says.

My conversation with him sounded like a negotiation.

“I’m mostly feeling better, but I still sometimes have sensations in my ribs, so do I still need to take it easy?” I asked.

“I have a lot of empathy. I know you don’t want to hear it,” he said gently. Nieman has run 58 marathons himself, so he knows the feeling. “You don’t want anybody telling you not to run, but this is where you’ve got to be really, really careful and just bide your time and slowly get back into it once you feel better.”

His advice to runners: listen to your body and don’t push yourself. That’s not an easy metric for marathoners who are used to pushing beyond what feels comfortable, but Nieman says exhaustion can exacerbate the nerve pain and make it all last much longer.

Other things to keep in mind: it’s possible that sunburns can impede your immune system, so cover up once you’re back out and running, says Jennifer Moffat, a SUNY microbiology and immunology professor and expert on chickenpox and shingles.

And, Moffat says, while you still have a rash, you’re contagious and can spread the virus to others through contact. If you’re at the gym or anywhere you might touch other people, you should have the rash fully covered.

She also advises keeping an eye on the other stresses around marathons, like not eating enough, not sleeping enough, and the mental stress around races.

“The anticipation, logistics, travel hassles, changes in environment and food, rivalries with other competitors, jet lag, time away from family, the cost can become overwhelming,” she says. “Getting to the starting line of a marathon is much more than showing up with your shoes tied.”

In fact, she says, it’s common for people to come down with other viral infections right before a race (the dreaded taper cold).

As for me, two months after my rash first appeared, I finally truly threw in the towel. I couldn’t keep up any kind of marathon training without making myself feel worse, so I switched to low-effort maintenance running and decided my BQ would have to come next year.

#8875. The Benefits of Biking for Seniors, Including the Mental and Physical Payoffs

You might find a few surprising advantages of cycling on this list.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

We know you think we’re going to tell you all the ways cycling improves your heart health and muscle strength—and it does, but guess what? According to a 2023 scoping review in Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, studies show that when older adults cycle regularly, their happiness improves and they are better able to maintain their quality of life.

In fact, even though many people associate aging with physical and mental declines, regular exercise—like a daily bike ride—can help slow or even reverse some of these effects.

“Regular physical activity helps seniors maintain good health, improve their quality of life, and increase their overall well-being,” Mary Sabat, MS, RDN, a personal trainer and dietitian in Georgia tells Bicycling. “It can enhance physical strength, flexibility, and endurance, making it easier to perform daily activities and maintain independence.”

Those are just few reasons why biking for seniors is so great—but here are all the advantages you gain when you start pedaling regularly.

While almost forms of physical activity improve physical and mental health, cycling is particularly well-suited for those in their golden years due to its accessibility. After all, cycling is easy on the joints, even for those with joint pain or injuries. “It can be tailored to individual fitness levels and adjusted to accommodate different abilities and physical limitations, too,” says Sabat. “Recumbent bikes, trikes, or electric-assist bicycles can be used to make cycling more accessible for those with mobility challenges or balance issues.”

Robert Patterson, a cyclist and lawyer, has been cycling for more than 40 years. He points out all the obvious aerobic and strength-building gains he’s enjoyed over the years, but also the psychological benefits. “Cycling also benefits my mental health. My attitude and overall focus are always improved by being on the bike,” he says.

Here are nine reasons, according to the experts, for you to saddle up and hit the road (or the gym) for a ride.

Aerobic exercise is the key to managing heart health. Because the heart is a muscle, it needs to be exercised on a regular basis to maintain its strength and optimal function. And because the heart and lungs work together with the venous system to deliver oxygenated blood to your muscles, any exercise that increases your heart rate and breath rate for an extended period of time will help improve your heart health and overall cardiovascular function.

Plus, as anyone who has ever pushed the pedals and pumped through a 20- or 30-minute bike ride knows, cycling will definitely get your heart rate up. The repetitive cycling motion qualifies as a moderate to intense form of aerobic exercise that you can easily adapt to your personal fitness level. This means that even if you haven’t exercised in years, by starting at a lower intensity and making adjustments to your workouts based on your heart rate, you can safely and effectively add cycling to your weekly routine.

“As individuals age, the risk of heart disease increases,” says Sabat. “Cycling is a low-impact aerobic exercise that helps improve cardiovascular fitness, strengthens the heart muscle, and enhances blood circulation. It can lower the risk of heart attacks, strokes, and high blood pressure, thereby promoting a healthy heart.”

In fact, a series of two 2019 review studies (part 1 and part 2) published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that all forms of cycling reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and also reduced the risk factor profile for poor heart health—meaning that cyclists had better body composition stats, blood lipid profiles, cardiorespiratory fitness levels, and more time spent exercising. All of these together help mitigate the risk for developing heart disease.

You can combat practically any chronic condition, including heart disease, along with type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and cancer with a regular ride. Exercise helps keep the blood flowing, systems moving, and cells turning over in a way that promotes overall health. For instance, high-intensity exercise (and high-intensity cycling, specifically) helps improve blood glucose response, according to research, which may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.

Even in the case of cancer, participating in a regular cycling routine has been shown to reduce the risk. For example, May 2020 study published in The Lancet found an association between participating in a daily bike commute and a 16 percent decrease in cancer mortality and an 11 percent decrease in cancer incidence.

“By incorporating a ride here and there into their routine, seniors can reduce the risk of chronic conditions. These conditions can be debilitating, but with regular exercise, seniors can take proactive steps toward prevention and management,” Josh Weight, a certified sports physiotherapist and the director of Gravity Physio in Australia tells Bicycling.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience regular joint pain associated with arthritis or previous injuries. In fact, according to the National Poll on Healthy Aging, about 70 percent of older adults report current joint pain. This can be exacerbated by extended periods spent sitting, or simply not moving around much, as sedentary behavior is directly associated with increased incidences of knee and other joint pain.

While on the surface this may not seem like a big deal, it can lead to a cascading series of events where joint pain or arthritis contributes to a reduced range of motion. This reduced range of motion can influence balance, coordination, and even the ability to perform everyday tasks. These issues can also contribute to a reduced quality of life and even an increased risk of falls. As such, any activity that can be done without contributing to joint pain while protecting and strengthening the structures that help stabilize the joints (muscles, tendons, and ligaments) is an important undertaking for older adults’ overall health and well-being.

“Cycling is a low-impact activity that puts minimal stress on the joints, making it an excellent option for individuals with joint-related issues. It provides a cardiovascular workout without placing excessive strain on the knees, hips, or ankles,” Sabat says.

Whether done on an indoor bike or a more traditional road or mountain bike, one thing’s for sure: Cycling works the legs. It takes muscular strength, power, and endurance to keep the pedals moving, especially when climbing a hill or ramping up the resistance. But it’s not just the legs and glutes that benefit—cycling can help build strength in the shoulders, upper back, and core, as well.

Of course, you may not be looking to build massive quads as one of your long-term fitness goals, but developing muscular strength isn’t just about looking strong—it’s about maintaining your quality of life.

Research estimates muscle mass begins to decline by 3 to 8 percent every decade following your 30th birthday, with those rates increasing further once you hit 60. This age-related muscular decline over time makes it more challenging to continue doing everyday activities like climbing stairs or carrying groceries. It’s important to participate in exercises, like cycling, that will help maintain or build muscle mass over time to safeguard your ability to perform these daily activities.

In fact, according to a 2015 review study published in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity, adults over 70 years of age experienced increased muscular strength and power when participating in a cycling exercise program at least three times a week for 12 to 16 weeks. This data flies in the face of anyone who believes they can’t develop muscle or strength as they age—it’s not only possible, it’s critical to overall health and functional ability.

One area in which cycling can be particularly beneficial is balance and coordination. This has ties to muscular strength, as strong, trained muscles tend to perform and react more quickly to stimuli than those that aren’t worked regularly. However, it also has to do with the unique requirements of cycling itself.

“Cycling requires balance and coordination to stay upright and navigate,” says Andrew White, a personal trainer and owner of Garage Gym Pro. “This can be especially beneficial for seniors as these abilities tend to decline with age, increasing the risk of falls and injuries.”

This isn’t just conjecture—a 2018 prospective study published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity found that older adults (between the ages of 65 and 85) who cycled daily had better balance, a faster pace while walking, and better self-reported lower-extremity function compared to those who didn’t bike regularly. Based on this study, it appears that cycling helps preserve balance and coordination which contributes to lower-body function that can help prevent falls.

Just as muscle mass tends to decline with age, an associated change in body composition takes place, which often leads to increased weight gain. And as weight creeps up, so do the risks for heart disease and chronic illness, particularly in populations considered obese.

Cycling and other forms of exercise can help keep weight and other disease risk factors in check. This is partly due to the muscle-protective benefits exercise offers, but also due to the increased calorie burn that occurs during moderate- to high-intensity exercise like cycling.

“Cycling can help seniors maintain a healthy body weight, reduce excess body fat, and prevent obesity-related health issues,” Sabat emphasizes.

It’s not unusual for seniors to experience social isolation that can contribute to physical and mental health decline. Changes in health, mobility, or driving status can keep seniors alone at home. This is unfortunate because strong social connections are positively associated with longevity.

Cycling can provide seniors with an accessible way to get out and about, and to also engage with other people of all ages. “Cycling can be an enjoyable and social activity for seniors. Exploring outdoor trails, participating in group rides, or engaging in community cycling events can foster a sense of camaraderie and connection with others,” says Weight.

And for seniors who want to start cycling, but don’t know how, community cycling clubs offer a great way to learn and connect at the same time.

In addition to the benefits of social interaction, cycling can boost mental health in a number of ways, especially if you’re riding your bike outside. “Cycling outdoors provides an opportunity to connect with nature, which can be therapeutic and stress-relieving,” says White.

In fact, according to a 2022 study published in the Journal of Affective Disorders, individuals who participated in outdoor cycling (or other outdoor activities like walking, jogging, or team sports), were less likely to experience depression than those who were inactive. Likewise, there’s evidence that even a single outdoor exercise session (like cycling) can impact mood, more than indoor exercise equivalents.

Even in the absence of an outdoor setting, physical activity as a whole is good for mental health. “Regular exercise releases endorphins which can elevate mood and reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression,” Sabat explains.

One final benefit of cycling for seniors: It can support cognitive function. “Studies have shown that physical activity can have positive effects on cognition and may help reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia in older adults. Exercise promotes better blood flow to the brain, stimulates the release of hormones that support brain health, and improves memory and attention,” Sabat shares.

Laura Williams, M.S., ACSM EP-C holds a master's degree in exercise and sport science and is a certified exercise physiologist through the American College of Sports Medicine. She also holds sports nutritionist, youth fitness, sports conditioning, and behavioral change specialist certifications through the American Council on Exercise. She has been writing on health, fitness, and wellness for 12 years, with bylines appearing online and in print for Men's Health, Healthline, Verywell Fit, The Healthy, Giddy, Thrillist, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and Runner's World. After losing her first husband to cancer in 2018, she moved to Costa Rica to use surfing, beach running, and horseback riding as part of her healing process. There, she met her current husband, had her son, and now splits time between Texas and Costa Rica.

#8872. Running Faster vs Running Longer: Which Should I Focus On First?

Both are key components of a smart training plan—but how you prioritize each one depends on your goal.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Runners have two main paths to choose from when it comes to running goals: run faster or run longer. Both will make you a stronger, fitter athlete—but training for one looks a little different than the other.

Should you focus on running faster to build power and strength, or should you go the distance to test your physical and mental stamina? There’s no right or wrong answer, but understanding the differences between these two approaches can help you make the most of your training.

Like so many questions in running, the answer depends on your current fitness level and your goals. But for most new runners, it’s generally better to start training to run longer.

“I think sometimes runners are quick to jump into trying to run all-out, whatever their goal race is, instead of just working toward being able to feel okay completing the distance first,” says Ruth Atkinson, VDOT-certified McKirdy Trained running coach based in Dallas. That means you probably want to think about the distance you want to cover first, whether you’re vying for your first 5K or have some shorter distances under your belt and are considering a half marathon or marathon.

There’s a saying in running: Start where you are. In other words, don’t put a time goal on a race when you start training. Instead, start training, see how your fitness improves as you get closer to race day, then set a time goal. Some research even indicates that building up your easy mileage will lead to better long-distance run performance compared to focusing on speed workouts: A study published in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research in 2021, involving 84 male runners, found a correlation between volume of easy runs—not tempo runs, not interval training—with world-class long-distance running performance scores.

One of the most important benefits of gradually increasing your volume is training your tendons, ligaments, joints, and bones to withstand the repetitive impact of running without overtaxing them, which might lead to overuse injuries. “Starting with distance gives your body a chance to catch up to the muscular capacity you need to develop to stay healthy and move forward,” says New York-based Nike running coach Rebeka Stowe. It’s generally easier and faster for beginners to build aerobic capacity compared to muscle strength, so you have to give your muscles enough time to build that strength.

Once you have a solid aerobic base—the foundational fitness you need to sustain your training—you could shift to more of a speed focus.

Not all running has the same effects on your body. When you’re training for distance, most miles will be at a low-intensity effort. (When it comes to rate of perceived exertion, this would be about a 4 out of 10 effort, or lower, with 10 being all out.) That easy, conversational pace may not feel challenging—although it will help you develop mental toughness by teaching you how to push through fatigue and discomfort as the miles add up—but it’s stimulating important physiological adaptations that will improve your performance at faster paces.

For starters, you’re improving your cardiovascular capabilities. “Your heart is a muscle,” says Stowe. “By running at a slower pace, you’re building that muscle’s capacity to pump blood to the rest of your body so it can handle higher intensity work later.” As your heart’s stroke volume increases with training, it beats less frequently to supply the same amount of blood to the body—meaning it’s becoming more efficient.

Slower runs also train your slow twitch (type I) muscle fibers, which allow you to sustain your pace over longer distances. These muscle fibers have a higher density of mitochondria and greater capillary density, both of which help you maintain your energy level.

In fact, aerobic exercise increases the number of mitochondria in your cells, according to research published in the American Journal of Physiology—Endocrinology and Metabolism, and can increase capillary density by more than 25 percent, an older study in Journal of Atherosclerosis and Thrombosis found. The more mitochondria you have, the more energy you can produce, and the greater your capillary density, the better blood flow to your working muscles. Both of those benefits translate to improved performance at faster speeds.

Speed work, on the other hand, acts almost like strength training, developing your muscles as you work against increased ground reaction forces.

“Challenging your body to run at a faster pace is going to call on more muscle fibers,” says Stowe. In this case, you’re working fast twitch (type II) muscle fibers, which are best suited for short, explosive efforts. These fast-twitch fibers also come into play at the end of a race for your finishing kick.

Picking up the pace also improves your cardiovascular capacity, but in a different way than easy running. Working at a higher intensity increases your VO2 max, “the maximum amount of oxygen that your body can use during exercise,” explains Atkinson. “The more you practice running at this pace, the easier it will be to translate that into holding faster paces for longer periods of time.”

Training for speed will also improve your lactate threshold—the intensity level at which lactate accumulates in the blood faster than you can remove it, leading to fatigue—so you can improve your endurance at faster paces.

To gain these benefits, you can base the pace needed off of your 5K time. If you don’t know your race pace for that distance, you can just go out and run 3.1 miles as hard as you can—it should be an 8 or 9 effort level on a scale of 1 to 10. VO2 max pace is a bit faster than 5K pace, while lactate threshold pace is a bit slower than 5K pace. (Keep in mind speed workouts aren’t always built around just these specific paces. A good training plan will have you holding speeds from mile pace or faster all the way up to marathon pace and slower, depending on your goals.)

Speed training also positively affects the density and structure of your bones, and may potentially prevent age-related bone loss, according to a research review published in 2023 in Sechenov Medical Journal—further bulletproofing your body against overuse injuries.

Another benefit of speed training: It requires a lot less time than building volume, which helps runners who are balancing training with other obligations.

When you train for distance, your workouts will focus on gradually building up the time or mileage you run. Long runs at a conversational pace will be the cornerstone of your plan, along with some moderate-intensity runs and recovery days.

“If you’re running four days a week, you’d have one day of speed and three easy days with higher volume, including a long run,” says Atkinson. Your speed workout would typically include longer intervals at goal pace, adds Stowe. “You should do a good majority of your speed volume at half marathon or marathon pace so that you become more efficient—and more comfortable—holding that pace,” she explains.

The goal, when you’re training to run longer, is to improve your aerobic endurance and teach your body to handle the physical demands of extended activity. As you progress, you’ll increase your weekly mileage to build the stamina you need to go the distance.

Training for speed generally aims to improve your pace over shorter distances. You might run shorter, more intense workouts but with more recovery time between efforts. Let’s say you’re training for a fast 5K race: “You would ease into it by doing 200-meter and 400-meter reps at goal 5K pace, because you’re not going to be able to sustain that pace over longer distances yet,” says Stowe. “As your training continues, you progress to 800s, mile repeats, even 2K repeats—you can work your way up to holding that goal pace in smaller chunks.”

If you’re still running four days a week, your training plan might include three easy runs and a speed workout, or two days with speed and two that are easy, Atkinson says. Your focus will be on maximizing your cardiovascular capacity, running form, and the ability to push your body to sustain those faster efforts. “The quality of your workouts will be a little bit harder, which means the quantity will be a little bit less to keep everything balanced,” she explains.

A good training plan incorporates speed and volume, because your body has different energy systems that respond to different stimuli.

“Think of it like a recipe,” says Stowe. “If you’re supposed to mix salt and sugar into something but you forget to do one, you’re not going to get the desired outcome. The taste is going to be off, right? If you want to optimize your outcome, you have to have speed and volume as part of your training, so you’re developing all of your systems.”

Starting with distance will help you build the foundation you need to develop speed. “If you spend a dedicated amount of time increasing your volume, you’re going to build a pretty robust aerobic system,” says Atkinson. “When you add speed work to that, you’re learning how to turn your legs over faster and become more efficient at faster paces. Then, you have the aerobic system in place to be able to hold the faster paces you can now run.”

For most runners, it’s a cycle. You may spend four to six months training for distance, and then two to four months working on speed; then you layer endurance back in and combine the two.

Both speed and distance training have their own set of benefits, and you can always mix and match, choosing what fits your current goals and lifestyle. Whether you’re training to run faster or longer, each step will bring you closer to becoming the strongest version of yourself.

#8871. Great Hydration is About More than Just Electrolytes

Harmless Harvest shelf-stable coconut water. (Photo: Harmless Harvest)

Hydration comes up a lot when we talk about performance and recovery. Are you drinking enough water? Are you getting enough electrolytes? Are you tracking your fluid intake? It can be overwhelming to keep tabs of every statistic and ounce, but the hype around hydration isn’t without cause. Hydration is not only an essential component of pre-, mid- and post-workout performance. It’s an essential part of everyday life.

Electrolytes are a particular point of focus among performance athletes. Electrolytes are the minerals that help maintain the balance of fluids inside and outside your body’s cells. This is a critical consideration when it comes to high-exertion workouts where you’re losing lots of fluids through sweat.

The market is more saturated (pun intended) than ever with tablets, powders and pouches galore to help you optimize and maximize your electrolyte intake. But hydration doesn’t have to be as complicated as all that—and the conversation surrounding electrolytes doesn’t have to be reserved for elite athletes. It can be an everyday consideration for your morning walk, a quick out-and-back hike, or your daily commute to the office. And it all starts with a single coconut.

That’s the mission behind Harmless Harvest, a California-based company championing the coconut, turning a remarkable fruit into a remarkable lineup of products. It’s new pantry-friendly coconut water contains one ingredient: 100% coconut water with no added sugar or preservatives. The simplicity of their products ladder up to the simplicity of the brand’s philosophy—that great taste, quality ingredients, and premium tasting hydration should be for everyone to enjoy. Uncomplicated hydration doesn’t have to be a statistic for you to overanalyze—it can be an intentional and enjoyable part of your everyday life.

So what’s so great about a simple bottle of coconut water? Well, it’s just that: the simplicity. All on its own, coconut water delivers naturally occurring electrolytes, including potassium, to support everyday hydration. Unlike the formulated hydration drinks, tablets and powders that rely on added electrolytes, coconut water provides those muscle-supporting, fluid-balancing minerals into every bottle of Harmless Harvest coconut water naturally. Every bottle is made with a single ingredient with that naturally sweet coconut taste that’s completely delicious and refreshing.

From your pantry to wherever the day takes you, Harmless Harvest’s newest coconut water makes it easier than ever to keep great-tasting hydration close at hand. With no refrigeration required, you can keep bottles at room temperature until you’re ready to enjoy. Grab a bottle on the way to yoga, before a big day on the slopes, or just on the way to work. And unlike the traditional flash pasteurization commonly used by beverage producers, Harmless Harvest’s optimized heat treatment and micro-filtration preserves the fruit’s natural sweetness and nutrients, so you’re getting everything the mighty coconut has to offer.

Another question you might be asking is why is Harmless Harvest’s coconut water pink? Harmless Harvest’s commitment to sustainability and environmentally conscious practices extends beyond the bottle, too. The brand works with coconut growers in Thailand to source ethically farmed, non-GMO coconuts and also invests in initiatives that support farmers and their communities. These conscientious business practices aim to bring you products that you can sip with peace of mind.
