#8859. All the Brooks Running Shoes and Apparel on Sale Now for Black Friday

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Many of us started running in a Brooks trainer, and with Black Friday deals in full swing, you can stock up on must-have Brooks gear or gift that friend you’re pushing to run their first 5K.

What makes Brooks trainers so popular? Their plush, slipper-like fit and comfy cushioning put them at the center of a Venn diagram where dad shoes and serious runner trainers converge.

Several top-rated models, like the Adrenaline GTS 25, are on sale at brooksrunning.com and sites like REI and Amazon. But sizes and colors are limited, so stock up now before they’re gone for good!

We’ve also included discounted Brooks apparel, so you can run in Brooks from head to toe all winter long.

Brooks Running Sale | REI Brooks Running Sale

The stability counterpart to the Ghost 18, the Adrenaline GTS is the shoe many of us ran in when we fell in love with running. The 25th iteration is the lightest yet, with a foamy midsole, the brand’s DNA Loft v3, to absorb shock and provide soft landings. The guide rails system is Brooks’s unobtrusive stability tech for neutral runners and overpronators alike. Dense foam on the medial and lateral sides acts as bumpers to help align your knee and ankle.

“This is a fantastic shoe,” said tester Chris Garges, an overpronator and heel striker. “I’ve run in every model Adrenaline dating back to the Adrenaline 3, and this is by far the best shoe in the series. I loved everything from the fit to the ride to the cushioning.”

Brooks wanted to change what we should expect when running in a max-cushioned trainer. “We noticed that for some people, they would start running in a neutral shoe and then their body would work extra. So the internal cost was actually increasing,” said Brooks Footwear PLM and BlueLine Director Nikhil Jain.

The team set out to create a shoe that would cut that internal cost. The Glycerin Flex has a decoupled heel and Flex Zone; these components allow your foot to flex naturally instead of working against a stiff, beefy platform.

“Testing the Brooks Glycerin Flex was a novel experience for me on multiple fronts,” said Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Not only was this the first Brooks running shoe I’ve ever run in, but it was also the first hyperflexible shoe that I have ever seen—and overall, it was a positive experience. The Glycerin Flex combines the benefits of a daily trainer that allows your feet to work and get stronger with the comfort and protection of a maximalist shoe.”

We like the Glycerin Max 2 for run/walking and recovery days. The shoe has 45 mm of DNA Tuned foam in the heel and a 6 mm offset. Its beefiness was off-putting for some, especially for runners hoping to get in some tempo work on their long runs. But testers said the cushioning was extremely comfy on slow days.

“I loved how comfortable the sneaker was. I instantly felt supported and it felt like I was walking on a bouncy pillow,” said wear-tester Steph Norman. “This sneaker would be great for easy/long miles where you do not have to worry about your feet hurting.”

The popular Brooks Ghost hits the trails. The shoe is outfitted for going off-road with 3 mm lugs on the TrailTack rubber outsole.

Our tester, David Hinkl, appreciated how the shoe protected his feet on gnarly surfaces. “The best part of the shoe for me was the sole,” he said. “It was beefy enough to prevent sharp rocks and pointy things from getting to my feet. Training is more fun when I don’t have to tiptoe across the trail.”

The Canopy is iconic. Despite the curtains of rain, monstrous winds, and cold temps, Des Linden was the first American woman to win the 2018 Boston Marathon after 33 years. And she wore the Canopy Jacket. This version of the Canopy (the original is also on sale with 30 percent off) can be packed into a little pouch that’s easy to store in the depths of an overpacked duffel.

The High Point keeps out the rain without overheating. Venting in the back allows airflow, while waterproof fabric and sealed inner seams keep you from getting soaked during a downpour. The jacket also packs down into a pocket.

These joggers are the softest joggers we’ve tested. They’re great for warmups, cooldowns, and traveling. I should know—I trekked Japan after running the Tokyo Marathon in these.

#8857. Runners of All Fitness Levels Benefit From the Run/Walk Method. Here’s How to Use It to Pace Smarter and Race Faster.

Think you’re too advanced for the run/walk method? Think again.

Many experienced runners often assume that the run/walk method is only suitable for beginners. There’s no way it could help you reach your goals or allow you to run faster paces, right? In reality, it could be the missing piece of your training and racing plan.

Andrea Dell, an RRCA-certified run coach based in Charlotte, North Carolina, believes run/walk has a place in your training—no matter your fitness level or your goals. In fact, she includes some form of the run/walk method in all her runners’ training, because it’s a tried-and-true strategy for tackling longer distances, recovering more efficiently, and even dropping minutes from your marathon time.

So whether you’re a couch-to-5K runner, a first-time marathoner, or a seasoned athlete, Dell lays out all the ways run/walk can improve your training and how to make the most of the method.

If you’re a first-time runner or someone following a couch-to-5K training plan, your run/walk intervals might look like 30 seconds of running followed by a 60-second walk interval.

If you’re a first-time marathoner or a more advanced runner, however, you might run for four minutes followed by 30-second walks. More advanced runners or those going for long distances might also use run/walk intervals during workouts such as Yasso 800s. To do it, run 800 meters at the prescribed pace, but instead of jogging between efforts, walk briskly to recover. This walk interval should be double the amount of time of the hard effort, Dell says.

While run/walk intervals can serve as a speed workout hack to help you get faster and pace more evenly (more on that below), they can improve your running in other ways, too. For example, try 90-second run intervals and 30-second walks for extra recovery on an easy run the day after a long run. This reduces the overall stress of the effort, but still gets your legs turning over so you can move through any soreness without stiffening up, Dell explains.

You can also use run/walk intervals during your weekend long runs to help you conquer the distance.

If you want to run farther distances, “run/walk keeps your heart rate low for long enough that you can maintain pace for a lot longer than you would expect,” says Dell. This makes it a lot more manageable to tackle a half or full marathon for the first time (or if you’re racing the distance again after a long time away).

Dell tells runners that if they can run six continuous miles, they’re capable of completing nine miles using run/walk intervals because the walk breaks reduce the overall intensity and effort of the run. This can provide a smoother transition to the half marathon for runners who just worked up to training for a 5K or 10K.

Run/walk intervals can also help runners increase their long-run distance during half or full marathon training, Dell says. “I’ve had athletes who either could not get over the half marathon distance to save their lives or blew up on runs multiple weeks in a row,” she says, but run/walk helped fix that.

If you tend to “bonk” around mile 13 of a 15-mile long run, using run/walk intervals for the first five miles will help keep your heart rate down longer so you can maintain your pace and build patience with the run. Then, you’ll be in a better position to complete all 15 miles without hitting the wall, Dell explains.

Runners who are just beginning to incorporate interval workouts into their training might struggle to switch between hard and easy paces. “Some people don’t know how to run at different paces. They only know their one pace and that’s kind of it,” says Dell. “So when they get into speedwork, their heart rates just spike so quickly because they’re not used to those faster paces yet.”

If you’re used to training at more intense speeds, but you struggle to stay in zone 2 on easy runs, run/walk can help you keep your pace and your heart rate down. Maintaining 30-second walk breaks and the run interval that works best for you (anywhere from 60 seconds to six minutes, depending on your fitness level and speed) will help keep your heart rate in the right easy zone.

Run/walk intervals can also help speed up recovery, Dell adds. When you’re doing speedwork, you can reduce your injury risk and recover faster by walking—instead of jogging—between efforts.

A lot of the time, runners tend to unknowingly speed up during the jog intervals, which leads to not fully recovering between each effort. That makes them more likely to experience cumulative fatigue, she explains. “This is really important for people who are doing half or full marathons for the first time, because they are just constantly building mileage,” and more work requires more recovery, she says.

Better quality recovery intervals mean better quality speed intervals, too. And walking instead of jogging in between your faster efforts allows you to push harder, both mentally and physically, Dell explains.

“Mentally, you’ll have an easier time pushing hard if you know there’s a true walk break coming. You’ll also have more leg turnover, feel speedier, and get your heart rate down [during the working sets],” Dell says.

Run/walk is also a great tool for splitting up an otherwise monotonous maintenance run, Dell explains. “Maybe it’s a Monday, or it’s cold outside, and you just don’t want to go for your run,” she says. Run/walk intervals not only help you keep your easy pace truly easy, but they also remove the mental pressure of trying to maintain one pace for the entire run.

“It’s mindless: You follow your watch’s beeps [for when to walk and run] and you can just listen to your music. Then all of a sudden, you’ve got your four miles done while leaving your analytical brain out of it,” Dell adds.

Every runner needs to learn how to switch gears between running and brisk walking on marathon race day, whether that’s to grab gels or water, navigate crowded courses, or keep moving if you hit the wall in the later miles, Dell says. “If you’re running the New York City Marathon and all of a sudden you blow up at mile 18 going up some of the bridges, it’s a good idea to learn how to [slow down] and restart your body at any point,” she explains.

Beginner marathoners and seasoned athletes alike can only benefit from adding run/walk to their training schedule. And who knows? You might like it so much, you run/walk an entire race and PR.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8856. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Yay! I’m thrilled to read about a city of the future, and I look forward to hearing more when you spend the winter there. I gave them my email address so I could hear more in the future.

Mr. Money Mustache April 8, 2023, 6:43 pm

Believe it or not, this is not a big problem in Phoenix and most other big desert cities. They have plenty of water for domestic use. It’s agriculture that uses the lion’s share of fresh water – about 80% of it in the Western US. Then our other industrial uses, then our houses are down near the bottom.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. A single patch of lawn watered in the desert will use more than an entire household, so as soon as you remove that you have made the whole city more sustainable.

Alas, here in the Denver area the lawn with the big sprinkler system still seems to be in style, despite the fact that our summer climate very closely resembles a real desert. The grass will die within a week or two if you leave it unwatered, which I think would be a great idea in most cases. There’s lots of cool stuff you can do with river rocks and native flowers and Yucca plants that takes almost no water to sustain!

Very accurate, MMM! I’ve got a good friend who works for whatever they call the “water” department of the city of Mesa (right next to Tempe), and whenever I bring up the metro Phoenix water supply issue, he basically says “we’ll be fine, but things will have to change with respect to agriculture in the southwest and lawns/golf courses”.

I worried about it for years, but a bit of research and several articles in the NYT helped calm me down. Here’s one: https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/05/22/climate/colorado-river-water.html .

TLDR: We’re going to have to continue to evolve what we raise/grow/eat to balance the demands on our planet, especially considering climate change (to the surprise of practically nobody reading MMM)

(In fact, it’s hard to find anyplace to live that isn’t a ten-minute walk from a grocery store and a few other amenities, such as hair stylists, cafes, restaurants, etc.) We’ve also been expanding our bike lanes, car sharing options, and car-free zones. Other European cities are making similar improvements on what were generally already more pedestrian- and bike-friendly urban plans. I hope that this project works well in Tempe and that more U.S. cities get on board.

I would say Vancouver Canada has benefited from similar urban design ideas where you don’t need a car to live here but still be able to reach all amenities. I get around by bike to get to work and do errands here in Vancouver, even with its hills. Its high ranking on the livability scale is pretty world renown. We own a car, but rarely gets used.

I was in Rome and I LOVE their car culture. If you drive a moped scooter in Italy, you get special traffic-bypassing privilege; such as driving on the centerline to bypass gridlock. It is perfectly safe because everyone is aware of it. Most city streets are primarily WALKED, with cars being a secondary form of transport. If you want to travel far, the train is less than $20, it goes 170mph, and is very enjoyable to travel on. Also, the cars are almost all manual transmission…. This has nothing to do with efficiency, but it is a very cool part of the culture. After spending a week there, walking over 10 miles per day, and riding around the countryside on a vespa, coming back to the USA felt sad. Everything is so spread out, and if I want to go 100+ miles, I’m forced to drive. Trains are incredible. Imagine taking a 170mph train and a folding bike to San Diego for the weekend. I’d be there a LOT.

I live in Madrid (Spain) now it’s the city center is much like you describe it. It was built centuries ago (started 500 years ago and evolved in tiers). Obviously, it was not designed for cars. There are still cars moving around, but it’s clear that they are the 2nd grade citizens here. Most transport is on foot and a super efficient metro system. Then, the medium and long range rail lines. Most people living here don’t have nor need a car.

I also live in Spain (A Coruña) and I was thinking the same as you Amir.

This video is good summary of Spanish cities from the perspective of someone from a North American”

‘Pedestrianized Streets Are Good, So What Are We Even Doing?’ https://youtu.be/7BRvk-_wM6U

In my city in Canada, people were protesting against the concept of 15 minute cities proposed by the municipal government. The protesters believe it is part of the plan but an authoritarian global world order power(s) that aim to confine people to geographic prisons and ban cars.

15 minute cities are a very sensible idea which became subject to a lot of mass hysteria a few years ago. Hopefully some common sense on the matter has returned.

#8854. What Top Tri Coaches Fix Between November and March

Top triathlon coaches share what they have their athletes work on in the off-season. (Photo: FinisherPix/Triathlete, Aaron Palaian, Oliver Baker, and courtesy David Tilbury-Davis)

One of triathlon’s attractions – and frustrations – is that there is always something to work on, and there are few better times to continue that never-ending quest for perfection than during the off-season.

With no race commitments, it gives triathletes the opportunity to step back, assess their strengths and weaknesses, and identify what to work on heading into spring.

For Northern Hemisphere athletes, that time is now. So, to help you along the way, we turned to four of the sport’s leading coaches to get their views — in their words — on what triathletes should focus on between now and March.

One of the world’s leading coaches and applied sports scientists in endurance sport, Plews has coached elite triathletes, including world champions Chelsea Sodaro, Javier Gomez, and Terenzo Bozzone.

He is also the founder of the coaching platform Endure IQ for both athletes and coaches. Plews himself is a former age-group Ironman world champion and still holds the fastest amateur time at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship.

“I never did proper strength training when I was younger, but now that I do a lot more, I’m seeing the benefits. But it is only as good as the quality and intent you put in. One of the big mistakes I see with many triathletes is that there’s no real intent.

“Get someone to help make sure you’re doing proper lifts. If you need to learn the correct movements, winter would be an ideal time. Then strength work needs to challenge the system. We typically talk “reps in reserve” when it comes to strength training [i.e., how many more reps you could complete before reaching failure].

“I’d advise working to two to three reps in reserve, but you can go to four if you’re not confident. But the main thing is you want to see a change in the speed of movement as you fatigue through the set.

“I would focus mostly on compound lifts: barbell hip thrusts, Bulgarian split squats, Nordic hamstring curls, and isometric holds and calf raises to add injury prevention. As time goes on, pair it with more plyometric and ballistic exercises, which might be a squat into a box jump.”

“Winter can be a period where you become unstuck from a psychological point of view. What’s important is to find balance. You want the volume, but don’t want to become stale so that by the time you get to the season, you’ve lost enthusiasm.

“If you really push the envelope early, especially with long, cold rides in January and February, by the time you get through to the season, you’re just sick of it. So, I think there’s a very fine line between doing too much training and not enough.”

The founder and head coach of NVDM Coaching in Austin, Texas, Van Der Merwe leads a team of more than 30 coaches supporting over 700 athletes. A former top-50 world-ranked junior tennis player from South Africa, she raced as a professional triathlete from 2010 to 2023 and has coached since 2009. She also leads Ironman U, Ironman’s official coaching certification program.

“Winter is when we raise the ceiling. We reverse periodize, so short, focused threshold and VO2 work comes before the long volume, because every triathlete races at a percentage of their FTP.

“If an athlete raises FTP from 220 to 235 watts this winter and rides an Ironman at 70% of it, race-day power goes from 154 to about 165 watts. Spring then becomes about extending that fitness.”

“Most athletes book a fit in spring, which leaves little time to adapt before racing. Our order is comfort first, then aerodynamics, then power, because the fastest position is the one you can hold for the whole bike leg and still run well afterward.

“In one study, the lowest torso angle tested cost riders about 16 watts at threshold compared with their own positions. Winter trainer rides are the perfect place to build into a new position gradually.”

“This is one most athletes never think about, and it can quietly derail a whole season. Vitamin D drops through the winter, especially for athletes training indoors at northern latitudes.

“A review of more than 2,000 athletes found over half had inadequate levels. Iron stores matter too, especially for female athletes. We ask athletes to get a baseline panel with vitamin D and ferritin now, so their doctor can address anything before the big training blocks start.”

Head coach at KIS Coaching, Cunnama is a former elite professional triathlete from South Africa who won major long-distance races, including Challenge Roth and Ironman Hamburg, and owns two top-five finishes at the Ironman World Championship in Kona. Following his racing career, he became a presenter with the Global Triathlon Network (GTN), sharing his knowledge and experience with a worldwide triathlon audience.

“Everyone knows they should work on their weaknesses over winter, but that usually translates to a broad goal like, ‘I want to work on my swim,’ which then turns into ‘more swimming, less biking and running.’

“I find it more effective to keep a balance in all three triathlon disciplines, but try to get ahead on the things that you always fell behind on last season. Determine which aspect of your training made you feel most underconfident, and then tweak your off-season training to target that area.

“For example, if you found that using paddles destroyed your arms, do extra paddle work. If hills were your nemesis on the bike, hit the hills (or simulate them on the trainer). Rather than tackling physical limitations, target the mental hurdles – use the off-season to get to a place where you love the sessions you hated last season.”

“It is hard to make changes to technique during the season when you have volume goals in training, because technique changes (or position changes on the bike) require you to only do as much of the new technique as you can sustain, and no more.

“You can’t ingrain a new technique when the second half of your session is falling back to the old technique! So, make those changes in the off-season and slowly build back that technique better. The advantage of triathlon is you have two other sports to keep you fit while you reset your technique in the third sport.”

A highly respected triathlon coach, Tilbury-Davis has worked with professional and age-group athletes since 1995. Through Tilbury-Davis Coaching, he has coached leading athletes such as Lionel Sanders and Ashleigh Gentle. Based in Finland, he works with a small group of international athletes.

“Efficiency of movement sounds vague, but while I’m a big proponent of doing strength and conditioning work throughout the year, winter is a time to understand that swimming, biking, and running all require expression of force from the core – when I say core, I effectively mean from the knees to the chest.

“You’re talking around 64 different muscles and creating the capacity to have a stable base to express force from will improve your body alignment in the water, your ability to maintain an aero position on the bike, and your ability to have hip extension and knee drive in the run. It centers around doing the kind of exercises that are multi-plane, multi-muscle recruiting as part of a several-times-a-week program.

“For example, you see a lot of triathletes train with a Masters group and the swim coach says to do a high elbow or chicken wing drill. The reality is that 99% of triathletes do not have sufficient mobility to swim in a manner that a swim coach would like. So, to step back, I would say to improve your swimming, go away and work on your thoracic and scapular mobility.”

“A lot of people don’t talk about saddle choice. We all buy expensive running shoes that are made out of expensive foam that breaks down over a period of time, but we forget that saddles are also made out of foam.

“If you’re serious about maintaining a good position on the bike, you probably should be changing your saddle once a year and for a pro that might be twice a year because the foam in the saddle breaks down the same way that the foam in a running shoe breaks down.”

“Get used to having to cope with uneven surfaces on the run, shortening and lengthening your stride length, stepping over rocks and roots, dealing with off camber, on camber, dealing with gravel, sand, mud, all of those proprioceptive stimuli that vary significantly improve your body’s ability to be efficient. A worst-case scenario for me would be an athlete that just runs on a treadmill the entire winter at a very narrow bandwidth of running paces.

“A good way of explaining this is that people talk about the way the Kenyans train. They do this famous long run in Iten where it’s a progressively descending pace. But what’s special about that workout is that they’re running on trails, gravel fire roads, wooded areas, and gradient changes. Probably the most powerful thing about that run is that they’re working on different surfaces, different terrains, different obstacles, different gradients, while they’re still working on a physiological stimulus.”

“That’s probably when people ask me what’s the number-one most important session for Ironman training: I would say go run on trails before anything else, because it builds resilience and strength, which is what you need for an Ironman.”

#8853. 853 Runners Were Disqualified From This Road Race. Many Broke the Same Starting-Line Rule.

More than 3 percent of finishers lost official results after organizers reviewed bib data.

Your race bib can tell organizers a lot more than how quickly you finished. At Spain's 61st edition of Behobia–San Sebastián, it also helped them figure out whether you started when you were supposed to. As it turns out, getting a little too eager at the starting line can be enough to cost you an official result.

Organizers confirmed that 853 participants were disqualified from the November 8 event, a popular 20K race that attracted 27,172 runners this year. According to Spanish outlets Mundo Deportivo and 3Cat, starting in an earlier wave than assigned was a major reason behind the unusually high number.

The race sorts participants into groups based on their previous performances, with staggered start times designed to help manage the crowds. Runners can move back to a later wave if they wish, but jumping ahead to an earlier one is grounds for disqualification. It's a rule that should sound familiar to anyone who's run a race with NYRR, as they follow the same policy and warn that moving into a faster wave or corral can cost runners their results.

With thousands of people lining up, slipping into an earlier group can go unnoticed, but timing chips attached to race bibs allow organizers to track when participants cross the starting line and other checkpoints along the course.

Other violations, including using another runner's bib without an authorized transfer, are against the rules and can also result in disqualification. However, organizers haven't provided explanations for every case, making it unclear how many involved starting-wave violations.

According to figures released by organizers, 29,301 people registered for the event, and 26,947 crossed the 12.4-mile course’s finish line in San Sebastián. Of those who completed the race, a little more than 3 percent were disqualified.

While it sounds like a lot, 853 is actually an improvement compared to previous years. In 2023, a whopping 1,327 runners were disqualified, followed by 958 in 2024 and 918 last year. So the numbers are heading in the right direction, although there's clearly still some confusion—or disregard—when it comes to following the pre-start rules.

Runner’s World has contacted race organizers for details about the disqualifications, including whether affected participants have an opportunity to appeal.

#8851. REI vs. Dick’s Sporting Goods Black Friday Deals, Which Is Better?

The two brands are known for wilding out on sales, but here’s how to find the best deals.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Your cart has been sitting there since October, and I get it. I’ve got a few (hundred) tabs open myself. As someone with many marathons, a few ultras, and more halfs and 5Ks than I can count, I can tell you the real Black Friday question isn’t whether to buy shoes and running gear; it’s where. REI and Dick’s are two of the names that come up the most often, and they handle the holiday very differently. REI is again giving its employees a paid day off on Friday, November 27, so its deals land early. Dick’s has typically stretched its sale across the weekend. Deciding who has the best deals comes down to these two questions: What are you actually shopping for, and how much do you need? Here’s how the deals stack up.

One thing both brands are doing, and doing pretty well, is taking some big-name running shoes and discounting them hard. Think Hoka, Asics, and Brooks top trainers with discounts of $50 or more, with deeper discounts on previous years’ models. The deals don’t match model to model, and each outlet has different shoes at different prices. For example, REI offers steeper discounts on Hoka, and Dick’s has better pricing on brands like Adidas.

The Hoka Bondi 9 is a favorite among distance runners, especially those with flatter feet. It has a supercritical foam midsole that makes it light and responsive, with a snug fit, a generously padded collar, and comfortable, max-stack cushioning. It’s a big improvement over the Bondis of antiquity, and it’s one of their most popular shoes overall. And the price difference between REI and Dick’s is significant, with REI the clear winner.

Can’t go wrong with the ultra-comfortable Adizero Evo SL from Adidas. It’s fun to run in; it’s bouncy, responsive, and keeps you happy on long runs. Dubbed by Jeff Dengate as the Shoe of the Year for 2025, this trainer remains one of our most beloved shoes of the past few years.

The On Cloudmonster 3 is the perfect mix of firm and cushioned, keeping you supported on your longest efforts, whether walking or running. It’s a max-cushioned trainer with On’s CloudTec technology that compresses and rebounds with every strike, making it responsive, a bit bouncy, and ready for high mileage.

REI is also known for its Co-op line of gear. It’s their own, high-quality gear that comes in at terrific prices. For Black Friday and Cyber Monday, many of those items are discounted even further, making it hard to say no to already affordable goodies. REI also offers a variety of smaller brands like Rabbit, which they are able to offer on sale. If you’re into smaller brands, or you’re a big fan of Co-op, REI is the place to hit up.

Rabbit makes great UPF-rated long sleeves that are perfect for layering on cooler days or staying cool in the sun on hotter days. This one has one of my favorite features—a watch panel that lets you wear the shirt over your hands with thumb holes, so you can still see your watch. The fabric is buttery, the seams are sealed, so they’re not itchy or irritating, and they launder like a dream.

REI makes really good hydration vests, often in a more expansive size range than other brands. I’ve tested this one, and I like it a lot. It has space for a bladder and two flasks, plus room for snacks, gear, and whatever you happen to take off during your run because you’ve overheated.

Some of the biggest sales at Dick’s Sporting Goods are on its biggest-ticket items like treadmills, running watches, and other exercise equipment. These are categories that REI doesn’t touch as much, and some not at all (treadmills). This area is where Dick’s really shines. You could get hundreds off this time of year, and you should take full advantage.

This is truly one of my favorite “get-up-and-run” treadmills, and for 40 percent off, it’s tripping into “cheap” treadmill territory. It’s a solid treadmill with a good-size deck, plenty of connectivity, incline, and speed, all at a fabulous price tag.

Suunto has improved so much over the past few years, and this is one of the best examples. It’s a dynamic, multisport running watch with terrific GPS, battery life, connectivity, and a family of apps to help keep you connected. It’s also one of the better-looking running watches available, and while that might not be the most important thing, it’s still worth considering.

Both brands have fantastic Black Friday discounts, but they look pretty different. Dick’s has the upper hand on big-ticket items, but their shoes are a bit more expensive. REI wins on shoe price, and in the smaller labels and private-label brands they’re known for. And both stores carry shoe brands the other doesn't. In the end, it’s about picking your faves and knowing what you’re shopping for.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. #8850. The Bivo Trio Mini Keeps Finding a Place on Our Bikes When the Temperatures Begin to Dip—Here’s Why

In a crowded category, the Bivo Trio Bottle ends up in our bottle cages for colder rides.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Your water bottles have probably frozen at least once if you ride outside in cold weather. Usually, it’s only a thin layer of ice on top or a clogged nozzle, but that’s enough to be annoying. If you ride at low enough temperatures with standard plastic bottles filled with plain water, it will inevitably happen. However, it’s important to stay hydrated on winter rides.

There are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides. Hot chocolate, coffee, tea, or Skratch Labs’ apple cider will warm your soul and lift your mood. And nothing hits better than a coffee stop in the middle of a cold winter ride, especially when conditions are dreary or sloppy.

Stainless insulated bottles broke into cycling about five years ago and have since exploded in popularity. They’re a proven way to keep water and hydration mix cool on the hottest summer days, and they can also keep hot drinks warm for many miles on winter rides.

The Bivo Trio Bottle, available in raw stainless steel and silicone-covered stainless steel versions, has become a bottle of choice on cold-weather rides. Read on to find out why, plus tips to prevent your bottles from freezing this winter.

Cyclists have many different methods (often handed down from one generation of riders to the next) to help prevent frozen bottles. One simple solution is to start your ride with hot water. However, depending on the temperature and ride length, this can also freeze.

Using insulated plastic bottles, adding a high-sodium drink mix, and wearing a hydration pack or vest under a riding jacket are all tricks I’ve used (with varying degrees of success) to keep my bottles from freezing. And some riders still swear by adding a shot of booze to their bidon. However, while these methods may prevent icing, they still result in a cold beverage during your ride.

It’s hard to miss the growing popularity of stainless steel water bottles in cycling. Their use has boomed in the last few seasons as more riders have become concerned about microplastic contamination. Plus, these metal bidons, particularly the Bivo bottles, are in the cages of many cycling influencers.

Stainless bottles typically feature a vacuum-sealed double-wall design with a coated outer and a bare stainless inner layer. Since metal bottles are rigid, you cannot squeeze them like plastic bottles. (It takes some getting used to if you haven’t ridden them before.) And while stainless bottles are much heavier than plastic models, they are heavy-duty and almost indestructible—they dent and scratch but rarely break.

Bivo is the trend-setting stainless option and commonly available from retailers like REI, Backcountry, Amazon, or your local bike shop. The Insulated Mini we tested is 17 ounces and costs $44, or opt for the 21-ounce model for $5 more.

I have ridden with insulated bottles at several points in my cycling life. But until last summer, I usually stuck with non-insulated plastic bottles for most of my rides, regardless of air temperature.

Generally, I prefer the feel of a regular bottle; 22-ounce Specialized Purist bottles are my go-to, and I occasionally carry a 10-ounce Purist Maker mug for a mid-ride coffee break. But I often skip stainless insulated bottles because they aren’t squeezable and weigh noticeably more than plastic bidons.

However, before a recent ride on a cold and blustery day, I filled an insulated bottle with hot chocolate and was pleased to have a warm treat throughout my 90-minute ride. So, like my insulated bottle test last summer, I applied a little science to see which insulated stainless bottles performed best in cold temps.

For this test, I gathered several popular metal insulated bottles. First, I evaluated the bottles by measuring water temperature over three hours in subfreezing conditions. Then, I used them on rides in cold weather to determine which worked best from a functional perspective.

While the intent was somewhat scientific, I also strove to be practical—these are tests anyone can do at home. This testing was not performed in a controlled environment or with professional-level, calibrated equipment.

Since it was below 32 degrees outside, I was able to perform outdoor freeze testing. Like my summer insulated bottle tests, I filled the selected bottles with 400 grams of tap water (heated to 212 degrees for this test instead of chilled water used in summer). Then I placed the filled bottles on my front porch in subfreezing temperatures; I did this after sunset so sunlight would not warm the bottles. Every 30 minutes, I checked and recorded the water temperature of each bottle, in the same order each time, with a digital food thermometer.

Following the initial three-hour test period, the bottles remained overnight in sub-freezing temperatures for an additional nine hours. This tested whether the contents would stay warm for a full 12 hours (as per some bottle makers’ claims). Additionally, for reference, I subjected a Purist Maker tumbler (with 200 grams of water), an insulated plastic bottle, and a standard plastic bottle to the same tests.

The following day, I evaluated the bottles’ on-bike performance on a short loop in my neighborhood. I tested their use with standard and lobster-claw gloves (such as holding, opening caps, removing them from cages) and their nozzles’ function while drinking hot coffee (a medium-roast pour-over with some oat milk for my tests 😉).

The results were clear: Insulated stainless bottles work very well in cold weather. They keep your beverage hot for an hour-long ride in 30-degree temps. For longer rides, your drink will experience some heat loss but will remain drinkably warm for three hours. The insulated metal bottles performed notably better than plastic bottles (insulated and non-insulated) for the full duration of the test.

After about three hours of exposure in the cold, the Bivo Insulated Trio Mini kept my coffee at a warm 119.8 degrees. This is only slightly below coffee expert James Hoffmann’s recommended coffee-drinking temp of 122 to 129 degrees. (Although I’m not sure Hoffmann would be pleased drinking three-hour-old brew.) In 12-hour testing, none of the metal bottles froze. Most bottles finished at room temperature after 12 hours outside in freezing temperatures.

On the bike, the Bivo valve works great, and the bottle texture isn’t overly slippery. The bottle shape is compatible with most cages, though it fits best in the Arundle Sport cage recommended by Bivo.

Nozzle Shield: Look for bottles with a cap that protects the nozzle. Typically, I’m not a fan of these shields when riding in warm weather—they flop around and get in the way when drinking. However, in the winter, caps keep road salt and slush off the bottle’s nozzle, and they also help prevent icing. Ones with a removable plastic or rubber shield are easier to clean; plus, you can use the bottles without the cap on warm days.

Vapor Pressure: Many of the tested bottles carry a warning about using liquids hotter than 180 degrees. This is to avoid scalding and burns from pressurized hot water when the cap or nozzle is opened. With insulated bottles, hot liquid heats the air inside the bottle enough to spray potentially near-boiling water into your mouth or onto your body.

Avoid this by letting your hot beverage cool slightly before pouring it into your bottle. For long rides (when using two bottles of hot drinks), save the hotter bottle for later in the day. This way, it has time to cool to a drinkable temperature.

Cage Compatibility: Since they do not deform or flex, metal bottles don’t pair with every bottle cage. Some stainless bottles have a loose fit in cages (bottles can even eject on rough roads), and some cage shapes do not allow some metal bottles to sit correctly, causing annoying rattling and buzzing while riding. Other cage-bottle pairings are so tight that it’s hard to remove the bottle while riding.

My advice: Check that your cages work before dropping up to $100 for new bottles that won’t fit. Some brands have specific cage recommendations on their sites. You can also read user reviews for the compatibility of different bottles and cages. Also, be sure to check the overall bottle height to be sure it fits in your frame.

Dropped Bottles: I do not recommend using metal bottles in mass-start situations; use plastic bidons for big group rides or races. When a metal bottle is ejected from a cage on a bump, or you drop one (as is prone to happen with cold hands or when wearing bulky gloves), it ricochets off the road surface more than a plastic bottle. And while metal makes these bottles more durable, they do not burst open on impact or crush if hit by other riders.

Bivo shook up the bottle market when it launched its stainless steel bottles. The small Richmond, Vermont-based company launched insulated bottles shortly after, and cyclists have fallen in love with them. They work well, look good, and don’t have a funky taste.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8849. Running for Time vs. Distance: Experts Explain Which Is Better for Your Goals

The pros and cons of training by minutes versus miles.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Whether your goal is to run a marathon or simply improve your fitness, following a solid training plan will help you stay consistent as you work toward that goal. But with so many options to choose from, finding the right training plan can feel tricky.

So where do you start? Consider this: Most plans fall into the very broad categories of time-based versus distance-based running. In other words, a plan prescribes runs in terms of minutes or in terms of miles. There’s no clear evidence that one is inherently superior for race-day performance, but each approach does have specific advantages and disadvantages.

To help you determine whether time-based running or distance-based running is right for you, we tapped three experts to explain the pros and cons of each. They break down exactly what to consider so you can pick the type of training plan that best fits your schedule, preferences, ability level, and race goals.

Distance-based plans, or those that provide specific mileage goals for each workout, are incredibly common. That’s in part because they make a lot of sense for runners training to race a certain distance, such as a 5K, 10K, half marathon, or full marathon. Runners need to prepare their bodies for the specific mileage of their chosen race, Janet Hamilton, CSCS, an exercise physiologist and the founder and head coach of Running Strong, tells Runner’s World. And following a distance-based plan is a great way to ensure you’re getting in the right number of miles.

Aside from preparing you physically for a race, distance-based plans can provide a powerful mental boost. Knowing you’ve successfully run a given distance before you toe the starting line—whether that’s logging three miles prior to attempting a 5K, or 20 miles in advance of a marathon—can give you confidence that you’ll be able to finish the race you’re gearing up for, says Jacob Phillips, a Texas-based run coach with RunDoyen.

Distance-based plans can also clue you into your current performance levels. For example, if you run six miles at a hard effort, you’ll get a good grasp on your 10K abilities. “You know exactly where you stand over the prescribed distance,” explains Ken Rideout, a masters marathon world champion and nationally best-selling author of the memoir, Everything You Want Is on the Other Side of Hard.

The biggest downside of a distance-based plan: If it’s not coupled with instructions on how to pace yourself or what effort level to strive for, then it’s up to you to manage those details. And in Hamilton’s experience, many runners, when left to their own devices, complete their workouts at lactate threshold pace. That’s about the same effort at which you’d race a 10K or half marathon—much faster than you want to do your daily runs.

While there are certainly benefits to running at faster paces, you don’t want to miss out on all the perks of easy-pace running. Keeping your daily runs at a comfortable, conversational effort helps develop slow-twitch muscle fibers, improves running economy, and may even reduce your injury risk.

Many beginner-friendly plans and run/walk programs use time as the main training parameter. One perk of this approach is that timed runs can be “a lot less intimidating” than distance workouts, says Rideout. “When you’re running a prescribed distance, you can’t help but notice, what was my pace? What were my mile splits?” he explains. But the format of a time-based run automatically reduces the prominence of those metrics, which can be helpful if you’re just easing into a running routine.

Experienced runners might find similar benefits to this approach. For folks who get frazzled by having to check their mileage throughout a run, or those who get obsessive about pace, a time-based plan may be a soothing alternative. “It’s not as stressful,” Phillips explains. “I think there’s a simplicity to saying, ‘Hey, you’re going to go out and just run for half an hour,’” without having to worry about completing a certain route or number of miles.

A time-centric approach can also encourage athletes to embrace easy-effort runs because it removes intrinsic pressure to run hard, says Phillips. After all, if time is the only goal, it doesn’t matter how fast you go—you’ll be successful in that day’s workout by simply moving for the prescribed duration.

This can also make time-based training a good idea for busy runners. Say you only have 30 minutes today to break a sweat. With a duration-focused plan, you’ll be able to complete your planned workout, even if variables such as the terrain you’re running over or your energy levels that day impact your usual pace. No matter what happens, you’re done in 30 minutes.

Opting for timed runs can also make sense for folks who are trail running in off-the-grid locations where there are no mile markers and GPS devices don’t always function well, says Hamilton. Instead of fixating on how far they’ve run—which may be challenging if not impossible given the circumstances—runners can be successful by simply going out for a certain number of minutes.

A duration approach may come in handy for traveling runners, too, says Hamilton. When you’re in an unfamiliar location, there’s no need to expend effort trying to figure out how to make a five-mile loop from your hotel. Instead, you can run out-and-back for 45 minutes and call it a day.

Lastly, because there’s less emphasis with time-based runs on achieving a certain pace, they can help you “get into different heart-rate zones and stay in a specific zone for a prescribed period of time,” says Rideout. This can be beneficial in improving your overall fitness, he explains.

Time-centric running isn’t for everyone. As we mentioned, if you’re training for a particular distance, a plan focused solely on duration may not give you the race-specific preparation—or confidence—you need to achieve your goal.

Additionally, time-based plans might not be the best fit for runners who are strongly motivated by tracking their daily and weekly mileage or hitting new distance-based milestones.

When comparing time versus distance running, know that “both ways can be very, very beneficial,” says Phillips. It all just boils down to finding the right plan that fits your goals and lifestyle.

In general, new runners will likely find success with a time-based approach, while more experienced runners, especially those targeting a specific goal time in a race, “tend to do a little bit better with a volume-based approach,” says Phillips.

Your personality and preferences for a training plan may also influence which philosophy to follow. “As a coach, I like saying ‘We did X amount of miles this week, and next week we’re going to do X amount of miles,’” says Phillips, noting that many of the runners he coaches also prefer to track their progress via distance logged week to week.

On the flip side, “there are some people who just don’t want that,” says Phillips. “They don’t want the stress of comparing week to week or even day to day, so I think it just comes down to what you enjoy more.”

Hamilton, for her part, tends to recommend plans that combine time and distance prescriptions—for example, run six miles in 60 minutes—because she finds this hybrid approach helps her athletes develop confidence in running certain distances while also keeping their pace in check.

Rideout is of the mindset that a well-rounded training plan will include both types of runs. “I try to always keep things fresh, keep my body guessing, and try to optimize performance all the time,” he explains. Regularly introducing different types of training—via time-centric workouts and distance-focused runs—is a good way to ensure your body continues to adapt and improve.

No matter what plan you choose, you can always sub one time-focused run for a distance-based workout, and vice versa, if you think it helps your mindset that day.

Jenny is a Boulder, Colorado-based health and fitness journalist. She’s been freelancing for Runner’s World since 2015 and especially loves to write human interest profiles, in-depth service pieces and stories that explore the intersection of exercise and mental health. Her work has also been published by SELF, Men’s Journal, and Condé Nast Traveler, among other outlets. When she’s not running or writing, Jenny enjoys coaching youth swimming, rereading Harry Potter, and buying too many houseplants.

#8847. The Runner’s World Guide to Recovery

Your guide to smarter recovery—from managing soreness and fatigue to easing back into running after a race, offseason, or injury.

What you do to recover between runs matters just as much as the miles themselves. But knowing what your body needs isn’t always straightforward. Should you head out for an easy run or take the day off? Is that soreness normal, or a sign of an injury about to derail everything? And which recovery tools are actually worth the hype?

This guide helps you navigate those decisions, starting with the fundamentals. Plus, we’ll help you choose a training plan to ease back into running after a race, your offseason, or an injury (both minor and burdensome).

Whether you’re bouncing back from a tough workout or gearing up for your next training block, start planning your recovery here.

Recovery doesn’t have to be complicated, but it does require giving the basics as much attention as your workouts. Easy runs, rest days, postrun fueling, and sleep all help your body manage the work you’re putting in. That means keeping most of your miles at a pace where you can comfortably hold a conversation, rather than turning every run into another hard effort.

How easy should your next run be? Take the quiz below to find out.

It also means taking at least one full day off from training each week—and more if you’re new to running or need extra recovery.

What you do after a run matters, too: Carbohydrates replenish energy stores, protein supports muscle repair, and sufficient sleep gives your body time to recover and rebuild.

Sore legs after a tough workout can come with the territory. But knowing when to take it easy—and when to stop running—isn’t always obvious. Before you push through discomfort, pay attention to how it feels, whether it’s improving, and how it affects the way you move.

If you notice these warning signs, stop running and seek guidance from a healthcare professional rather than trying to push through.

While dynamic stretches are ideal before your run, practicing static stretches postrun—where you hold a stationary position—can help ease tightness while your muscles are still warm.

#8846. Best Winter Cycling Gloves for Cold, Wet, and Windy Rides

We rode through freezing rain, sleet, and biting wind to find the best winter cycling gloves that stay warm, dry, and secure when conditions are at their worst.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Nothing ruins a chilly, crisp day on the bike faster than frozen fingers. Besides being uncomfortable, numb hands can make it difficult to shift gears or feel your brake levers, turning a cold ride into a potentially unsafe one.

The right pair of winter gloves will keep your hands warm without making it difficult to operate your bike’s controls. But finding that pair isn’t always as simple as checking the temperature rating on the packaging. How warm your hands get, the weather conditions, and the type of riding you do all play a role.

For example, on a 35-degree road ride, you’ll likely want a much warmer glove than you would for a mountain bike ride at the same temperature. Higher speeds on the road mean more windchill, while a slower, harder effort on the trails can leave your hands sweaty in gloves that are too warm. If you ride throughout the winter, it’s worth owning a few different pairs to cover the range of conditions you’ll encounter.

I tested more than 40 glove models in temperatures ranging from the low 60s to below 20 degrees, then narrowed the field to my six favorites. I’ve included recommended temperature ranges for each, but consider those a starting point. If you tend to run cold or have Raynaud’s syndrome, you may want a warmer glove; if your hands sweat easily, a lighter, more breathable option might work better.

More Winter Gear Advice: Our Expert Swears by This Three-Layer Trick. ● The Best Men’s Winter Cycling Jackets ● The Best Winter Cycling Hats

Perhaps my all-time favorite version of my all-time favorite glove, DeFeet’s Duraglove has been around for ages and has remained mostly unchanged. It’s very comfortable, has great dexterity, and provides good grip. Plus, it has touchscreen functionality. DeFeet offers two versions of this glove: The plain Duraglove ET and the Duraglove ET Wool Blend featured here, which uses a merino wool blend.

I’ve found this version to be the warmer of the two. I’ve worn this glove into the low 40s during high-intensity rides and stayed comfortable. Because this knit glove is incredibly breathable, it’s still comfortable to wear as the day warms into the mid-to-high 50s. The Duraglove is unsuitable for rainy rides as its knit construction will quickly soak up water.

These Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be as warm as they are. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no issues.

They use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a big fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

Near-freezing temperatures with rain are probably the most challenging conditions to ride in. But for some, it’s unavoidable. Glacier Glove’s Ice Bay is as good as it gets for these conditions. It’s constructed with 2mm-thick, fleece-lined neoprene and is as waterproof as any piece of clothing could be.

These gloves have incredible dexterity given their warmth. The long cuff is easy to tuck under your rain jacket to keep water out. The downside of a neoprene glove is that it does not breathe at all. That’s partly how it keeps your hands warm, but it only works as long as you keep the gloves on. If you take them off, your now-sweaty hands will get quite cold quickly, and your formerly toasty gloves (lacking body heat) will be cold and wet with sweat. Despite these drawbacks, if it’s cold and rainy and I need to be out riding, these are the gloves I reach for.

These pricey gloves are the warmest five-finger gloves I’ve tried that still let me move my fingers. Gore took inspiration from high alpine mountaineering for the design. The outer shell uses a Gore-Tex ePE liner that is highly wind- and water-resistant. For insulation, Gore used a PrimaLoft lining. It features one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios. All of this results in a glove that can be comfortable down to and below freezing, depending on your pace and specific riding conditions.

I’ve used similarly warm gloves from other brands, and they've often been far too bulky to feel useful. These still maintain a good bar feel and let me freely articulate my fingers. While they have touchscreen compatibility, I found them a little too bulky to quickly type out a text message on an iPhone.

We’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

The gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

The secret to the dexterity is the PrimaLoft Gold insulation, which provides exceptional warmth without adding bulk. Most very warm gloves are also very thick, which makes it difficult to locate the proper shifter and grip your brake levers. This pair keeps my hands warm on long weekend rides and daily commutes, even when temperatures dip below freezing, without getting in the way.

Bar Mitts may look unconventional, but riders who use them swear by their added warmth and control. Designed to work with gloves, these neoprene covers attach to your bar and enclose your bike’s shifters and brake levers. They add significant wind protection and help keep your hands shielded from the elements.

Several Bar Mitt variants are available for road, mountain, and townie-style handlebars. Be sure to check details and confirm fitment with your bar/shifter combo before you order.

Glove fit is subjective. They should fit in the Goldilocks range. If your gloves are too big, you risk losing grip on the handlebar and controls. But a glove that’s too tight can prevent you from comfortably grasping the handlebar or grips.

An easy way to spot a glove that’s too big is if you have a lot of fabric bunching in your palm. It’s always worth trying new gloves on your bike to see how they feel on the bars, since labeled sizing can differ from brand to brand.

If you’re riding in temperatures below the mid-40s or closer to freezing, you want a glove with some insulation. In the most basic definition, insulation is filling used to capture and hold onto warmth. The most familiar insulation for outdoor use is down, often found in puffy jackets. In gloves, you are most likely to find down in very bulky mittens, which are very warm but lack the dexterity for cycling.

Most cycling-specific gloves use synthetic insulation from companies like Polartech or PrimaLoft. These materials are most often used on the back of the hand to protect from wind and minimize interference with the handlebar feel. Thin, grippy material is generally found on the palm. Many brands use leather on the palms for improved grip and durability, so watch out for this if you avoid buying animal products.

For the interior of the glove, look for polyester or Merino wool. You want something that wicks sweat and keeps your hands dry—sweaty hands can quickly turn into frozen prunes.

Gloves with appropriate breathability for the temperature and your riding effort keep your hands warm and dry. The warmer the temps, or the higher your effort, the more breathable you’ll want your gloves.

Regionally, humidity also plays a part in selecting the right glove. If you ride somewhere cool and dry, such as Colorado, where it might be in the 30s with low humidity, you likely will be able to use a lighter pair of more breathable gloves. These can do a much better job keeping you warm because they transfer moisture away from your hands more effectively. If you ride in the Northeast, the same pair of gloves might feel too cold at the same temperature, since humidity is often much higher. For these conditions, you’ll want a glove with better wind and waterproofing at the expense of breathability.

Once you figure out the glove warmth you need for your riding, consider other features before buying. Something I find very important in gloves meant for frigid weather is long cuffs. Cuffs make it easy to tuck the glove under or sometimes over your jacket sleeve, keeping your wrists warm and stopping cold air from entering your jacket.

The palm construction of a glove is also worth careful examination. A common feature is padding. Some riders prefer padded gloves, while others do not. Padding matters less the warmer a glove gets, since the palm becomes bulkier with insulation. For thinner gloves, a seamless palm is the way to go. It minimizes any chance of irritation and improves handlebar feel.

If you ride with a smartphone or have a touchscreen computer, gloves that interact with these devices are great. The less you need to remove your gloves in the cold, the happier your hands will be.

Finally, a soft, large terrycloth nose-wipe section (preferably along the thumb or index finger) is good if you’re a heavy snotter.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.
