#8819. ‘At 60, I Went From Zero Running Experience to Finishing the NYC Marathon Within a Year. These 5 Strategies Got Me to the Finish.’

A first-time marathoner over 50 shares the training, mindset, and support that carried him 26.2 miles.

I’ve never been a runner. Before this past year, the last time I ran was a local 5K on a whim with my daughter about a decade ago. I didn’t prepare for it at all, so it was challenging, and I never ran again after that.

Then, this past May, I signed up to run another local 5K, two months before I turned 60. Working in an office full of runners—I’m an editor at Popular Mechanics and we share an office with Runner’s World—I just wanted to prove that I could do it.

I went on a handful of runs before the race in an attempt to prepare, but I couldn't really make it past 1.5 miles. I got really frustrated. Leading up to race day, I saw how hilly the course was and decided to just wing it. If I had to walk at some points, I’d walk… and that’s what I did on most hills, because I didn’t quite have the stamina to make it through.

But all the runners around me were so inspiring; it felt like we could all make it through together. I saw someone in front of me going about the same pace, and that helped pull me to the finish line. I finished in 35:16, averaging an 11:20 pace.

A few months later, I got the opportunity to run the New York City Marathon. I was hesitant to accept, because I didn’t think I could run that far, but a few of my colleagues pushed me to say yes and really believed in me. So I signed up.

GET YOUR ZERO-TO-MARATHON TRAINING PLAN HERE

When I started marathon training, I followed the Runner’s World six-month zero-to-marathon training plan. I skipped a few weeks ahead because I had already worked up to running five miles and the plan starts with walking.

My training experience was far from perfect, but I learned that as a beginner, you have to just start and go from there.

To be totally honest, I didn’t train for the marathon as much as I probably should have. I started training around early August by running three times a week on local trails in the evenings, averaging three- to five-mile easy runs. I also made sure to add hills to most of my runs to get my quads ready for the hills in New York.

My training came to a bit of a halt after the first few weeks of training, when I realized I probably needed to contact my cardiologist. A couple of years ago, the doctors told me I have an enlarged aorta (the largest artery in your body that carries blood from your heart to the rest of your body), which the doctor attributed to my physically demanding years as an ironworker.

The problem with an enlarged aorta is that if it ruptures, you could have a fatal heart attack with little to no warning signs. Thinking about this made me nervous to train out of fear I might put too much stress on my heart.

So I called the doctor and scheduled an appointment, but they had to reschedule it for the last week of October and I wouldn’t be able to do imaging until November. But I told the nurse practitioner about my marathon training, and the doctor gave me the go-ahead to continue running with caution. I decided to stick with it knowing I didn’t have any symptoms or immediate concerns.

However, I did miss many of my long runs and I was pretty stressed that I wasn’t keeping up with the training plan. Once race day got closer, I grew tired of being hesitant and ran a 15-mile long run, which is the minimum distance run coaches recommend to cover in marathon training. Thankfully, I felt really strong through every mile and fueled well, which gave me reassurance for race day.

I also did about four of the threshold interval workouts in the beginning of the zero-to-marathon training plan, naively thinking they would be easier than easy runs because they included two-minute breaks…but they were not. I remember one workout in particular: eight sets of one-minute threshold efforts with one minute of recovery between each, along with a two-mile warmup and cooldown and some 30-second pre-workout strides. It was harder than I thought, but I got through it.

Toward the end of my training block, I noticed my pace naturally getting faster, which boosted my confidence and made me think I could potentially aim for sub-five hours on race day.

I also have a very basic strength routine that I do three to four times a week with a 35-pound kettlebell, which I kept up with throughout training, and I think that helped keep me strong and durable enough for the race.

I typically do a combination of 20 to 50 kettlebell swings, 10 weighted goblet squats, and 10 push-ups. I think the kettlebell is one of the greatest weight tools there is; I don’t have to go to a crowded gym and I can fit in a sufficient strength workout at home. The key with my strength routine is to not stop and complete the reps continuously.

I also incorporated two to three sets of five to 10 minutes of continuous jump rope between some of my strength sets at least once a week. This meant I snuck in some plyometric work to build my power and durability.

For people out there who think that they can’t train for and run a marathon, you can. I loved reading Runner’s World articles and training plans. If you follow a plan, even loosely, you can get to the finish.

The morning of the race, I felt very anxious. I traveled from Princeton, New Jersey, that morning, making a stack of six large pancakes (my go-to fuel source) and ate three before I left my house, saving the rest for the bus ride to the start line.

I felt a sense of imposter syndrome at the starting line, which I think goes hand in hand with being a writer. Whether it was my early years of being a screenwriter or adjusting to a new job at Popular Mechanics, I constantly dance with a feeling of “why am I here?” Those feelings came flooding back at the marathon. I thought to myself, “I’m not a runner…what am I doing here?” But I’ve learned the only way to work through that is to just do it, and take the first step.

With 12 gels on me and a 17-ounce handheld bottle of electrolyte mix, I made my way through the race, maintaining an easy effort. I felt like I could breathe through my nose if I wanted to for most of the time.

Some of my favorite parts of the race were running past buildings I’ve worked on and listening to the crowds. I didn’t turn on my music once during the whole race because the cheering was so loud and gave me so much energy.

There’s something particularly special about the creative, weird, and wonderful energy in the New York City Marathon. It was touching to see how such a big city comes together on this day, and not out of tragedy. I had never even been to a marathon before this, so that part felt really powerful. We’re living in a time of uncertainty, so it’s nice to know that people are still there for each other in the way they should be.

By the time I got past the halfway mark of the race, I realized sub-five was out of reach and I adjusted to sticking to my goal of simply finishing. I found my family around mile 17, which gave me the courage to keep going despite miles 19 and 20 hitting me hard.

I finished in 5:18:56, greeted by my colleagues holding my medal for me at the finish line. I felt like I proved that you can do anything you put your mind to, and I was so glad that my family was there to watch me finish, too.

The same thing that pulled me through my 5K happened around mile 18 or 19 of the marathon. I looked up and saw a woman wearing a hydration vest with a sign on her back printed in pink that read, “22 weeks pregnant.” I thought to myself, “Oh my god. I’m following you because you’re my new inspiration.” If she was running this race pregnant, there was no way I was giving up.

At mile 20, I knew I wasn’t going to be able to break five hours, but I’m grateful and proud I made it past mile 15 because that was the farthest distance I’d gone. I saw my family spectating at mile 17, and I think if I had seen them at an earlier mile, I would’ve struggled more to keep going.

My family really believed in me along the way. They made “Team Smith” shirts, and a bunch of my friends and family members came in to watch, including my son FaceTiming in from Paris. I only got to see them for a minute, but that’s what carried me for the last nine miles.

For me, half the battle of the race was mental. I thought to myself that anything after 15 miles would feel like driving at night: Your headlights only show you 50 feet in front of you, so only focus on that. You can’t see the whole road out to where you’re going, but you can keep going bit by bit. I told myself I could go another two miles at a time, and before I knew it, I was at the 23-mile mark.

My marathon experience brought me back to an early point in my career, when I graduated from film school in Ithaca, New York in 1988, lived in Los Angeles for a little while, then moved back home to New Jersey. People told me I would never sell a script living in New Jersey, but I sold four. Then, people told me I would never get a movie made, but I did. I really wanted to prove these things to myself, and I treated 26.2 miles the same way.

I also have three kids in their early and mid-20s. I wanted to set an example for them that you can do anything you set your mind to, and to reiterate a value that holds up in our family: to never, ever give up.

When I think about what my kids experience, I notice a lot of pressure on their generation on social media to not fail at a goal they set. In my work life, the only way I ever learned anything new with tools or construction was by trying, messing something up, and then trying to do it better. The entire marathon experience emulated that belief for me: The only way to succeed at anything is to fail a lot. That’s how you learn, grow, and get better.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and currently competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#8818. How Yonatan Katz Cracked the Boulder Nobody Could Solve at the World Climbing Series

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Climbing is what happens when you take a gym rat’s obsession with grip strength, remove the floor, and let gravity do its thing. There’s no bench to lie on, no belt to tighten, and no place to hide a weak link. You have to get your body up a wall using holds that sometimes look so bleak the edge of a credit card looks like it might offer more purchase. And if you screw up, you better hope your rope is knotted correctly.

That was on full display at the World Climbing Series bouldering finale in Salt Lake City, October 16-18. In the men’s final, Israel’s Yonatan Katz won gold on only his second start in the senior international series. He went into the final problem behind Britain’s Maximillian Milne and came out the winner after pulling off a move nobody else in the final had managed.

Here’s how it happened. The last boulder was a nasty coordination problem. Before Katz stepped up, the other finalists who had attempted it hadn’t even reached the scoring zone, a designated hold partway up the route. On his fourth try, Katz got past the zone and reached the top. He finished with 69.7 points. Milne couldn’t answer on his turn and took silver with 59.7. Japan’s Rei Kawamata was third with 54.2. For a sport that looks, to outsiders, like a bunch of people climbing a wall, there was a hell of a lot of drama hanging off those holds.

The women’s final the next day had its own story. France’s Oriane Bertone won with 84.6 points after being the only finalist to complete the first boulder. Britain’s Erin McNeice finished second with 69.7, barely ahead of Japan’s Mao Nakamura at 69.6. McNeice didn’t win that night, but she won the season-long Boulder title. She’d opened the series in 11th place and followed it with a gold and four silvers.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Sorato Anraku had already locked up the men’s overall championship after winning five of the six bouldering events. Then he failed to advance from qualification in Salt Lake City. Even the guy who dominated the season can get humbled by a fresh set of plastic holds. If bodybuilding judges replaced their comparison rounds with problems that changed every week, we’d see a few interesting faces backstage.

Bouldering is done on relatively short walls with thick mats instead of ropes. The athlete has to solve a sequence of moves, reach designated holds, and control the top. Strength matters, obviously. So does the ability to position your hips, push through your feet, generate momentum, and decide what to do before your forearms turn into concrete. Some moves are slow and surgical. Others look like a gymnast being thrown into a hardware store. The best climbers aren’t simply pulling themselves upward. They’re figuring out how to make the least-wasteful movement possible under pressure.

There’s a lesson in there for anybody who trains. A giant back and a crushing handshake don’t automatically make you good at something that requires timing, balance, and technical skill. Nor does being smaller make you weak. Climbing exposes the difference between owning strength and knowing how to use it. And if you’re tempted to try it, start with an introductory session, not an advanced overhang and a heroic declaration. A 2026 review of 45 climbing-injury studies found frequent problems involving fingers, hands, shoulders, and ankles. Those little finger pulleys weren’t designed to absorb your entire ego on day one.

I like sports that punish bullshit. Climbing is high on that list. There’s no score for looking intimidating while you chalk your hands, and no bonus for explaining how strong you’d be if the holds were bigger. Katz won because he solved a problem that had stopped the others. McNeice took the season because she kept delivering. The wall doesn’t care about your résumé, your physique, or your excuses. It only cares whether you can get to the top.

#8817. The Best Power Racks of 2025: Our Top Picks for Strength Training

Our expert shares his experience, and an Olympic lifting titleholder shares advice on choosing the best option so you get stronger with this home gym staple.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

A power rack allows you to safely perform weightlifting exercises like barbell squats and bench presses, without a spotter, in your home gym. Add-on accessories like pull-up bars, dip stations, and resistance bands can help you get the most out of your power rack, giving you the tools for a versatile full-body workout.

Whether you have limited space or are looking for a budget-friendly power rack, there are options that may work for you. We compiled a list of the best power racks for your home gym with all the details you need to find the right equipment to take your fitness routine to the next level in 2024. Shane Sevcik—a USAW-1 (USA Weightlifting) certified coach, current USA Weightlifting Foundation board member, state record holder, and Masters Pan American and World title holder—also shares his insights into what to look for in power racks.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

The REP Fitness PR-1000 Power Rack has a four-post frame made from 14-gauge steel with laser-cut holes spaced two inches apart. There are two pull-up bars—one is 1.25 inches thick, and the other is two inches thick—so you can do accessory work such as pull-ups and grip exercises without using additional space or buying a separate piece of equipment. The pull-up bars are strategically placed on the rack, spanning the front and back posts, contributing to the overall stability. There are built-in weight storage pegs on the back base for additional sturdiness. You can customize the rack using multiple accessory options such as safety straps, a dip station, and more.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., CF-L1, used this rack to do exercises like squats, bench press, strict press, pull-ups, and more for almost two years. He describes it as an intermediate or beginner rack and noticed movement while un-racking 350 pounds. “The rack held the weight just fine, but there was some swaying after I removed the bar. I’d recommend it to a beginner or someone who doesn’t lift to that capacity because I was happy with it otherwise.”

We like that the PR-1000 comes with chrome-coated safeties extending past the rack, offering an additional place for a barbell. The numbered uprights allow you to adjust the safeties or J-hooks quickly and never have to worry about your bar being crooked. “The J-hooks were easy to move, and the hole spacing of one inch is adequate to get the bar lined up where you need it,” Lunsford says. “I can attest to the functionality of the safeties; they worked great for me when I failed a heavy bench over 250 pounds.”

The Titan Fitness T-3 Series Power Rack is a wall-mounted power rack that folds to a closed position, which only sticks out five inches from the wall. The bolt-down uprights and side bracings keep it stable, so you feel comfortable lifting weights to 1,100 pounds. Those who want to use the dual pull-up bars for dynamic movements such as kipping pull-ups or toes-to-bar benefit from the added stability the floor attachment provides. The rear pull-up bar is two inches thick, and the front pull-up bar is the industry standard of 1.25 inches thick.

This rack is made from 11-gauge steel and features two-inch by three-inch tubing. Typically, newer racks have three-inch by three-inch steel tubing, so attachments from other brands may not work. Lunsford says, “A rack is an essential piece of fitness equipment. What sets them apart is the build, value, and accessories. A full power rack of this style with a weight capacity of 1,100 pounds for around $400 is an excellent bang for the buck.”

Lunsford says the brand uses manufacturing processes to elevate the overall quality. “The holes are laser cut instead of punched, and the brand uses robot welders instead of guides operated by humans.” This technique allows for more efficiency, precision, and consistency in enhanced craftsmanship. The laser-cut holes are two inches apart, and the bench and clean pull zone have Westside hole spacing—holes in the upright that are closer together for more precise positioning.

Free shipping is available on all Titan products, and a one-year warranty covers manufacturing defects and issues that may arise while using the product. One callout we have is the rack does not come with safety arms, which range in price from $90 to $190, depending on which type you get. The rackable weight capacity is 1,100 pounds, but the included J-cups are rated up to 1,000 pounds, so if you want to move heavier weights, you’ll need to upgrade the J-cups.

Titan offers several accessories for purchase separately, including safety bars or straps, stabilizer feet, spotter arms, pin and pipe safety set, or an extension kit to upgrade to six uprights. Other customization options include choosing from a black, red, or blue rack color, two rack depths and heights, or adding a four-pack of weight plate holders.

At only 72 inches tall (six feet), the REP PR-1050 Short Power Rack is a solution for home gyms with low ceilings, such as garages or basements. This equipment has a sturdy yet compact footprint of 58 by 48 inches and supports up to 700 pounds.

While this power rack is short, it provides a solid range of features. It comes with dual pull-up bars (supporting up to 400 pounds), numbered upright holes spaced two inches apart, rear base weight horns, chrome-coated safeties, and plastic-lined J-cups. It’s also compatible with various add-on attachments, including cannonball grips for grip strength exercises and landmine attachments for exercises including landmine presses and rows.

The Fringe Sport Retractable Power Rack is an excellent option if your garage or home gym is tight on space because it is compact and easily stored. This convenient home power rack can be retracted and folded inward or outward for storage. When retracted, it only sticks out five inches from the wall. It has a compact base and can support up to 800 pounds.

The uprights are two-by-three-inch 11-gauge steel and feature Westside spacing in the bench zone. You can set the rack’s 1.25-inch diameter pull-up bar to multiple heights. It’s 91 inches tall, which may not be ideal for low ceilings.

The unit comes with J-hooks coated with ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMW), a strong, abrasion-resistant material, to protect your barbell. Fringe Sport provides an installation video to help guide you through the installation of this power rack. It includes four mounting brackets and six detent pins to lock the rack in position.

The Sunny Health & Fitness Power Zone Strength Rack Power Cage Squat Rack has a pulley system attachment for lat pulldowns and adjustable resistance you can load with weight plates up to the 352-pound limit. You can use the lat pulldown attachment for exercises like upright rows and curls. When you aren’t using the attachment, built-in safety hook latches provide easy storage for the top long or short lever bar.

This power rack has features to help you get a well-rounded workout. The adjustable angled pull-up bar has four positions, including wide and narrow grips. The J-hooks have 18 vertical height settings, and the spotter bars with safety latches help you squat with heavier weights. There are six resistance band pins, for additional resistance against the bar.

The Rogue Fitness R-3 Power Rack is the most compact option in Rogue’s R-Series and is an excellent option for a home garage gym. This power rack comes in two height options—90.4 inches or 84.4 inches—so it works in garages and home gyms with low ceilings.

This rack is made of heavy-duty 11-gauge steel with Westside spacing (a type of spacing that allows for granular control of bar placement, such as barbells and safety bars) through the bench in a one-inch pattern and two-inch spacing above and below the bench. The unit is compatible with various Rogue Infinity Series add-on attachments, such as the Rogue Matador, fully adjustable dip handles, or a bar hanger for barbell weight storage.

The unit has a 43-inch pull-up bar, infinity J-cups, pin/pipe safeties, and four band pegs. You can customize this rack by adding a bar, bench, or plates to your purchase on the Rogue Fitness website. This unit is versatile enough for various exercises, including low rows, pull-ups, chin-ups, squats, bench presses, powerlifting, CrossFit, and Olympic lifting.

The Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has an official weight capacity of 800 pounds. This unit can help anyone hit their goals, from beginners to elite powerlifters.

Like all good squat racks, the Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has solid steel safety arms rather than hollow tubes. It features two rear stability bars. Thanks to 19 adjustable height levels, you can use the unit for various exercises besides squats, including pull-ups, chin-ups, bench presses, and overhead presses. And it’s $299, the most affordable option on our list.

It has a multi-grip pull-up bar and two 23-inch safety bars with chrome locks. While it doesn’t come with J-hooks, dip bars, or plate storage attachments, one-inch holes allow you to use this equipment with standard-sized attachments.

A power rack—or power cage—has four uprights designed to serve as a base for powerlifting, Olympic lifting, and other strength training. They are commonly used with a barbell but may have optional attachments for non-barbell exercises using cables or body weight. A full power rack allows athletes to lift inside or outside the cage. Half racks have two uprights, so athletes must lift outside the rack because there is less depth.

Research links strength training, including weightlifting, to long-term health benefits like reducing disease.

A power rack provides equipment, like safety bars, to help you lift heavy weights safely without a spotter. Some power racks come with add-on attachments, such as pull-up bars and dip bars, to help you get a well-rounded workout. Additionally, most power racks are compatible with accessories you can buy for an extra price to customize your workout for your needs.

Exercisers use a power rack for strength training, Olympic lifting, and powerlifting. Additional attachments, such as a dip station or pull-up bar, allow you to use it for bodyweight exercises. Some have pulley systems for other resistance exercises.

Correctly using a power rack can successfully enhance strength training. “It’s all about consistency,” Sevcik says. “Make sure you have some kind of progressive overload built into your programming.”

Power racks provide a safe lifting experience, which is of utmost importance, especially if you plan on training alone. The safety straps, pins, or arms—also called safeties—are a critical safety feature. “One of my biggest pet peeves is when I see people who don’t know how to set the safety arms the right way and have the pins set way too low,” Sevcik says. “The purpose of those safety arms is to give you a safe way to bail out of a lift. Otherwise, you’re just using a power rack as a big immobile squat stand.”

So, what is the correct way to set up the safety arms? “To set them up for squats, put the unloaded bar on your back and squat down to the deepest position you can get yourself into,” Sevcik says. “The safety bars should be about an inch and a half or one notch lower than your bottom position, so if you ever fail on a squat, all you do is sit your butt down to the very bottom.”

Many come with safety arms, pins, or nylon straps, but some budget options may require purchasing them separately. If you’re new to using a power rack, we recommend asking a fitness professional for guidance on different exercises and safety.

Before purchasing, measure your space and look at the rack’s total footprint. While measuring the floor and comparing it to the base is essential, ceiling height is another crucial factor. You may need a shorter option if you use your rack in a basement or a room with low ceilings.

You can retract and store a folding power rack if you’re limited in space or need room for other activities. It’s a good idea to consider your height and weight when looking at the dimensions, especially if you plan to use the pull-up bar or other attachments. You may want to leave space on each side for accessories so you can attach them on the sides if necessary. We recommend you keep the space around the rack clear of obstructions, particularly in front, so you can safely complete your lifts or bailout.

Power racks come in a variety of styles, colors, and materials. Some construction and style factors to consider include:

The power racks on this list have capacities ranging from 700 pounds to 1,100 pounds. The lower and middle weight range will likely work for you if you are a beginner or intermediate exerciser. If you are an advanced athlete, you may want to opt for a power rack with a high weight capacity and heavy-duty steel. Attachments such as safety arms, J-hooks, or pull-up bars have varying weight limits. Always stay within the recommended weight range for your safety.

How much you’re willing to spend depends on your budget and training style. Many racks on this list include a basic setup, with the option to add accessories as needed, which cuts the cost. Other racks come fully loaded with accessories, so they are incredibly versatile. However, these options cost more, so it is crucial to consider the features and whether or not they are helpful for your workout style and goals. The racks on this list range from around $299 to $965, and many brands offer free shipping.

Power racks come in various styles and features. The following sections break down Sevcik’s power rack must-haves.

Sevcik says to look for thick, heavy-duty steel such as 11-gauge. “A rack made out of thicker steel creates more leverage on the uprights. Especially when you add those attachments.”

“I think a big must-have a lot of people overlook is to make sure your J-cups, or J-hooks, have some coating on them to preserve the knurling on your bar,” Sevcik says. “If you’re doing a bench press or deadlift, [knurling] is no big deal, but if you’re an Olympic weightlifter, that’s where my snatch grip is holding onto, and I want it to be as sharp and aggressive as possible.”

“I would make sure you have enough hole patterns to make a lot of adjustments. Sometimes, they’re too spaced out, for example, in two-inch increments instead of one,” Sevcik says. “I like to have the added adjustability, especially for those heavier weights.”

Sevcik says having the option to do pull-ups is a good idea. “They’re one of the most basic, fundamental movements. Plus, if you dedicate the square footage to put the rack in there, you’ll want to get as much utility as possible because you are sacrificing some real estate.”

“It’s important to have the option to add accessories,” Sevcik says. “You might not want a dip bar right now, but down the road, you may decide to incorporate more dips in the training program, and it sure is nice to have your power rack as your one central piece of equipment.”

Many power racks come with attachments, though certain brands require you to purchase add-on attachments separately. Some of the power racks on this list come with pull-up bars (chin-up bar), safeties, and J-cups included, while others do not. It’s important to read the details of what comes with your unit to know what additional purchases you’ll need to make to achieve your desired power rack workout.

We considered the following while choosing each product on this list:

We chose budget-friendly and high-end options suitable for any fitness level and listed several compact and folding options for those with limited space. We also spoke to Shane Sevcik, a USAW-certified coach and competitive athlete, about essential add-ons and safety features.

Research suggests 30 to 60 minutes a week of muscle-strengthening exercises can benefit your health. With the help of a power rack, you can achieve a wide range of strength training fitness moves without needing a spotter. A power rack can add convenience to your workout by enabling you to get a safe weightlifting workout anytime from the comfort of your home gym.

A full power rack has four to six uprights attached by cross members, creating a cage to lift in. A squat rack—also called a squat stand—is typically two uprights and weighs less than a power rack, making it more portable. Power racks are more versatile, with the option to add accessories, while squat racks usually do not.

If you choose a freestanding power rack, anchor it following the manufacturer’s instructions to ensure it’s safe and secure.

Generally, a freestanding power rack should be a few feet from the wall so you can perform exercises comfortably and safely. Always refer to the manufacturer’s guidelines and recommendations when setting up your rack.

Common gauges are 11-gauge and 12-gauge, with lower numbers providing thicker and stronger steel; however, these tend to be more pricey options. A thinner 14-gauge steel is slightly less sturdy but likely works well for a general home gym setup. We chose racks ranging from 11-gauge to 16-gauge to suit various budgets and fitness levels.

Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC, is a writer and editor in the fitness and nutrition industries. She has contributed to PowerliftingTechnique, FeastGood, Garage Gym Reviews, BarBend, and Fitbod. When she's not working, you can find her training in her garage gym; cuddling with her dog, Charlie; trying to keep her two cats, Raven and Riley, from destroying her house; or hanging out with her family - all with a cup of coffee close by.

The Breaking Muscle newsletter is everything you need to know about strength in a 3 minute read.

Breaking Muscle is the fitness world’s preeminent destination for timely, high-quality information on exercise, fitness, health, and nutrition. Our audience encompasses the entire spectrum of the fitness community: consumers, aficionados, fitness professionals, and business owners. We seek to inform, educate and advocate for this community.

#8816. After Hitting Rock Bottom, an Army Veteran Went for a Run With a Plan to End His Life. Then He Heard a Familiar Military Command He Couldn’t Ignore.

For years, Jeremy Hurtt asked himself: “Why should I be alive when better people weren’t?”

Editor’s Note: This story contains a mention of suicide. If you or someone you know is struggling with suicidal thoughts or self-harming behaviors, call or text 988 to get help from the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.

Jeremy Hurtt woke up that winter morning in 2014, and after staring at the ceiling for a few minutes, headed out for a run, thinking it may be his last.

He headed toward the spot where the run—and everything else—could end. An overpass above an interstate in the town of Benton, Arkansas, a mile from the house he had been crashing in for the past few weeks, sleeping on a cold floor, getting by on the generosity of a friend. Money had troubled Jeremy for years. He did odd jobs around town for a few bucks, but mostly was bumming $10 and $20 from friends just to get by. He was 34 years old, with nothing in the bank, no home, no car, not even a driver’s license. All these little indignities, piling up, had started to bury him.

Since finishing a deployment in Iraq in 2008, there’d been lots of days when Jeremy felt down, depressed—and seemed different from the playful, clownish, upbeat guy his Army pals and others had come to know. “He was no longer good-time Jeremy,” one friend says. “He was withdrawn, reclusive.” But he never seriously thought about hurting himself. Until that morning when the indignities were too many, and his mind couldn’t stop wondering why he was still alive and better people weren’t.

The overpass was a destination he had crossed before. On walks and runs when he was up for it. At that early-morning hour, semitrucks would be rushing below. He, on the other hand, wasn’t rushing, running at his usual 8-to-9-minute pace, which let his mind race ahead. Running was something he had done occasionally, a means to an end after his return home from Iraq, a way to stay somewhat fit. That morning, running was the means to get where he needed to go.

He thought of what would happen if he decided to jump. About the driver whose vehicle would likely strike him once he landed on the road. He didn’t want to cause another person pain. He knew from his time in Iraq the pain that comes with sudden death. But even this good intention couldn’t deter him from running ahead.

He gave little thought to what might happen if he didn’t jump.

He neared the overpass. A short way to go. The sound of semis intensified. Just a little farther. A railing on the overpass to climb over. The poor driver. One more step.

And then he heard something else. Words in his head.

If you’ve been in the military, you know Charlie-Mike. You may have heard the call, the command. Jeremy followed it often when stationed in Iraq in the mid–to-late aughts. It was a time when improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and explosively formed penetrators (EFPs) got mentioned on the nightly news as often as sports scores and tomorrow’s forecast. When American troops tried to end chaos in a country exacerbated by American miscalculation.

Charlie-Mike is military code: Continue the Mission. Move forward. In the face of adversity. No matter what.

There was no shortage of adversity in Iraq, which the U.S. invaded in 2003. By the time the U.S. Central Command announced the final withdrawal of troops this past September, more than 4,300 American troops had been killed. Jeremy Hurtt served there for 15 months, during the 2006–2008 surge. What he saw and heard, and those he met and those he lost, remain fresh in his mind. He and his troop—Alpha 3/61—were fired upon often; sometimes they stopped until they heard the command. Like the memories of friends who didn’t come home from their deployment, he’s never forgotten Charlie-Mike.

At that moment atop the overpass, Charlie-Mike dominated his thoughts—pushing out all others. It triggered, he says now, “a moment of clarity.” Everything is a mission. “You’re not done,” he recalls thinking that morning. “You’re not done until you get to where you’re supposed to be.” To him, that meant he couldn’t stop running—or living.

Jeremy ran until he was back at his friend’s house. He had a plan, one he put into action a couple of days later. And as the plan unfolded in the weeks and months that followed, the running intensified. Longer and longer distances. Not fast miles, just miles.

But as much as he’s run in the years since that January morning, Jeremy has never outrun what ultimately brought him to the overpass in the first place.

Jeremy Hurtt comes from Harrison, Arkansas, a town in the Ozarks. When he was a kid, the town had maybe 9,000 residents. “It’s big,” Jeremy, now 47, says with a slight chuckle. “There’s not a town that size for 90 minutes in any direction. Growing up, my cousins called me a city boy because I was from Harrison.”

In many ways, it had the comforts—and trappings—of the South. Like nearby Bull Shoals Lake, filled with smallmouth bass that made for easy fishing. Jeremy’s dad, a semipro fisherman, showed him all the tricks. Come the fall, football ruled. University of Arkansas Razorbacks, with their wishbone offense. When he wasn’t watching them on TV, Jeremy played ball himself. Even though he was barely 5 feet when he got to high school, he earned a spot as a wide receiver and safety on the school’s team. But for all the fun, at home his mom, Frances, kept priorities in order. “She was definitely one of those Bible-thumpin’ Southern Christian Baptists,” says Jeremy’s older brother, Jason. “We were raised in the church, and we always had that voice in our head, even when she wasn’t around.”

After high school, Jeremy followed many of his classmates to the University of Arkansas. He liked being away from home, living in the bigger city of Fayetteville, far from his mother’s rules. He was social, made friends easily, and bonded with many over his love of the Razorbacks. He attended games, as well as the pre- and postgame tailgates. He could go out on a Saturday night, and Friday and Thursday, too. The parties and the drinking came easy for the garrulous kid from Harrison. But his grades suffered, and by the end of his freshman year, his time in college had ended. Jeremy, who friends say was one of the smartest guys they knew, was “asked not to come back” for year two.

That summer, back in Harrison, he kept drinking, hanging out, working a dead-end job at a local newspaper. It was leading nowhere, and that didn’t sit well with Frances. One night he returned home to some tough talk. “My mom basically came to me,” he remembers, “and was like, ‘You’ve got a decision to make; you’re not going to sit here forever. You’re gonna figure out what you’re doing next.’” She’d already done some groundwork for him, talking with a local Army office. Jeremy followed up with a recruiter, thinking it would “get her off my back.” Instead, he was tantalized by prospects of a steady paycheck and career options following his service time. And, the recruiter told Jeremy, it was peacetime. There was no war to worry about. Jeremy enlisted right away and within days was headed to basic training.

It was September 1998. Peace wouldn’t last forever.

These days, Jeremy Hurtt loves to run hills. He’ll track his runs, aiming to hit 2,000 feet of elevation during a 13-miler. The effort calms him, lets him think. “The feeling of pushing yourself,” he says, “and trying to improve yourself.”

Running and hillwork weren’t always his forte, though, especially in boot camp where, as a college dropout, he was learning what discipline was all about. “I never was a huge running fan,” he says, “and I hated hills. I just couldn’t stand it, you know? I’d get halfway up a hill and just want to quit.”

After basic training, he was first stationed in South Korea and then assigned to a communications role in Washington, D.C. Some days he worked in the Pentagon. Life was good. He made friends with the other enlisted soldiers, who got to know Jeremy as the quick-witted guy from the Ozarks. The one who’d send his buddies off-color emails to get a chuckle or impress them by demonstrating how to download music for free. “I was always trying to make people laugh,” he says. They loved hanging out with him, especially after a cocktail or two. “He was a really smart guy, really funny, and he definitely enjoyed the world he was in,” says Dillon Cunningham, who was stationed with Jeremy at the time. He pauses a moment. “And then, you know, 9/11 happened.”

Jeremy was not in the Pentagon on September 11, 2001, when a hijacked American Airlines plane crashed into the building, killing the 64 passengers on board and 125 military and civilians; he was doing fieldwork a few miles away. Amid the horrors and chaos of the events unfolding, it would take days before he could contact his mother and tell her he was OK.

Until 9/11, Jeremy’s path in the Army had gone according to plan. “My idea was [not] to go anywhere near combat,” he says. But the terrorist attacks that took nearly 3,000 lives changed his mind. One of his grandfathers had served in World War II. Jason, his brother, was already stationed in Turkey with the Air Force. Jeremy no longer wanted to serve within the relatively safe confines of his communications posting, testing radios and satellite switches. In 2003, he asked to be assigned to a cavalry unit so he could prep for deployment. He was 25 years old. “It was just a feeling that this is the moment for my generation,” Jeremy says. “I wanted to be directly involved in whatever came next.”

It would take three years before Sgt. Jeremy Hurtt learned what next involved—and how it would test him like no hill ever could.

Come fall in the Ozarks, the Buffalo River, where Jeremy and his friends used to raft in the summer, is still just deep enough for one last excursion. And the Arkansas Razorbacks are back on the field, offering once more a promise to their diehard fans.

But in the fall of 2006, Jeremy was in Iraq and missed all that. Home was 7,000 miles away—and somehow felt even farther. On his first full night in Baghdad, a rocket struck his barrack. It didn’t explode, and no one was injured, but Jeremy now had firsthand experience of combat life. “It wasn’t like that all the time,” he says. But it was clear to him that “there are people who want me dead. They are going to try to kill me.”

For much of his time, Jeremy and his troop were on security detail. They patrolled sectors in Sadr City and East Baghdad, scanning rooftops and street corners, searching for “high-value targets” to capture or kill. “There’s some combat; occasionally people shoot at you,” he says. “It’s a lot more common for them to try to blow you up.”

He recalls just one of many incidents. One afternoon in 2007, Alpha 3/61 was southwest of Sadr City. They were in six armored vehicles, Jeremy with his M240 machine gun on lookout in the third Humvee. Without warning, an EFP, the most lethal form of homemade explosive used against Coalition troops during the war, tore through the backside of the lead Humvee. The warhead narrowly missed Sgt. Matt Haeffner, Jeremy’s roommate, who sustained a concussion in the blast.

As Haeffner recalls, Jeremy was one of the first in his troop to check on him. “We’ll be friends forever because we shared crazy moments like that,” says Haeffner, who was awarded a Purple Heart following the EFP attack. “My wife calls it trauma bonding.”

Not all of Jeremy’s friends in Iraq made it home. Sgt. Eric Snell, a father of two, was killed during a small-arms fire in Baghdad. He was charismatic, Jeremy remembers, a former pro baseball player with the looks of a model. And there was Sgt. Alexander Fuller, who died when his Humvee struck an improvised bomb. “His wife was pregnant with their first child,” Jeremy says. Jeremy knew both Snell and Fuller from his earliest days in the Cavalry. And then there were the eight men from his troop who died in a vicious battle in Afghanistan. That was hard on Jeremy, who, by then, had finished his deployment and was back in Arkansas and a world away from the fighting.

The distance added to his sense of guilt. Should he have re-upped for another tour and gone with his former troop to Afghanistan? Why did Snell and Fuller die, and not him? Why did the dumb drunk, as Jeremy thought of himself, get to live and those men did not?

“I always thought it’s a trade that anybody would have made. If you could trade me for Fuller and he gets to see his daughter grow up—I think people would make that trade,” Jeremy says. “And keep Snell around for his kid; that trade would make sense.” He pauses for a second. “To me, it just always seemed like a cruel joke—those people didn’t get to experience their lives, and I was still here.”

So he’d keep asking himself, “Why should I be alive when better people weren’t?”

Back in Arkansas, Jeremy didn’t forget what he saw, and what he was missing. He couldn’t find much work, but found plenty to drink. Within a year of returning home, his weight went from 170 pounds to 230. In Iraq, he ran occasionally, when the situation allowed, sweating in the desert heat. So when he got prodded by friends to enter a local weight-loss competition, he turned to running to peel the pounds away. “I was running up and down hills and in the heat and humidity of Arkansas,” he says, “so it came off pretty quickly.”

Bringing order and routine to other parts of life proved more challenging. For a time, he returned to the University of Arkansas, starting fresh. He tried majoring in broadcasting but never made it to graduation. He found a variety of part-time jobs, including production work at an ESPN radio affiliate. Nothing stuck. A girlfriend came and went. Alcohol was the only constant.

Fireworks on the Fourth of July or at a football game made him edgy. He’d drive through an underpass, see trash on the side of the road, and wonder if it was concealing an IED. He’d suddenly remember Snell. “He was my favorite soldier ever, and got killed the day I went on leave,” he says, his eyes watering. He waits a moment. “That all rolled up into the guilt, everything, I felt for a lot of years afterward.”

Friends and family noticed a different Jeremy from the one they knew before deployment. “I remember linking up with him a few times, catching up, and it was like a shell,” Dillon Cunningham recalls. “He was there, but there wasn’t anything solid in there. You could quickly tell he was not operating at the specs we used to expect from him.”

Once they began to notice the changes, his friends and family began to worry.

Twenty-two. It’s a number “that really sticks heavily in most military guys’ heads,” Jason says. For nearly a decade, 22 referred to the number of deaths by suicide among U.S. military veterans each day. Several suicide prevention organizations have 22 in their names. The number is on flags and tattoos to promote awareness. Various versions of a 22 Push-Up Challenge ask participants to do 22 daily push-ups for 22 days. Even though the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs downgraded the number of suicides to 17.7 per day in 2024, 22 remains code for those in the know.

Jason worried his brother might become a statistic.

“The power that the brain has when you get yourself in certain situations—if you don’t have those people to talk to, you do just fall down a drain,” Jason says. “And the unfortunate thing is, so many people don’t know who to talk to. A perfect example is Jeremy; he lost his buddies. Those may have been the guys he talked to and that he felt good with. Well, they’re gone, and so he starts going down that drain.”

Jason became Jeremy’s lifeline. On that morning in 2014, when Jeremy didn’t jump from the overpass, he got back to his friend’s house and called his brother, who was living outside of St. Louis, several hundred miles away. He didn’t talk about his suicidal thoughts, but asked for help finding work, getting back on track. Jason didn’t hesitate. He got Jeremy a job on his crew that worked on upgrading cell towers. He’d be on the road a lot, and the hours would be unpredictable, but the work would be steady and bring in a paycheck—and a group of coworkers to be around. And after his shifts, Jeremy could go for a run, which he often did, in the same pair of basketball sneakers he wore to work.

Jeremy never sought professional counseling, but he suspects he was suffering from PTSD. Getting psychological help is not something many veterans choose to pursue, his brother says. “When you come home, and you go talk to someone that has the sheepskin on the wall,” Jason says, “they say they know how a brain works. [But] you start talking to them, and there’s a major disconnect. These people have no idea what you’re talking about.”

Jeremy found a different kind of help, a different way to cope. The simple act of putting one foot in front of the other that brought clarity to his mind like nothing else. It interrupted the repetitive negative thoughts rumbling in his head. “So many troops find things to soothe their pain—if that’s gentlemen’s clubs, beer, drugs, whatever,” says Jason, who now works as a helicopter pilot for the FAA. “Jeremy was smart enough to channel that into running, and running was that savior for him.”

Jeremy started paying off debts. With the technical skills acquired from his past communication job, he eventually got a job with a company doing software testing. By 2018, he had saved enough to buy a place in a wooded, secluded area back in the Ozarks. Hills were nearby. That was when his love for accumulating elevation kicked in. He entered some races—he’s run the Little Rock Marathon three times, with a PR of 4:55:58—but preferred running solo.

And on those solo runs, he could finally start processing what he lived through in Iraq.

Jeremy has never mentioned his run to the overpass to Jason or Matt Haeffner or Dillon Cunningham. In fact, the only person he’s told is his wife, Stacie. They met online before his deployment to Iraq and stayed in touch for nearly a decade. In 2014, they reconnected. Stacie was living in Nashville at the time, and Jeremy was in the area working on a cell tower job. They went on a few dates, kept texting and calling when Jeremy’s job was done and he was back in Arkansas. Then, at the end of 2019, when Jeremy was living alone in his house in the woods, he texted Stacie that he wanted to be more serious. “He had been running,” she remembers, “and he was like, ‘I really think we’re supposed to give this a real shot.’ I was like, ‘OK, let’s figure this out.’” She packed up and moved to Arkansas. “We were engaged in a few months,” she says with a smile.

And by 2021, they were married. Friends from around the country came to the wedding. They saw the Jeremy they remembered from before Iraq. Sort of. The night before the wedding, a group of Army friends got together in his house. The laughter was flowing, and so were the drinks. But before it got too late, Jeremy told his buddies he was headed to bed. “You can imagine military guys—we were like, ‘Oh, come on, man. You’re getting married. Screw that,’” Dillon says. “And he was like, ‘I gotta run a half marathon in the morning. I run a half marathon every Saturday.’” On the morning of his wedding, Jeremy ran, showered, and made it to the ceremony with time to spare.

This past June, Stacie and Jeremy welcomed a new member to the family. Baby Josephine. She keeps Mom and Dad busy, so Jeremy has cut back on running. He might get a short one in during the workweek. Come the weekend, though, Stacie gives him the green light and lets him go long. And at an 11-minute pace, he runs his half marathon.

“I don’t think it was trivial that I ran to that overpass,” he says, sitting in the den of their home outside of Houston, where they moved just before Josephine was born. “There’s something that happens in a run where, like, I have breakthroughs and insight. And I think that’s what happened that day. The mile I took to run to that overpass gave me just enough to be in a moment. It all kind of clicked into place.” Jeremy waits a second. He thinks back a dozen years. “I was—excuse my frankness—bullshitting away the opportunity. I had to be here, in this experience of being alive.”

Just then, Josephine starts stirring. Jeremy Hurtt has to go. He has a mission to get back to.

Charles Butler, a former editor at Runner's World, now teaches journalism at the University of Oregon. With Matt Long, he wrote The Long Run: A New York City Firefighter's Triumphant Comeback from Crash Victim to Elite Athlete.

#8815. The Glute Training Guide for a Stronger and More Powerful Posterior

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Not every muscle gets immortalized in a rap song, but the glutes do more than look good in pants. Beyond the vanity benefits, the glutes help you do fun things in and out of the gym.

Although the gluteus maximus gets all the attention, the gluteus medius and minimus provide the stability that lets the glute max do its job better. That’s why it’s important to focus on all three, not just one.

Compound lifts hit them hard and heavy, but isolation exercises are necessary to train all glute functions and muscles. You can also load them in different ways: from a lengthened position (think RDL) and from a shortened position (think Hip Thrust).

Understanding those differences, rather than choosing sides in the great squat-versus-hip-thrust debate, is key to better glute training.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gQnMPHoDGEc

Each glute muscle has a different role, and understanding them will help you train them more effectively.

It’s the largest and most superficial of the three muscles, and it’s responsible for much of your backside’s size and shape. Although it’s best known for hip extension and external rotation, some lower fibers can assist with hip adduction depending on hip position, while the upper fibers assist with hip abduction.

The gluteus medius sits on the lateral side of your pelvis, partly beneath the gluteus maximus. Its primary job is hip abduction, but it also helps stabilize the pelvis. It also has different muscle fibers that perform different jobs. The anterior fibers assist with hip internal rotation, while the posterior fibers can contribute to external rotation.

The gluteus minimus is the smallest and deepest of the three, sitting underneath the glute medius. It assists with hip abduction and internal rotation while helping control the femur’s position within the hip joint. It also works with the glute medius to stabilize the pelvis when one foot leaves the ground.

The hip is a ball-and-socket joint that allows your hips to flex, extend, abduct, adduct, and rotate. But not everyone’s ball-and-socket joint is built the same way.

The depth and orientation of your hip socket, the angle of your femoral neck, and how much your femur rotates forward or backward vary from person to person. These structural differences influence exercise selection and positions.

Some squat with a narrow stance and toes pointed forward, while others go wider with toes pointed out. Your hip anatomy, mobility, strength, and limb length all influence what position works best for you. Adjusting your stance, foot position, and range of motion can help you find positions that load the glutes effectively and work with your anatomy.

Your glutes are among the body’s most powerful muscles, and paying attention to your backside pays off in more ways than one.

Glutes give you the horsepower to do the things you enjoy, from squatting to sprinting to other daily activities. The stronger they are, the more force they can produce, especially when you pair that strength with power training.

In many unilateral movements like walking, running, walking upstairs, and single-leg RDLs, smaller glute muscles control your lower-body position. Weakness can show up in a loss of balance, excessive wobbling in a single-leg stance, or your knee caving inward during squats and deadlifts. You don’t want any of that.

Your hips, knees, and lower back are teammates, and when one struggles, another may compensate. Weak glute med and glute min can cause knee valgus, which your knee ligaments don’t like. Weak hip extension strength or limited hip mobility forces the lower back to do a job it’s not designed for. Training the glutes for strength and mobility prevents this.

Almost every powerful lower-body movement involves the glutes.

During sprinting, the gluteus maximus drives powerful hip extension. When you cut, land, or change direction, all three glute muscles help control the hip and pelvis as your body absorbs and redirects force. The glutes also contribute to rotational movements, such as swinging a bat, throwing a punch, and a golf swing. Their ability to produce force and rotate helps link lower-body movement to upper-body power.

Here’s what your glutes need to grow bigger and stronger.

Compound exercises such as barbell squats, Romanian deadlifts, and barbell hip thrusts let the glutes produce force alongside the quads, hamstrings, and adductors, making them an excellent foundation for building strength and muscle.

Deep squats, front-foot elevated split squats, and deficit reverse lunges put a loaded stretch where you need it most. Because the hips are flexed and the glutes are lengthened, they can build greater muscle. Bonus points for using a controlled lowering phase.

Barbell hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickback variations emphasize hip extension as the glutes approach their shortened position, given their smaller range of motion.

Neither approach is better, but both can help develop the glutes.

Hip abduction machines, lateral band walks, and side-lying hip raises train the gluteus medius, minimus, and the upper fibers of the gluteus maximus. These improve hip stability, allowing the glute max to work more effectively.

Seated band hip internal rotation, cable hip external rotation, and seated 90/90 hip rotations rotate the thigh within the hip joint while keeping the pelvis and lower back locked in. Rotational training supports hip stability, health, and more complete lower-body development.

The dreaded Bulgarian split squats, single-leg RDL’s, and step-ups train one leg at a time, improving hip stability. Unilateral exercises challenge the glutes to produce force and stabilize the pelvis, improving balance while strengthening imbalances between sides.

You don’t need 15 different glute exercises, but the right combination of movements that cover their various functions without turning every leg day into a marathon.

Start With Compound Bilateral And Unilateral Lifts

Compound lower-body lifts are the foundation of glute training because they let you go hard and heavy while other muscles join the party. But here’s an important distinction: Many compound lifts don’t isolate the glutes.

Compound lifts build strength and muscle, but moving more total weight doesn’t always mean the glutes get all the love. Squat depth, torso angle, hip position, and exercise technique influence how much work the glutes perform.

You need more than one type of hip-extension exercise because different movements challenge the glutes at different muscle lengths. Romanian deadlifts, full-range-of-motion squats, and front-foot elevated split squats load the glutes when they’re lengthened, while hip thrusts, glute bridges, and cable kickbacks emphasize tension closer to full hip extension, when the glutes are shorter.

Both can build size and strength, and each offers something the other doesn’t.

Don’t get caught up in the Team Squat versus Team Hip Thrust debate. Include exercises that challenge the glutes at both longer and shorter lengths, use a full range of motion you can control, and overload when you can.

Debates don’t build muscle. Training does.

Compound exercises train the glute med and mini, but direct hip-abduction exercises give them extra attention. When they’re stronger, your glute max can go to work unencumbered.

Broad jumps, sled pushes, hill sprints, and lateral bounds powerfully train the glutes and fire up your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which drive many of your gains. These exercises are great if you want your strength to carry over to athletic activities.

Your glutes can only work within the ranges your hips can access and control. Include half-kneeling hip flexor stretches with a posterior pelvic tilt, adductor rockbacks, 90/90 hip rotations, and prying squats in your warm-up to prepare for the work ahead.

The trick to training your glutes well is balancing heavy lifting, muscle-building work, and stability exercises while giving your backside enough time to recover. Here’s how to make it work.

Perform lower-body compound exercises, both bilateral and unilateral, with challenging weights. Maintain your technique and rest two to three minutes, or longer, between sets. Focus on progressive overload without sacrificing range of motion.

Again, use compound lower-body exercises that hit both lengthened and shortened positions, with a controlled eccentric contraction and full range of motion, training close to technical failure. Although muscle growth can happen across a wider rep range, this range balances load, effort, and fatigue.

Perform power movements early in your workout when you’re fresh, focus on maximum movement speed and quality, and rest 2 minutes or longer when needed to maintain explosiveness.

Hip abduction machines, cable abductions, and side-lying variations allow you to focus on the smaller glute muscles. Use controlled reps, avoid momentum, and progress the load.

Single-leg RDLs, step-ups, and Bulgarian split squats build strength while challenging stability. Only progress as your strength and balance improve.

Your weekly training volume should include all glute-focused exercises. Use the following table as a guideline, not a rule set in stone.

Some exercises train several qualities at once. A Bulgarian split squat challenges glute strength, muscle growth, and stability, but you don’t count the same set three times. Assign each set to its primary programming purpose (muscle/stability) when using the table.

For most lifters, two to three sessions per week is a good starting point.

Beginners can split their weekly work into two sessions, while intermediate lifters can use two or three. Experienced lifters focused on glute development will benefit from spreading the work over three sessions to maintain training quality.

Training your glutes isn’t rocket science, but you can make it harder than it needs to be. Here’s what to watch for and how to fix it.

Hip thrusts and bridge variations are excellent for building the glutes from the shortened position, but making them your only option misses opportunities to challenge the muscles at longer lengths and train hip abduction and stability.

The fix: Combine hip thrusts with RDLs, squats, split squats, and direct hip abduction exercises to cover more of the glutes’ functions.

It’s tempting to focus on exercises where you can really feel the squeeze, but muscle growth isn’t determined by how hard you can contract your glutes at lockout. RDLs, deep squats, and front-foot-elevated split squats challenge the glutes at longer muscle lengths, providing a different training stimulus.

The fix: Include at least one exercise that loads the glutes during greater hip flexion.

When chasing the squeeze or extra ROM in a hip thrust, deadlift, or RDL variation, some lifters extend their lower back instead of their glutes. Overarching your back at the top creates movement that doesn’t originate in the hips and shifts the focus away from where it belongs.

The fix: Keep your ribs over your hips, extend through your hips, and stop when you reach lockout.

The gluteus maximus gets the glory, but the smaller glute muscles help stabilize your pelvis, support the ball-and-socket movement, and produce hip abduction. Relying on compound lower-body exercises may leave these muscles undertrained.

The fix: Include band, cable, or machine hip abduction variations to give these smaller muscles the attention they deserve.

There’s one camp that says all you need for glutes is squats. Another camp says hip thrusts are all you need. Opinions run wild, so let’s separate fact from fiction.

Squats are fantastic for building glutes from a lengthened position, but the glutes need more than that, as they don’t challenge every glute function.

The truth: No one doubts squats are great for glutes, but training from a shortened position and direct hip-abduction exercises provide a different stimulus that can enhance muscle development.

Doing a set of hip thrusts tells you you’re engaging your glutes, but just because you “feel” it more doesn’t mean hip thrusts are better than squats for building muscle. Greater muscle activation during an exercise doesn’t necessarily translate into greater long-term muscle growth.

The truth: Research comparing hip thrusts and squats shows both build the glutes effectively, despite their different mechanics. For some, it comes down to personal preference.

Influencers with great glutes will scream from the rooftops that you can isolate and build an upper-glute shelf and a better lower-glute hamstring tie-in. But here’s some fact behind that fiction: The glute maximus has different fiber orientations that contribute to hip extension, abduction, adduction, and rotation.

The truth: Certain exercises and hip positions can shift the emphasis toward different glute regions, but you cannot turn off one area while training another. This is similar to what I explored in the upper- and lower-ab training myth.

If you walk up the stairs or sit down in slow motion after glute day, you might assume you’ve had the greatest glute workout ever. Hold your jeans.

The truth: Extreme muscle soreness usually signals a new training stimulus or heavy eccentric loading, and it isn’t a reliable measure of muscle gain.

Adjust the loads, sets, reps, and exercise variations to match your experience and recovery. Perform them as standalone sessions or fit them into your existing program.

Rest periods: Rest two to three minutes after each superset and 90 seconds between exercises.

Progressive overload: When you reach the upper end of a rep range with clean technique, increase the load slightly.

Manage weekly volume: The full-body workout includes nine glute-focused resistance sets, while the lower-body workout includes 11. Keep that in mind when combining these into your current routine or performing both in the same week.

People rap about and admire the glutes, but they’re the engine that makes the body roar in and out of the gym.

Building stronger, more muscular glutes takes more than hip thrusts and band booty burners. Train the glute max through all its functions, give the med and mini some love, and combine exercises that challenge your backside in lengthened and shortened positions. Include unilateral training, progressive overload, and adequate rest and recovery, and your jeans will thank you.

One last thing. Turn around and admire your handy work.

The Hand-To-Knee hip thrust will hone your technique and build force.

If you’re looking to build a bigger booty, you may need to stick with the basics.
